name: Stroke, Ring, Crack
idea: Every hit is a Stroke, taken at once. A struck body then rings: it takes a further 50% of that Stroke as Ring over 3 s. Weight lowers Stroke. Muffling cancels Ring: knee-deep water, cloth armour, or 3 bodies within 1 m. But a muffled body cannot ring a heavy blow out: any single Stroke above 20% of its greatest health deals the excess again as Crack, which lowers greatest health until the vigil ends. Light hits want loose targets; heavy hits want crowded ones.
source: A struck bell keeps sounding unless cloth, water or a hand damps it, and a bell struck while held cannot vibrate freely and cracks.
nearest: Path of Exile armour, which is good against small hits and poor against large ones, and ordinary damage-over-time riders. Here the split comes from whether the body is muffled by water, cloth or a crowd, which the player changes by moving.

notes.where: Path of Exile's Ignite and Bleed (a share of every hit is taken again over a few seconds), the Endurance/Health split in Pillars of Eternity and Eclipse 8 permanent damage in Risk of Rain 2 (heavy hits shave greatest health for the run), and Path of Exile's size threshold for a savage hit. No game known where crowding, water or cloth decides which of the two a hit becomes.

Aesop's Oak and the Reed (what cannot give way breaks under the great blow) and the stock 'frozen body shatters under a heavy hit'; lingering after-harm is an ordinary bleed. The muffling by water, cloth or crowd is not in any of them.

name: Clapper to Bell
idea: Blows and bodies have Weight. A blow under 1/40 of the body's Weight is a Tap: half harm. Between 1/40 and 1/20 it is a True stroke: full harm, and the body rings, passing 30% to every body of its own weight class within 3 m. Over 1/20 it is a Breaking stroke: full harm plus 25% as Crack (greatest health lost for the vigil), and nothing rings. Size shows the five weight classes. Protection is being unlike the blows aimed at you; gear changes your Weight.
source: A clapper is matched to its bell at a few hundredths of the bell's weight: too light gives a thin sound, too heavy cracks the bell.
nearest: Over-penetration in tank games, where a shell too strong for its target does less. Here the fit of blow to body decides whether harm spreads by resonance to like-sized neighbours or is spent on one body.

notes.where: Ragnarok Online's weapon-versus-size table and StarCraft: Brood War's concussive and explosive damage against small, medium and large units; World of Warships' overpenetration bands for a shell mismatched to its target. The matched band that spreads harm to same-size neighbours is in none of them.
The singer whose matched note shatters the glass (stock; Oskar in The Tin Drum) and Goldilocks 'just right' fits; in games, over-penetration. The spread to like-sized neighbours is its own.

name: Copper, Tin, Rope and the Temper
idea: Copper: +6 health and +1 Weight per point. Tin: +2% Stroke and +0.1 s Ring length per point. Rope: -1% sigil interval and +1% pickup reach per point. The share of Tin in Copper plus Tin names the character's Temper: under 15% gun-metal (Crack taken -40%), 15 to 25% bell-metal (resonance and Ring you cause reach 50% farther), over 25% mirror-metal (Stroke +25%, Crack taken +40%). Sigils and gear ask for amounts (Tin 30) or for a Temper (bell-metal only), so one point can win or lose an item.
source: Bell metal is about four parts copper to one of tin; less tin gives tough gunmetal, more gives hard, brittle, white speculum or mirror metal.
nearest: Attribute requirements in Diablo-style games. Differs in that the ratio between two attributes, not only their size, puts the character in a named state and decides what can be equipped.

notes.where: Golden Sun, where the mix of Djinn elements set on a character names its class; Tyrogue in Pokemon, which evolves by whether Attack is above, below or equal to Defence; alignment-restricted gear in Knights of the Old Republic; plain attribute requirements in Diablo II and Path of Exile.

The four humours, where the proportion of fluids names a temperament, and Mistborn's Allomancy, where an alloy off its ratio does not work. A ratio of two attributes naming an equip state is not in either.

name: Swing
idea: Built by hits. Each hit arriving from the opposite side to the previous hit (directions more than 120 degrees apart) adds one Swing; a hit from the same side as the previous one removes one. Swing never fades with time. At 6 the body goes right over: it is flung 4 m along the last hit's direction, deals its own Weight as Stroke to every body it passes, and lands with Swing 0. Keepers need 12 and are flung 1 m. Catch a heavy body between two sources.
source: A bell is raised by alternate pulls, handstroke and backstroke, over many strokes until it turns right over.
nearest: Flanking bonuses in tactics games and stagger meters. Differs in that only alternation of sides builds it, same-side hits undo it, and it never times out.

notes.where: Left-right cross-ups in fighting games and Fiora's Vitals in League of Legends (the next hit must come from another side), stagger gauges that end in a launch as in Final Fantasy XIII, and thrown bodies that harm what they pass (Earth Spirit's Boulder Smash in Dota 2, bumps in Into the Breach). A meter that only alternation builds and that never decays is not known.

The cartoon and anime beat of a body knocked back and forth between two fighters, and rocking a cart until it tips; in games, stagger meters and flanking. Alternation-only build that never fades is its own.

name: Sent Hunting
idea: Put on one body by certain sigils. Every 0.75 s the body trades places with the nearest body within 2.5 m that is farther from the player; it cannot attack while trading. After 6 trades, or when nobody is farther, it turns and trades forward the same number of times, then the condition ends. Any shove while hunting costs it one extra trade back. Elites make 3 trades; keepers are immune. It removes a dangerous body from the front rank for a known time.
source: In plain hunt a bell moves one place per row to the back of the row and then returns the same way.
nearest: Position-swap spells such as Vengeful Spirit's swap in Dota. Differs as a lasting state that walks one enemy to the back of the crowd place by place and then brings it back.

notes.where: Knockback and shuffle in Darkest Dungeon, which send a front-rank enemy to the back by swapping it past those behind so it cannot use its front-rank attacks; Terror in Diablo II and other fear effects that send one enemy away for a known time. The stepwise walk out and the mirrored walk back are in neither.

Only the progression of a country dance (a couple working down the set and back, as in Strip the Willow) and the plain hunt itself; no story, creature or spell I know walks a foe to the back of its own crowd and returns it.

name: Clocked
idea: Put on the player inside the 5 m ring of a tongueless bell or by a keeper's call; lasts while in the ring plus 2 s. No sigil casts by itself. Each time the thumb lifts so the character stops, the next sigil in order, lightest first, casts once at +50%. Stops closer together than 0.3 s do nothing. Each cast made this way has a 3% chance to crack that sigil: half harm until the next gate.
source: Clocking is sounding a still bell by pulling its clapper against it by hand, a practice known for cracking bells.
nearest: Silence effects that stop casting. Differs in that casting is handed to the thumb's stop-and-go rhythm instead of being taken away.

notes.where: Archero's core rule, also the Soldier in Brotato: the character attacks only when the thumb lifts and it stands still, and players stutter-step to fire. Clocked is that rule switched on inside a zone and made one cast per stop.
notes.mutation: Make the player the clapper instead of making the stop the trigger: inside the ring a sigil speaks only when the character's body bumps the tongueless bell or another heavy body, once per touch, so casting is bought by walking into things. Keep the +50% and the 3% crack on each forced cast.

notes.where: Red Light, Green Light (Squid Game) and SUPERHOT's time-moves-when-you-move, turned round; silence curses in general. Casting on each stop is its own.

name: Half-muffled
idea: Leather on one side. Every second blow the afflicted makes is an echo: 25% harm, no condition applied, and it lands where the previous blow landed instead of being aimed. Lasts 10 blows. Enemies get it from cloth and leather effects; the player gets it from mourner dead, and then every second cast of each sigil is the echo. A cast made at the same instant as two other sigils is never muffled. Two seconds in water soaks the leather off.
source: Half-muffled ringing straps leather to one side of each clapper so that every second row is a faint echo of the first.
nearest: Blind and weaken effects. Differs in being strictly every second blow, and the echo repeats the last place struck rather than missing at random.

notes.where: Encore in Pokemon (the victim is forced to repeat its last move), Weak in Slay the Spire and blind effects for the feeble blow, and Spell Echo in Path of Exile for a repeat on the same spot. A debuff that makes exactly every second blow a faint copy of the one before is not known.
The nymph Echo, who can only repeat the last thing said, plus ordinary weaken and blind effects. The echo landing on the previous spot is its own.

name: Odd-struck
idea: The afflicted speaks early on one stroke and late on the next: its attack or cast intervals alternate between half and one and a half times the normal time, so blows come in quick pairs with a long gap. The average rate is unchanged. Lasts 20 s on enemies and until the next gate on the player. On an enemy the long gap is the moment to walk in. On the player, standing still for 4 s re-hangs the bell and ends it.
source: An odd-struck bell sounds sooner after the pull at one stroke than at the other, and its ringer has to compensate.
nearest: Attack-speed slows and hastes. Differs in keeping the average rate and only pairing the blows, which helps or hurts depending on what the pairs are used for.

notes.where: Echo Sabre in Dota 2, which turns a steady attack into two quick blows and a gap, and burst-fire guns such as Dahl weapons in Borderlands; roll-to-cleanse blights in Monster Hunter for the stand-still cure. As a debuff that keeps the average rate it is not known.
The stock enemy rhythm of two quick strikes then a long recovery window, and the lub-dub of a limping gait used as a tell in horror. Keeping the average rate while pairing blows is its own.

name: Turned
idea: Applied by lathe-work: a keeper, turner dead, some sigils. Each application takes one turning: -8% Weight, lasting the whole vigil, impossible to cleanse or heal, up to 5. A Turned body is shoved 8% farther and rings 0.5 s longer per turning; at 3 and at 5 it drops one weight class. At 5 it is tinny: its own Strokes deal half. On the player, turnings are made good only by recasting at a gate, which costs 10% of carried loot per turning.
source: A founder tunes a bell by turning metal off its inside on a lathe, and metal removed cannot be put back.
nearest: Stacking armour-shred debuffs. Differs in being permanent, capped, and changing what size of body the victim counts as.

notes.where: The Poison Mushroom in Super Smash Bros. and Reduce in Dungeons & Dragons (smaller, lighter, flung farther, hitting weaker), stacking armour shred such as The Black Cleaver in League of Legends, and Slay the Spire curses that last the run and are removed at a merchant for gold.

Undead level and ability drain in Dungeons and Dragons (the shadow's Strength drain, the wight's lost levels, bought back only by a paid Restoration) and Dark Souls II hollowing, a stacking uncleansable loss undone only at a price. The shrink-ray size drop is the other half.
notes.mutation: Make a turning a re-tuning, not a drain: each cut also quickens the body (shorter interval, faster step), so it trades mass for speed and a thinned body is a different instrument rather than a weaker one; let the player refuse the gate's recast and keep a deliberately turned character.

name: Ringer
idea: A tower ringer who kept hold of the rope. The thumb is the rope: every reversal of direction of more than 120 degrees is a pull and makes the starting sigil speak at once, at most once per 0.4 s; it also casts by itself every 3 s. Starting sigil Tenor Stroke: a heavy ring 2.5 m around the Ringer. Lifting the thumb for 1 s sets the bell mouth-up, and the next pull is doubled. The Ringer fights by rocking back and forth inside the crowd.
source: A ringer makes the bell speak by alternate pulls, handstroke and backstroke, and can set it balanced mouth-up at rest.
nearest: None known for reversing the movement stick as the attack trigger; the nearest is stand-still charging in survivor games.

notes.where: Charge inputs in fighting games (hold back, then forward), the stick waggle that charges a mini-turbo in Mario Kart 64 and the dash in Katamari Damacy, and Archero's stop-to-shoot for attacks driven by the movement thumb. Reversal of the movement stick as a class's attack trigger is not known.
Quasimodo as the figure of the tower ringer; for the input, alternate-direction waggling as in Track and Field. No story or game I know makes reversal of the walk the stroke itself.

name: Strickler
idea: A founder's mould-maker. Button one plants a spindle. While the Strickler is within 6 m of it a rigid strickle board joins them; the board scrapes every body it passes over (starting sigil Strickle: harm per sweep, and scraped bodies are pushed along the board toward its outer end). The thumb therefore walks circles: a faster orbit means more scrapes. A full turn closes the mould: the swept circle becomes a loam wall for 3 s that bodies cannot cross. Walking past 6 m drops the board.
source: A bell mould is shaped in loam by a strickle board swept round a central spindle.
nearest: Tether weapons that harm whatever crosses a line between player and anchor. Differs in that the line is a rigid sweep the player orbits, and a completed turn closes a wall.

notes.where: Hammerfight and Brutal.io (a weapon swung on a tether by moving in circles), Io's Tether in Dota 2 (a line between two points that affects what crosses it), Mario's Fire Bar, loop-closing in Pokemon Ranger and Qix, and ring walls such as Disruptor's Kinetic Field.

The magic circle that becomes a barrier the moment it is closed (Dresden Files, salt circles in folk horror), tetherball and the maypole; in games, Qix-style enclosing. The rigid scraping board is its own.

name: Tuner
idea: A foundry tuner with a case of forks. How far the thumb is pushed sets the note of the starting sigil Fork. A slow walk (under 40% push) sounds tenor: a heavy ring 6 m wide every 2.4 s. A full run sounds treble: a light ring 2 m wide every 0.6 s. There are five steps between. Heavy notes shove and fit heavy bodies; light notes fit the small. The Tuner changes what is being hurt by changing pace, not by choosing a target.
source: A ring of bells runs from the light, quick treble to the heavy, slow tenor, and a tuner works by comparing notes.
nearest: None known for walking pace choosing the size of the weapon; the nearest is weapon-swap buttons.

notes.where: Focus mode in Touhou and the laser in DoDonPachi, where moving slowly and the shape of the shot are tied together; Brotato items keyed to standing still or moving. Depth of stick push choosing among five sizes of one weapon is not known.
The Pied Piper, whose choice of tune decides which creatures are moved, and Touhou's focus mode, where moving slowly changes the shot. Pace as a five-step scale of blow size is its own.

name: Quarter-jack
idea: A clock-striker figure come down from its tower. Its starting sigil Jack's Hammer has no interval of its own: it strikes on every quarter of the toll (every 18.75 s) in a 5 m arc where the thumb points, at six times normal harm, and on the toll itself it strikes as many times as tolls have sounded this vigil. A clock hand circles the Jack. Between quarters it only ticks: one light tap per second on the nearest body. The thumb's work is being in place at known instants.
source: Quarter-jacks are mechanical figures on clock towers that strike the quarters and the count of the hour on bells.
nearest: Beat-locked attacks in rhythm action games. Differs in long fixed periods tied to the district bell and an hour count that grows as the vigil goes on.

notes.where: Beat-locked attacks in Crypt of the NecroDancer and Hi-Fi Rush, Jhin in League of Legends (fixed cadence, heavy fourth shot), and Clock Lancet and Pentagram in Vampire Survivors (clock-ordered and very slow weapons). A class whose weapon is slaved to the run's own difficulty clock is not known.

The clockwork man of stock (Tik-Tok of Oz, the clockwork droids of Doctor Who) and the cuckoo that calls the hour's count; in games, beat-locked attacks. Striking the vigil's own hour count is its own.

name: Conductor
idea: The Conductor's sigils keep no separate timers: they speak one after another in a row, lightest first, one row every 4 s. Button one calls Bob: the sigil about to speak trades places with the one after it, from then on. Button two calls Single: the sigil about to speak speaks twice and the last in the row is skipped once. A sigil hitting a body already hit this row by the sigil before it deals +25%. Starting sigil Treble: a light dart at the nearest body within 8 m.
source: Change-ringing bells sound one after another in rows, and a conductor calls bob or single to bend the pattern.
nearest: The fixed spell order on a Noita wand. Differs in that the order is changed live by two calls and pays for consecutive places striking the same body.

notes.where: Noita wands without shuffle, which cast their spells in a fixed order, and the deck queue in One Step From Eden; combo chains that pay for following the previous hit, as in Final Fantasy XIV. Two live calls that permute the order are not known.
Dorothy L. Sayers's The Nine Tailors, where a conductor calls bob and single; in games, the fixed spell order of a Noita wand and combo chains. Live reordering of automatic casts is its own.

name: Roper
idea: A rope-maker who walks backward paying out line. A rope lies along the last 12 m of the path walked. Starting sigil Sally: every body that crosses the rope pulls it, and each pull rings one stroke, a 2 m ring, at the rope's far end, its oldest point. More crossings mean more strokes, up to 8 a second. The thumb draws the rope across the horde's road and parks its far end where the crowd is thickest. Standing still for 2 s coils the rope in.
source: A bell is rung from a distance by a rope, and ropemakers walk backward down a ropewalk laying the rope out behind them.
nearest: Damaging trails and tripwires. Differs in that the rope does no harm: enemies crossing it are the trigger for strokes that land somewhere else.

notes.where: Sensors wired to traps in Evil Genius and tripwire-to-dispenser builds in Minecraft (a crossing here fires something there), the trailing tail of Snake and Tron, and Shadow Pinion in Vampire Survivors (a trail weapon that changes when the player stops).

The tripwire strung with tin cans or bells (stock of siege and zombie stories), the spider striking where its web is plucked, and the Tron or Snake trail. A harmless line whose crossings strike at its far end is its own.

name: Stander
idea: Grows from the Ringer. New rule, the Set: when the Stander stands still for a whole second, every sigil stops and stands mouth-up, and each further second held, up to 3, stores one more stroke in each. On the next step they all come down in order, lightest first, 0.1 s apart, each cast repeated once per second held. But the stay breaks if a single blow takes more than 15% of health while set: the stored strokes are lost and no sigil casts for 3 s.
source: A bell set mouth-up rests against a wooden stay that is made to break if the bell is pulled too hard.
nearest: Charge-and-release attacks. Differs in holding every skill at once, releasing them in a fixed order, and a break rule tied to one heavy blow rather than to any hit.

notes.where: Unleash in Path of Exile (a spell stores up to three extra repeats while it is not cast and lets them all go at once), charge shots from R-Type and Mega Man, stand-still bonuses in Brotato, and Focus Punch in Pokemon for a charge lost to a hit.
notes.mutation: Store weight, not seconds: while set, every body that comes within 2 m leans on the stay and adds its Weight to the store, the release is scaled by the weight leaning at the moment of the step, and the stay breaks when the leaning total passes a shown limit. The player judges how much crowd to let pile on, not how long to hold a charge.

notes.where: The stationary charge-up that a hard hit interrupts: Goku gathering the Spirit Bomb, the iaido stance before the draw, any interrupted spellcast. Storing every skill and releasing them in order is its own.

name: Composer
idea: Grows from the Conductor. New rule, Truth: every row the Composer's sigils ring is remembered until the next toll. Each row whose order has not been rung since the last toll adds 1 Truth: +3% harm and +1% pickup reach. Ringing an order already used makes the touch false: Truth drops to 0 and cannot build again until the toll. With 4 sigils there are 24 orders and about 18 rows between tolls, so the Composer must keep calling changes and never drift back to an old row.
source: A peal must contain no repeated row; a single repetition makes the whole performance false.
nearest: Style meters that punish repeating a move, as in Devil May Cry. Differs in that the thing not to be repeated is the whole order of the automatic casts, remembered between tolls.

notes.where: The Eye boss blind in Balatro (no hand type may be repeated this round) and its Obelisk joker, the stale-trick penalty in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, and the style meter in Devil May Cry. Tracking the permutations of automatic casts is not known.
The true peal of The Nine Tailors, spoiled by one repeated row; in games, Devil May Cry's style rank that punishes repetition. Applying it to the order of automatic casts is its own.

name: Gallery-walker
idea: Grows from the Tuner. New rule, walls carry: any sigil cast while the Gallery-walker is within 2 m of a wall does not spread outward. It runs along that wall in both directions for 20 m at 10 m/s, following corners and curves, and strikes every body within 1.5 m of the wall once at full harm with no falloff. Cast in the open, sigils behave as normal. The player fights by hugging masonry and dragging the horde along it.
source: In a whispering gallery sound clings to a curved wall and travels its whole length with little loss.
nearest: Wall-hugging missiles in old shooters. Differs in being a rule on every skill the character has, switched on by where the player stands.

notes.where: Search Snake in Mega Man 3 and the ground-hugging missiles of Gradius (shots that crawl along surfaces), Wall Creep enemies in The Binding of Isaac, and wall-slam positioning in Hades. As a rule on every skill, switched on by standing near masonry, it is not known.

A Link Between Worlds, where Link merges into a wall and travels along it round corners, and Zelda's wall-crawling Sparks; fire running a powder trail. Making it a rule on every skill by where one stands is its own.

name: False-bell Maker
idea: Grows from the Strickler. New rule, the mould fills: bodies that die inside the swept circle drop nothing; each adds its Weight to the mould. When the mould holds 40 times the character's own Weight a bell is cast at the spindle. It stands 30 s, blocks movement, and answers every Stroke of the player's that lands within 4 m of it with a 5 m ring of the same harm. Then it cracks and pays out all the withheld drops at once.
source: In the old method a clay false bell fills the gap between core and cope and is broken out so the metal can take its place.
nearest: Kill-fuelled summons. Differs in giving up drops for a time, getting an object that answers the player's own blows, and receiving the drops back when it breaks.

notes.where: Corpse-fuelled summons of the Diablo necromancer and Shadow Fiend's Necromastery in Dota 2, Mirage Archer and ancestral totems in Path of Exile (a stand-in that repeats your blows), and uncollected materials banked for the next wave in Brotato. Withheld drops paid back when the summon breaks is not known.

Lafcadio Hearn's 'The Soul of the Great Bell', where a body goes into the metal so the bell will cast, and the golden calf made of offerings; in games, kill-fuelled summons and loot pinatas. The withheld-then-returned drops are its own.

name: Pulled-off
idea: Grows from the Quarter-jack. New rule, the hammer can be pulled off: holding button one at a quarter holds the Jack's stroke back. The next quarter then strikes for both, and a third held quarter makes three, the most. Letting go releases at once where the thumb points. If the hammer is still pulled off when the district bell tolls, the swinging bell smashes it: the stored strokes are lost and the Jack only ticks until the following toll.
source: Clock hammers must be pulled clear before the bells are swung, or the turning bell smashes them.
nearest: Stored charges on abilities. Differs in the store being wiped, and the skill lost for a whole toll, if it is held across the district's own clock.

notes.where: The Great Sword in Monster Hunter (hold the charge past its third level and it weakens), cooking a grenade too long, Rumble's overheat lockout in League of Legends, and ordinary stored charges. A bust deadline set by the run's own clock is not known.
Cinderella's stroke of midnight, a held gift lost when the clock strikes, plus ordinary stored charges. Losing the store to the game's own toll is its own.

name: Backward-ringer
idea: Grows from the Roper. New rule, the alarm: button two turns the ring backward. While backward, sigils speak 40% more often and all drops are worth 30% more; but the city hears an alarm, so enemies arrive 40% faster and every second spent backward takes one extra second off the time to the next toll. Turning forward again takes 6 s, during which both penalties stay and neither bonus does.
source: Ringing the bells backward, in reverse order, was an old alarm for fire or attack on a town.
nearest: Self-imposed difficulty such as Curse in Vampire Survivors or Heat in Hades. Differs in being flipped live during the fight, eating the toll clock, and taking strokes to undo.

notes.where: Snuffing the torch in Darkest Dungeon (a live choice of more loot and harder hits on both sides, costly to undo), calling the next wave early for a bonus in Kingdom Rush, and run-long dials such as Curse in Vampire Survivors and Heat in Hades.
notes.mutation: Make the alarm a place rather than a rate: while backward, every enemy in the district goes to the rope's far end instead of to the player, each second still costing a second of toll clock, and on turning forward the whole gathered crowd comes for the player at once. The price is the clock and the pile-up, not a more-danger-for-more-loot dial.

notes.where: Noise draws the horde: the church bell in The Walking Dead, the car alarm in Left 4 Dead, Bloodborne's bell-ringing woman; Curse in Vampire Survivors. A live toggle that eats the toll clock is its own.

name: Bow Wave
idea: Every 0.8 s a ring is born at the player's feet and grows at 6 m/s to 9 m, harming each body once as it passes. Rings stay centred where they were born. Because the character moves at about 4 m/s, rings bunch up ahead and string out behind: bodies in front are struck about five times as often as bodies behind. It picks no target. The player makes it work by walking at whatever should die, and wastes it by running away.
source: A moving source crowds its wavefronts ahead and stretches them behind, which is why its note falls as it goes past.
nearest: Pulse and nova skills in survivor games. Differs in that rings do not follow the player, so the direction of movement sets the rate of hits.

notes.where: Expanding pulse rings left at their origin, as in Frost Nova in Diablo and the pulse weapons of survivor games. No game known that tunes ring speed against walking speed so that the bunching ahead is the point.

Only the physics demonstration itself (a boat's bow wave, the Doppler diagram); novas left where they were born exist, but I know no story or game where walking toward a target is what raises the rate of hits.

name: Far Carry
idea: Every 5 s a stroke sounds from the player and lands in two places: on every body within 3 m, and on every body between 10 and 13 m away. Nothing between 3 and 10 m is touched. Harm in the far band is 150% of the near. It picks no target. The player makes it work by keeping the pack either at arm's length or at the far edge of the screen; it is useless at the middle distance where such fights usually happen.
source: A great sound is heard near its source and again far off, with a zone of silence between where the sound has bent overhead.
nearest: Ring-shaped and donut-shaped areas. Differs in two bands at once, with the dead middle as the thing the player has to play around.

notes.where: Darius's Decimate in League of Legends (outer ring strong, inside weak), point-blank and donut blasts paired in Final Fantasy XIV fights, and the minimum range of the Siege Tank in StarCraft. One player skill with two live bands and a dead middle is not known.

Only the retold anecdotes of acoustic shadow in Civil War battles (unheard nearby, heard far off) and artillery's minimum range; no skill or spell I know hits near and far together with a dead middle.

name: Beating Pair
idea: Two forks sound from the player, one pulsing every 1.0 s and one every 1.1 s, each a 4 m ring. A pulse's harm is multiplied by how nearly the two forks are sounding together: 3 times when they coincide, almost nothing when they are half a beat apart. So the skill swells and fades once every 11 s, shown on a meter. The player walks into the crowd as it swells and out as it fades. Anything that changes one fork's rate changes the length of the beat.
source: Two notes slightly apart beat: their loudness rises and falls at the difference between their rates.
nearest: None known; the nearest is weapons with strong and weak phases on a fixed timer, but here the cycle comes from two rates the player can alter.

notes.where: Distant only: Convention of Elements in Diablo III (a power window that rotates on a fixed timer) and lining up two cooldowns in World of Warcraft. No game known where the phase between two pulse rates is the damage multiplier.

Power that swells and fades on a cycle: Sir Gawain's strength waxing to noon, the Great Conjunction of The Dark Crystal, spring tides when sun and moon agree. Two alterable rates making the cycle is its own.

name: Still Points
idea: Every 12 s a fork is planted where the player stands and lasts 12 s. A standing wave runs along the straight line from fork to player, up to 14 m. Every 2 m from the fork is a loud point, a 1 m circle that harms twice a second; halfway between loud points are still points where no body, the player included, takes harm from any sound. The pattern is measured from the fork, so stepping nearer or farther, or swinging round it, lays loud points on the pack.
source: Waves meeting between fixed ends make a standing wave with still nodes and loud points at fixed spacing.
nearest: Beam or tether skills between the player and a placed object. Differs in the harm being a row of points with safe gaps, moved by the player's distance and angle.

notes.where: Mario's Fire Bar (a pivoted row of harm with gaps), Technology Zero in The Binding of Isaac and Io's Tether in Dota 2 (harm strung between two points), and safe spots inside boss patterns.

Only the classroom standing wave (Kundt's tube) and, at a distance, safe gaps in a bullet pattern; I know no fiction or game with a player-laid row of loud points and immune still points measured from a planted object.

name: Whistle
idea: Every 4 s the skill counts the bodies within 8 m by weight class and whistles the note of the commonest class. Every body of exactly that class within 8 m takes full harm and hums for 2 s, passing 20% of any harm it takes to like bodies within 2 m. Bodies of other classes are untouched. Elites count as a class of their own. The player makes it work by fighting crowds of one kind and leading the odd ones away first.
source: The blind carillonneur Jacob van Eyck found a bell's separate notes by whistling each pitch until the bell answered it.
nearest: Skills that hit every enemy of one type on screen. Differs in choosing the majority kind near the player by itself, which the player steers by herding.

notes.where: Synchronoise in Pokemon (strikes only bodies sharing the user's type), the Colour Bomb in Candy Crush and the Hypercube in Bejeweled (every piece of one kind), and Extinction in Magic: The Gathering. Automatic choice of the majority kind, steered by herding, is not known.
The sound that harms one kind only: Slim Whitman's yodel bursting the Martians in Mars Attacks!, the dog whistle, the Piper's rat tune. Choosing the commonest kind nearby by itself is its own.

name: Sifting Plate
idea: Every 15 s a square of ground 8 m across under the player trembles for 3 s. Its still lines are a cross through the centre and a circle of 3 m radius. Every pickup inside, and every body lighter than the player, is drawn at 3 m/s toward the nearest still line for as long as the trembling lasts. It does no harm. Drops end up in lines that one walk collects; light enemies end up in lines that narrow sigils rake.
source: Sand on a vibrating plate is thrown off the moving parts and gathers along the still nodal lines, drawing Chladni figures.
nearest: Vacuum pulls and pickup magnets. Differs in sorting things onto a fixed pattern of lines instead of to a point or to the player.

notes.where: Dark Seer's Vacuum in Dota 2 and Graviton Surge in Overwatch (pull to a point), and the Vacuum pickup in Vampire Survivors. Sorting drops and bodies onto a figure of lines is not known.
Only Chladni figures as imagery (the sand patterns of The Rings of Power title sequence); vacuums and magnets pull to a point, and I know nothing that sorts drops and bodies onto nodal lines.

name: Wall Answer
idea: Every 3 s a shout leaves the player toward the nearest wall within 15 m, in a lane 2 m wide at 20 m/s, harming each body it passes. It strikes the wall and returns down the same lane at half harm. Bodies in the lane are hit twice, and a farther wall gives a longer lane and a longer wait between the two hits. With no wall in reach it does not cast. The player makes it work by keeping the horde between self and stone.
source: An echo is a sound returned from a wall after the time it takes to travel there and back.
nearest: Bouncing and returning projectiles. Differs in aiming at masonry instead of enemies, so the player's position against the walls is the aim.

notes.where: Sivir's Boomerang Blade and Ahri's Orb of Deception in League of Legends (out and back down a lane, hitting twice), Runetracer in Vampire Survivors, and Camille's Hookshot, which works only on terrain. A skill that aims itself at the nearest wall is not known.
The sonic scream of stock (Black Canary, Banshee, Skyrim's Fus Ro Dah) crossed with the returning boomerang, and Echo answering from the cliff. Aiming at masonry rather than at foes is its own.

name: Cope and Core
idea: Every 10 s two loam walls rise around the player: the core at 2 m and the cope at 4.5 m. They stand 3 s and block bodies. Whatever stood in the gap between them is in the mould: after 1.5 s metal is poured and every body in the gap takes heavy harm. Bodies inside the core, next to the player, and bodies outside the cope are untouched. The player makes it work by holding the crowd two to four metres off, neither closer nor farther.
source: A bell mould is an inner core and an outer cope, and the bell is the metal that fills the gap between them.
nearest: Donut-shaped blasts in boss fights. Differs as a player skill whose walls hold the crowd in the band, with an inner circle that spares the enemies nearest the player.

notes.where: Donut-shaped blasts in Final Fantasy XIV, Bone Prison in Diablo II, and Disruptor's Kinetic Field followed by Static Storm in Dota 2 (a ring wall, then harm inside it).
The dwarves drowning Smaug in a mould of molten gold in The Desolation of Smaug, boiling oil on besiegers, and the boss-fight donut blast. A moat of walls that spares the nearest foes is its own.

name: Belled One
idea: Every 14 s a bell is hung on the nearest ordinary body within 6 m. For 8 s it is the wether: it walks straight away from where the player stood at the cast, at 3 m/s, and every non-elite body within 6 m of it follows it instead of the player. When the bell falls off, or the wether dies, its followers stand lost for 1.5 s. The player aims it by where they stand at the cast: the flock is led directly away from that spot.
source: A bellwether is the belled sheep that the flock follows, so that one animal leads and locates all the rest.
nearest: Decoys, taunts and charm effects. Differs in the lure being one of the crowd, moving, and steered only by where the player stood when it was belled.

notes.where: The pipe bomb in Left 4 Dead and the L.U.R.E. in Deep Rock Galactic (the horde follows the lure, not the player), Attract in Diablo II (the lure is one of the crowd), and Mirage's decoy in Apex Legends (a lure that runs off in a straight line).
notes.mutation: Do not lead the flock away; reshape it: the belled body keeps hunting the player as before, but every ordinary body within 6 m falls into single file behind it, each walking in the footsteps of the one ahead, for 8 s. The player gets a column to rake with lane skills and steers its head by their own movement, which no decoy does.

notes.where: The Judas goat and the Pied Piper: one of the herd leads the rest away. In zombie fiction it is leading the herd off with a noisemaker (The Walking Dead, Land of the Dead's fireworks), and in games the Left 4 Dead pipe bomb the horde chases. Belling the cat supplies the hanging of the bell.
notes.mutation: Tie the bell to Weight so it sorts rather than lures: only bodies of the wether's own weight class follow it, and the bell jumps to the heaviest follower every 2 s, so the cast pulls one size of dead out of a mixed crowd and lines it up for weight-matched strokes.

name: Slapback
idea: A sigil with no stroke of its own. Every Stroke the player's other sigils land is repeated at the same spot 2 s later at 40%, and again 4 s after the first at 15%, each as a 1.5 m circle. At most 60 echoes are kept; the oldest are dropped. The player makes it work by retreating over the ground just fought on, so that the pursuing horde walks through the echoes of the last fight.
source: An echo returns a sound after a delay, and each further return is fainter than the last.
nearest: Repeat-cast modifiers such as Spell Echo in Path of Exile. Differs in repeating at the place after a delay, so ground already fought over becomes the weapon.

notes.where: Earthquake's aftershock and Spell Echo in Path of Exile, Luden's Echo in League of Legends, and Cosmic Clones in Super Mario Galaxy 2 (your own past replayed behind you). A capped trail of fading repeats of every hit, left on the ground, is not known.
Nigel Kneale's The Stone Tape, where a place replays what happened in it, and Echo; in games, Spell Echo and delayed after-images. Ground already fought on becoming the weapon is its own.

name: Leather
idea: The sigil casts twice as often, but every second cast is an echo: it is not aimed, it lands where the cast before it landed, at 30% harm, and applies no condition. On a sigil that leaves something on the ground, the echo renews that thing instead of placing a new one. Cost: the sigil's reach is cut by 20% and the binding fills two sockets. It pays only when enemies keep coming through one place.
source: Half-muffled ringing puts leather on one side of each clapper, so every second row is a faint echo of the first.
nearest: Faster-but-weaker supports. Differs in the weak cast being an unaimed repeat on the same ground rather than a smaller copy of a normal cast.

notes.where: The Spell Echo and Unleash supports in Path of Exile: the spell is cast about twice as often, the repeat goes to the same place, and with Unleash the repeat is weaker.
notes.mutation: Send the echo to the other side: every second cast lands at the point directly opposite the last landing, mirrored through the player, at 30% and with no condition. The modifier then pays when the player stands between two packs and is no longer a weaker repeat on the same ground.

notes.where: Echo again, the faint repeat of the last thing uttered, on top of ordinary faster-but-weaker supports. The unaimed repeat on the same ground is its own.

name: Louvres
idea: The sigil stops aiming. Its effect leaves the player in four fixed lanes along the map's compass lines, north, east, south and west, each 2 m wide and as long as the sigil's reach; whatever shape the sigil had is cut down to those lanes. Harm +50%. Cost: nothing between the lanes is touched, and the lanes stop at walls, so the player has to line the horde up on the cross.
source: A belfry lets its sound out only through the louvred openings in its four faces.
nearest: Fixed-direction weapons in survivor games. Differs in being a socketed change to any skill and locked to the map rather than to the way the character faces.

notes.where: The Bomberman blast: four lanes on the map's axes that stop at walls and miss everything on the diagonals. Loki's Horns in The Binding of Isaac puts that cross on whatever the character fires.
notes.mutation: Hang the lanes on the district's bell tower instead of the compass: the cross always has one arm pointing at the tower, so it turns as the player circles the landmark. Lining the horde up then means choosing where to stand relative to the tower, which a fixed cross never asks.

notes.where: Bomberman's blast: a cross along the four grid directions, as long as the bomb's reach and stopped by walls. The rook's lines in chess are the older picture. A player who knows Bomberman will see it at once.
notes.mutation: Hang the lanes on the district's bell tower instead of the compass: one lane points at the tower, one away from it and two run along the circle round it, so the cross turns as the player moves and lining up the horde means choosing where to stand relative to the landmark.

name: Second Voice
idea: When socketed, the binding is given a second sigil the character owns. A cast made while the character is moving is the sigil's own. A cast made while the character stands still takes the second sigil's shape and conditions, with this sigil's harm. Cost: both voices are at 75%, and the lent sigil's own interval is 25% longer. One socketed skill becomes two, chosen cast by cast by lifting the thumb.
source: Ancient Chinese chime bells give two different notes from one bell, depending on whether they are struck at the centre or toward the side.
nearest: Stance-switching weapons. Differs in the switch being whether the thumb is moving, and the second form being borrowed from another skill the character owns.

notes.where: Functions slotted into one another in Transistor (one skill lends its shape to another), the Siege Tank in StarCraft and Bastion in Overwatch (a different weapon when planted), and Shadow Pinion in Vampire Survivors (one behaviour moving, another on stopping).
Two-natured figures of stock (Janus, Jekyll and Hyde) and stance weapons in games. Borrowing the second form from another owned skill, switched by stillness, is its own.

name: Balance
idea: The sigil's projectiles do not vanish at the end of their reach: each stops there and stands mouth-up for up to 4 s. The first body to touch a standing projectile tips it, and it falls on that body for double harm. Cost: harm on the way out is halved, and at most 12 can stand at once (the oldest falls harmlessly). The player lays a fence at the sigil's full range and backs the horde onto it.
source: A bell rung full circle can be set at rest mouth-up, balanced, until a touch brings it over.
nearest: Mine and trap supports in Path of Exile. Differs in the line of traps always forming at the skill's full reach, bought with a weakened outward flight.

notes.where: Decelerating Shot in Noita (any projectile slows to a stop and hangs as a hazard), Anti-Gravity and Pop! in The Binding of Isaac, Arc Warden's Spark Wraith in Dota 2, and the trap and mine supports in Path of Exile.
notes.mutation: Let weight, not first touch, tip it: a stood projectile ignores any body lighter than the sigil's own weight class, each light body that passes sets it rocking for +20% harm, and only a body heavy enough brings it over. The fence becomes a filter that saves itself for the big one instead of a row of proximity mines.

notes.where: The bucket balanced over the door, the deadfall and the laid minefield of stock; in games, trap and mine supports. Traps forming only at the skill's full reach is its own.

name: Open Lead
idea: Every fourth cast of the sigil is left out: a beat of silence. For that beat (one interval long, at most 1.5 s) the player is damped: harm taken is 40% less and no condition can be put on them. Cost: a quarter of the sigil's casts. Two sigils with Open Lead whose silences fall together deepen the damping to 60%. A mark on each sigil shows its count, so the player can read when the quiet beat is coming.
source: Ringers leave one blow's silence after every second row, the handstroke gap or open lead.
nearest: Guard effects on a cooldown. Differs in buying the guard with missing casts on a fixed count that the player can read and line up across skills.

notes.where: Laurel in Vampire Survivors and Safer Spaces in Risk of Rain 2 (a guard that returns on a timer), and every-fourth counters such as Jhin's fourth shot. Paying for the guard with a missing cast on a readable count is not known.
The Defend command of turn-based role-playing games, a turn given up for a guard, and the rest in a bar of music. A readable fixed count that can be lined up across skills is its own.

name: Teller
idea: The sigil's hits deal nothing when they land. Each hit is counted on the body it struck. The counts are told when the character next stands still for 0.5 s, and on every district toll: every counted hit within 12 m lands at once, with 3% more for each hit in that body's count, up to 60% more. Cost: counted bodies keep walking unharmed until told, and a count is lost if its body gets more than 20 m away. Moving builds the count; stopping spends it.
source: The passing bell tells a death to the parish by a count of strokes.
nearest: Mark-and-detonate skills and stored-hit effects such as Impale in Path of Exile. Differs in nothing landing until the player stands still or the district bell tolls, so the thumb decides when the debt is paid.

notes.where: Twitch's Contaminate and Kalista's Rend in League of Legends (hits are counted on each body and cashed on command, more per stack, on everything in range), Explosive Arrow in Path of Exile, and Oracle's False Promise in Dota 2 for harm held back and landed later.
notes.mutation: Tell the counts as a running tally rather than body by body: on standing still the counts are read out smallest first, 0.1 s apart, each count rolling into the next body's, so the last body told takes the sum. The player decides who is told last by whom they have struck most, which a stack-and-detonate skill does not offer.

notes.where: 'You are already dead': Kenshiro's strikes in Fist of the North Star and the stock anime cut that lands only when the swordsman stops and sheathes (Zoro, Vergil's Judgment Cut End); the Five Point Palm of Kill Bill. In games, Explosive Arrow in Path of Exile: hits stick, count up and go off together for more per count.
notes.mutation: Let the telling pay out on the parish and not on the counted body: when told, each body rings its count as that many strokes on its neighbours while taking none itself, and a count is never lost by distance, so a heavily counted body is a loaded bell to be herded into a crowd before the player stops.

name: Rounds
idea: Holds 30% of the pool. While kept, the character's sigils give up their separate timers and ring in rounds: one row every 4 s, each sigil speaking once, lightest first, evenly spaced. A sigil deals +20% to a body for each earlier place in the same row that already hit it, so the fourth sigil lands at +60% on a body that took the whole row. After every second row one beat is silent. The bonus starts after 8 rows; the pool returns 8 rows after letting go.
source: Rounds is the bells sounding one after another from lightest to heaviest, and raising or lowering a bell takes many strokes.
nearest: Fixed cast order on a Noita wand. Differs as an optional kept state that pays for consecutive places landing on one body, with a slow raise and a slow lower.

notes.where: Fixed cast order on a Noita wand, one-two-three combo chains in Final Fantasy XIV (each step stronger for following the last), and reserved auras in Path of Exile.

Rounds as rung in The Nine Tailors, and the stock combination attack where each blow sets up the next; in games, combo chains and Noita wand order. The slow raise and lower of a kept state is its own.

name: Hand on the Bell
idea: Holds 25% of the pool. While kept, the character is damped: no after-harm can sound in them (harm over time of any kind ends at once and cannot be applied), and they cannot be shoved. But a damped body cannot ring a blow out: any single blow over 20% of greatest health also lowers greatest health by half the excess until the next gate. It is safe against a crowd of small dead and dangerous against one heavy stroke.
source: A hand laid on a bell stops its ringing at once, and a bell struck while it is held is the one that cracks.
nearest: Auras that give immunity to damage over time. Differs in the built-in price: while it is up, big hits become lasting loss.

notes.where: Trade-off keystones and reservations in Path of Exile (Petrified Blood, Unwavering Stance, Chaos Inoculation), and Eclipse 8 in Risk of Rain 2 for hits that shave greatest health.
Aesop's Oak and the Reed once more: the thing that will not yield to small winds is the one the storm breaks; in games, immunity auras with a drawback. Big hits turning into lasting loss is its own.

name: Curfew
idea: Holds 20% of the pool. While kept, experience does not come to the character: each drop lies under a cover where it fell, cannot fade and cannot be picked up. When the vow is let down (8 s to lower), and at every third toll, each cover within 15 m lifts and its embers fly in worth 20% more, plus 5% for each toll they lay covered, up to 40%. Covers farther away stay. The character levels late and in lumps, and has to be standing where the fighting was.
source: The curfew bell ordered hearth fires covered for the night, and a covered ember stays alive until it is uncovered.
nearest: Leaving experience gems on the ground for a later vacuum pickup in Vampire Survivors. Differs as a kept state that pays interest by tolls and ties the payout to where the kills were made.

notes.where: Experience gems left lying for a Vacuum in Vampire Survivors, the Piggy Bank's interest in Brotato, and interest on unspent gold in Teamfight Tactics. A kept state that buries experience where it fell and pays by tolls is not known.
The banked ember and the buried hoard dug up later, Aesop's ant laying by; in games, leaving gems for a late vacuum in Vampire Survivors. Interest counted in tolls and tied to place is its own.

name: Quarter-turn
idea: Choose one aimed sigil. For the rest of the vigil its aim is turned a quarter circle clockwise from the direction the character walks, and it strikes fresh metal: +30% harm. Taking it a second time on the same sigil turns it another quarter, so it fires behind, for 15% more. A third turn is never offered. The player decides during the vigil which sigils fire ahead, which sideways and which behind.
source: A worn bell is quarter-turned on its headstock so the clapper strikes fresh metal, which can be done only once or twice.
nearest: Weapons with fixed firing directions in survivor games. Differs in the player assigning directions to skills during the run, with a limit of two turns each.

notes.where: Back Shot in Thunder Force and the tail gun in Gradius, Mom's Eye and The Wiz in The Binding of Isaac (shots sent backward or off-axis), and the fixed directions of Knife, Axe and Whip in Vampire Survivors.

The broadsides and stern chasers of sailing ships (Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, Sid Meier's Pirates!), guns fixed sideways and astern of the course. Assigning them skill by skill with a two-turn limit is its own.

name: Maiden Voice
idea: Choose one sigil that has taken no chime this vigil. It becomes maiden: +60% harm and +20% reach for as long as no chime is ever taken for it. The first chime taken for it afterwards ends Maiden for good. Offered only while such a sigil exists. The player picks one sigil to leave untouched, and must then refuse its upgrades every time they are offered.
source: A maiden bell is one that came out of the mould in tune and has never been touched by the tuning lathe.
nearest: Bonuses for empty sockets or for having no modifiers. Differs in being a standing bet against that one skill's own later upgrades, made in the middle of a run.

notes.where: Eviolite in Pokemon (a large bonus for as long as the holder stays unevolved), and Stencil Joker in Balatro and empty-socket uniques in Path of Exile (pay for what is left unfilled).

Samson's uncut hair and the maiden-only unicorn: power that lasts exactly as long as the thing stays untouched and is gone for good at the first touch. In games, the Vow of Poverty of Dungeons and Dragons (Book of Exalted Deeds), a standing bonus kept only by refusing what is offered.
notes.mutation: Make it a wager on when to break the vow, not a vow kept for ever: every chime refused for the maiden sigil is banked on it unsounded, and the player may end Maiden at any toll to ring all banked chimes together as one outsized upgrade of a shape no single chime gives.

name: The Lathe's Cut
idea: Choose one sigil and cut it. It goes up one note for the rest of the vigil: interval 20% shorter, harm 12% less, Weight one class lighter. Each sigil shows its cuts as rings. A fourth cut on the same sigil makes it tinny, halving its harm, and the cut is still offered. Nothing can undo a cut. The player decides how thin to turn each sigil knowing that only one direction exists.
source: Tuning turns metal off the inside of a bell, and metal removed cannot be put back.
nearest: Attack-speed-for-damage trades. Differs in being one-way, counted per skill, with a known point of ruin that the game will still let the player reach.

notes.where: Soy Milk in The Binding of Isaac and the many faster-but-weaker items in Brotato: fire more often, hit softer, stack it as far as you dare. Over-enhancement cliffs in MapleStory for a step that ruins the thing and is still offered.
notes.mutation: Cut the note, not the numbers: a cut leaves interval and harm alone and only moves the sigil one weight class lighter, changing which bodies it rings true on, and the fourth cut takes it off the bottom of the scale so it rings true on nothing. The choice becomes which size of enemy each skill is tuned for, with the same one-way ruin.

notes.where: The folk tale of the tailor who cuts the coat down to a button, and The Fisherman and His Wife, where one ask too many leaves nothing; in games, speed-for-damage trades. A ruin the game still offers is its own.

name: Muffle the Toll
idea: The next district toll rings muffled: danger does not rise and rewards do not rise. The toll after it rings for two: danger and rewards rise two steps at once, and if that toll is the eighth, the keeper arrives with one extra toll's strength. Only one muffle can be held at a time. The player buys 75 quiet seconds now and pays with a double step later.
source: A muffled bell sounds faintly, and in half-muffled ringing the open stroke always follows the muffled one.
nearest: Items that delay difficulty. Differs in moving one step of the district's clock onto the next toll instead of removing it.

notes.where: Events that delay the rebel fleet in FTL, time stops such as the Orologion in Vampire Survivors, and the difficulty clock of Risk of Rain. Moving one step onto the next toll rather than removing it is not known.
Bargains for borrowed time: Godfather Death, Death shut in the pear tree, the debt that returns doubled. In games, items that delay difficulty. Moving one step onto the next toll is its own.

name: Drill the Crack
idea: Offered only when the character has lost greatest health to Crack. The crack is drilled wider so its edges no longer touch. All Crack already taken becomes permanent for the vigil and cannot be recast at a gate, but no further Crack can be taken from any source this vigil, and any sigil cracked by clocking regains its full harm. The player locks in today's loss to end the risk of more.
source: A hairline crack buzzes because its edges touch; drilling it wider stops the buzz, which is the wide gap seen in the Liberty Bell.
nearest: None known; the nearest is cleansing a curse, but this fixes the loss in place in order to stop it growing.

notes.where: Amputating a limb in RimWorld to stop an infection, trauma in Blades in the Dark (take a permanent scar and the stress track clears), and Omamori in Slay the Spire for immunity to curses bought ahead.
Cutting off the bitten limb to stop the spread (Hershel's leg in The Walking Dead) and cauterising a wound: a fixed loss accepted to end the risk. As a level-up pick it is its own.

name: Trade Clappers
idea: Choose two sigils. They exchange intervals for the rest of the vigil: each keeps its own shape and harm but casts as often as the other did. The one that became faster deals 15% less harm per cast; the one that became slower deals 15% more. Offered at most twice a vigil, and never for the same pair twice. A slow heavy sigil can be made the quick one, at the price of slowing something else.
source: A clapper is matched to its own bell, and a bell hung with another bell's clapper speaks differently.
nearest: None known for swapping the timing of two owned skills; the nearest is cooldown-reduction upgrades.

notes.where: Speed Swap and Power Swap in Pokemon (two creatures exchange a stat), and moving a spell between a fast and a slow wand in Noita. Exchanging the timers of two owned skills as a run pick is not known.
Only body-swap comedy at a great distance (Freaky Friday, The Prince and the Pauper); I know no story or game where two powers trade their tempo and keep their shapes.

name: The Wether
idea: A risen drover with a bell at its neck (a bright cone under a sphere head). Ordinary dead within 8 m do not chase the player; they follow 2 m behind the Wether, which circles the player at 7 m and cuts in every 6 s. It harms only by leading the flock over the player. Kill it and its flock stands lost for 3 s, then hunts singly. The player kills the bright bell first, or spares it to keep thirty bodies in one readable clump.
source: A bellwether is the belled sheep the rest of the flock follows.
nearest: Pack-leader enemies whose death routs the pack. Differs in the flock steering by the leader's path, which can make the leader worth sparing.

notes.where: The Dancing Zombie and its backup dancers in Plants vs. Zombies (a leader with a formation in tow), Elites leading Grunts in Halo (kill the leader and the pack loses its head), and the head-led chain in Centipede.

Big Daddy leading the dead in Land of the Dead, the Night King whose fall drops his army, the Piper at the head of the rats; in games, snake formations following a head. A leader worth sparing to keep a clump is its own.

name: Tongueless
idea: A risen bell on legs, mouth-down, with nothing hanging inside: a hollow tapered cylinder, dark within. It is slow and heavy, makes no sound, and a dark ring 5 m wide on the ground moves with it. Inside the ring the player is Clocked: sigils cast only when the thumb stops, one per stop. It does no harm itself; the horde around it does. The player must stay out of the ring or fight in stop-and-go steps, and should kill any Tongue heading for it.
source: A bell blamed for a riot in Uglich in 1591 had its clapper, called its tongue, torn out before it was sent into exile.
nearest: Silence-aura enemies. Differs in turning the player's casting manual inside the ring instead of switching it off.

notes.where: Silence-aura enemies and the Suppressor elite affix in Diablo IV (a bubble that changes how you must fight), Riki's Smoke Screen in Dota 2, and Archero's stop-to-shoot rule, which is what the ring imposes.
The Gentlemen of Buffy's 'Hush', walking bringers of silence, and living bells such as Pokemon's Bronzong or the temple bell of the Dojoji legend. Turning casting manual instead of off is its own.

name: Tongue
idea: A fallen clapper, an iron ball on a shaft, swinging end over end, 2 m a hop, lying still 0.6 s between hops. Where the ball will land is marked 0.5 s ahead and harms a 1 m circle. It ignores the player and travels toward the nearest Tongueless within 30 m; if it arrives the two join into a Tolling Bell elite that strikes a 6 m ring every 4 s. With no Tongueless about, Tongues hop at the player. Kill them while they lie still.
source: The clapper hangs inside the bell and strikes the sound-bow, and clappers do break off and fall.
nearest: Enemies that merge into a stronger one. Differs in two unlike halves, a silent bell and its lost clapper, seeking each other across the field.

notes.where: Flood infection forms in Halo and the Infector in Dead Space (a small hopping thing racing to a body to make a worse enemy; kill it on the way), two Templar merging into an Archon in StarCraft, and slimes merging into a King Slime in Dragon Quest.
The Headless Horseman seeking his head, the severed hand crawling home (Evil Dead II), Plato's split halves; merging enemies in games. Two unlike halves, one of them harmless alone, is its own.

name: Overthrown
idea: A bell on its wheel that has gone over the balance and cannot stop: a broad cylinder rolling in straight lines at 5 m/s, turning only when it meets a wall, harming and shoving every body it crosses. A line on the ground shows its path 6 m ahead. Hits from in front, against its motion, slow it one step of five; hits from behind speed it up one step. Slowed to nothing, it lies helpless for 5 s. Stay off the line; strike it head-on, never from behind.
source: A bell pulled too hard breaks its stay and swings over and over; pulls with the swing raise a bell and pulls against it lower it.
nearest: Charging and rolling-boulder enemies. Differs in its speed being set by which side the player's hits arrive from.

notes.where: Bonewheel skeletons in Dark Souls and Flame Wheels in Hades, a kicked Koopa shell in Super Mario (straight lines, turning only at walls), and knockback that slows whatever is shot head-on in Nuclear Throne. Five speed steps set by the side the hit comes from is not known.
The rolling boulder of Raiders of the Lost Ark, Zelda's straight-line blade traps and the kicked Koopa shell. Speed set by which side the hits come from is its own.

name: Rattler
idea: A tall thin risen sexton carrying a wooden plank and mallet (a long box and a small cylinder). It keeps 10 to 12 m from the player, circling, and never attacks. Every 3 s it knocks, and each knock takes 2 s off the time to the next district toll; a ring flashes on the toll clock when it does. Three Rattlers left alive bring every toll about 30 s sooner. The player must break off from the horde and run them down.
source: When bells are silent, wooden clappers and struck planks are used to call the hours in their place.
nearest: Enemies that attack a shared resource, such as torch-snuffers in Darkest Dungeon. Differs in attacking the vigil's clock itself, pulling the tolls nearer.

notes.where: Doom-adding cultists in Arkham Horror: The Card Game (Acolyte, Wizard of the Order: they keep away, do not attack, and push the agenda clock each round until hunted down), Avatar facilities in XCOM 2, and the fleeing scout in FTL.
notes.mutation: Let the stolen time be held, not lost: each knock moves 2 s from the toll clock into the Rattler's plank, shown as a growing tally, and killing it gives those seconds back doubled. The player chooses between running it down at once and letting it fill to push the next toll later, which a plain doom-ticker never allows.

notes.where: The grey gentlemen of Michael Ende's Momo, who steal people's time, and the ticking crocodile that brings Hook's hour nearer; in games, foes that attack a shared resource. Striking the run's own clock is its own.

name: The Row
idea: Six dead ringers shoulder to shoulder, a wall 9 m wide that walks at the player at 1.5 m/s and harms on contact. Five are grey and cannot be harmed or pushed. One is lit, the lead, and it takes all harm for the row. Each second the lead passes to the next ringer along, to the end and back. When a ringer dies the row is one shorter; the last one alive is an ordinary body. The player backs away, keeping sigils on the lit place.
source: In plain hunt one bell moves a place at a time along the row to the end and back while the others keep ringing.
nearest: Enemies where only a lit weak point can be hurt. Differs in the weak point walking a line of bodies on a fixed pattern that can be learned.

notes.where: The advancing rank of Space Invaders, council bosses where only one member can be hurt at a time (the Spirit Kings in World of Warcraft), and shell-game enemies hidden among copies. A weak point that walks a line of bodies to the end and back is not known.

The Cylon eye or KITT's scanner light running along a row and back, the shield wall, and the stock 'only the real one among the copies can be hurt'. A learnable pattern over a shrinking row is its own.

name: Bell-bearers
idea: Four dead carrying a great bell mouth-down over themselves: a bell with eight legs. Strokes cannot reach the bearers and do not harm the bell. But every Stroke on the bell makes it ring over the heads beneath: the bearers take that Stroke as after-harm spread over 3 s, and heavier Strokes ring 1 s longer per weight class. Light fast sigils barely trouble them. Each dead bearer slows it; with one left, the bell drops and pins it. It wants one heavy stroke, or a detour.
source: The sound under a struck bell is at its fiercest, and a great bell's low hum outlasts all its other notes.
nearest: Shielded carriers that must be flanked. Differs in the shield being the way in: hitting it harder is what hurts those beneath.

notes.where: The battering ram in Age of Empires II (a carried shell that shrugs off light fast hits and wants heavy ones), Lead and Ceramic bloons in Bloons TD, and the Zombie Bobsled Team and Parasol Zombie in Plants vs. Zombies.

The Dojoji legend, where the monk under the temple bell is killed through the bell, and the cartoon gag of ringing a bell over someone's head; Blasphemous has giants carrying great bells. The shield being the way in is its own.

name: Mould-walker
idea: A hollow figure of loam, dung and goat hair: a mould walking without its bell (dull brown boxes, visibly empty through a slot). It takes no harm. Each hit fills it instead, shown as bright metal rising in the slot; it is full after harm equal to its greatest health. When full it sets: it becomes a bronze copy that casts, once, the last sigil that struck it, back at the player at 150%, then stands inert and brittle. Finish filling it with the weakest sigil, or leave it.
source: A bell mould is an empty shape of loam, horse dung and goat hair that gives its form to whatever metal fills it.
nearest: Enemies that absorb and then reflect, and mimics that copy a power. Differs in the player choosing which of their own skills is copied, by which one lands last.

notes.where: Mirror Move and Bide in Pokemon (return the last move used on it, or the harm stored), the Bomb in Final Fantasy, which swells with each hit until it goes off, and Rubick's Spell Steal in Dota 2.
The clay golem, Marvel's Absorbing Man, and Gogo of Final Fantasy V, who gives back the last thing done to him; Kirby's copying. An unkillable mould the player chooses how to finish is its own.

name: The Conductor of the Dead Band
idea: Six bells hang round the arena. Each tilts mouth-up 0.6 s before sending a 40 degree wedge of harm, and they speak in a row shown as six numbered lamps. Phase one: rounds, 1 to 6. Phase two (at 70%): changes; from one row to the next a bell only keeps its place or swaps with a neighbour, so each row can be read from the last. Phase three (at 30%): firing, all six at once after 2 s; bells the player cracked earlier stay silent, leaving safe wedges.
source: In change ringing a bell may only keep its place or swap with a neighbour from one row to the next, and firing is every bell struck at the same instant.
nearest: Pattern-memory boss attacks. Differs in the pattern following the change-ringing rule, so it is predicted rather than memorised, and in the player preparing the last phase by cracking bells.

notes.where: Numbered-order mechanics in Final Fantasy XIV such as Limit Cut (attacks resolve in a displayed sequence), and cutting a tail in Dark Souls or Monster Hunter to remove one of the boss's attacks for the rest of the fight.

The undead maestro and skeleton band of the danse macabre, the killing bell-chamber of The Nine Tailors, and Simon-style pattern bosses. A pattern predicted by the neighbour-swap rule, and silenced bells as safe wedges, is its own.

name: The Flogged Bell
idea: A great bell carried by the dead. Phase one: tongueless, it charges along a line shown 1 s ahead, shedding four dead at each wall it hits. Phase two (at 60%): re-tongued, it tolls every 6 s after a 1.5 s swell, filling the arena; the only safe ground is the sound-shadow behind a heavy dead body, so the player spares big dead and stands in their lee. Phase three (at 25%): it tells the player's years, one stroke per character level, then lies spent 8 s.
source: Sound casts a shadow behind a solid body, and the passing bell gives one stroke for each year of the life.
nearest: Hiding behind pillars from an arena-wide blast in raid fights. Differs in the cover being enemies the player must spare, and the final count being as long as the character's own level.

notes.where: Hiding behind the Comets from Behemoth's Ecliptic Meteor in Monster Hunter: World, behind Garuda's pillars in Final Fantasy XIV and behind ice tombs at Sindragosa in World of Warcraft; Level 5 Death and Tonberry's Karma in Final Fantasy for attacks keyed to the character's own numbers.

Sheltering behind a pillar from the dragon's breath, the human shield, the cuckoo counting one's years, the charging Bell Carrier of Blasphemous and the flogged bell of Uglich. Cover made of foes that must be spared is its own.

name: The Tuner at the Lathe
idea: The arena is the inside of a bell, a round floor 16 m across. Every 8 s the keeper cuts: a groove 1.5 m wide appears as a ring at the player's distance from the centre, shown 1.5 s ahead. Grooves are permanent; crossing one costs 8% health and a 1 s slow. Phase two (at 60%): two rings per cut. Phase three (at 30%): he stands at the centre and can be harmed only from uncut floor. Where the player stands at each cut decides what floor is left.
source: A founder tunes a bell by turning rings of metal off its inside on a lathe, and metal removed cannot be put back.
nearest: Boss arenas that crumble over time. Differs in each loss being a ring whose radius the player picks by where they stand, kept for the whole fight.

notes.where: Grobbulus in World of Warcraft's Naxxramas and the Shaper's vortex pools in Path of Exile: a lasting hazard is laid where the player stands, for the whole fight, so the fight is about where to drop them and how much floor is left. Also Ghom's gas clouds in Diablo III.
notes.mutation: Make the grooves cut sound rather than skin: crossing costs nothing, but no stroke, the keeper's or the player's, carries across a groove, so each cut splits the floor into concentric bands that can only be fought within. The player's standing distance then decides which band the keeper ends in and whether there is room to share it with him.

notes.where: The crumbling arena of stock and the shrinking floor of Poe's 'The Pit and the Pendulum'; Blasphemous's Jondo is the inside of a great bell. Permanent rings at the radius the player stands on is its own.

name: The Founders' Sink
idea: Look: soot-black ground, loam-brown furnaces (tapered boxes), cylinder chimneys, cone slag heaps and round casting pits 4 m wide with ember-orange rims, plus bronze and verdigris green. Special: each pit holds a buried bell still cooling. Any Stroke landing in a pit is answered 1 s later by a 4 m ring of the same harm that strikes the dead and the player alike. A pit answered more than 3 times in 5 s cools too fast and cracks, dead for the vigil. Use the pits without hurrying them.
source: Bells are cast mouth down in a pit and cooled slowly for days; cooled too quickly, they crack.
nearest: Arena hazards that both sides can set off. Differs in pits that repeat the player's own blows and are spoiled for good by overuse.

notes.where: Explosive barrels, the arena traps of Hades and one-use environmental traps in Monster Hunter (hazards either side can set off, some spent after use).
The forge level of stock (the Sammath Naur, the forges of Erebor, the casting pit of Andrei Rublev) with hazards either side can set off. Pits that repeat a blow and are spoiled by hurry are its own.

name: The Hanging Quarter
idea: Look: oak-brown frames (boxes), lead-grey floors, and ropes hanging everywhere with sallies as striped cylinders in wool red, white and blue. Special: about forty ropes hang at fixed spots, each tied to a bell overhead and to a marked circle on the floor 5 to 10 m away. Anything walking through a sally pulls it, and 1 s later a heavy stroke lands on that rope's circle, on whoever is there. The dead blunder through ropes and ring them. The player learns which rope strikes where.
source: A tower bell is rung from the floor below by a rope with a woolly striped grip, the sally.
nearest: Pressure-plate traps in dungeon games. Differs in a whole district of them that the horde sets off by itself, each with a fixed distant landing spot to learn.

notes.where: Arrow traps in Spelunky and the pressure plates of Sen's Fortress in Dark Souls (enemies trip them too), and sensors wired to distant traps in Evil Genius.

The trapped temple of Raiders of the Lost Ark (tread here, the dart flies there), the cartoon rope that drops an anvil, and servants' bell-pulls. A whole district of them rung by the horde is its own.

name: The Blue Line
idea: The tree is a page of rows, eight places wide and sixty rows deep, a node at every place. A character's path is one line down the page: each point bought must be in the next row, in the same place or a neighbouring place. Classes start in different places. Three printed lines also run down the page on fixed zigzags (the treble: place 1 to 8 and back). A node where the character's line meets a printed line is doubled, so planning means timing sideways steps to meet them.
source: Ringers learn a method as a blue line drawn down a page of rows, and steer by where they pass the treble.
nearest: Lattice route maps such as the one in Slay the Spire. Differs as a fixed skill grid with a keep-or-step rule and printed weaving lines to intercept.

notes.where: The act map of Slay the Spire (one step per row to a neighbouring node), one-pick-per-tier talent rows in World of Warcraft, and the Sphere Grid of Final Fantasy X. Printed weaving lines to intercept are not known.
Only the Plinko or Galton board and the route lattice of Slay the Spire, both distant; I know no skill tree walked as one line down a page that pays for crossing printed weaving lines.

name: Five Notes in Tune
idea: The tree is drawn as the inside of a bell in five bands: hum, prime, tierce, quint, nominal. Each point cuts one node from a band for a small gain, never refunded. The number of cuts in a band is that note's pitch. When two bands stand in a true interval (hum twice the prime; tierce 6 cuts per 5 of prime; nominal equal to hum) a large harmonic bonus is on. One cut too many puts the pair flat and the bonus off until the other band catches up.
source: A founder tunes five partials by turning metal from different bands inside the bell; true intervals between them make it sound in tune, and metal cannot be returned.
nearest: Attribute-threshold bonuses. Differs in bonuses depending on exact ratios between counts, which one cut too far loses.

notes.where: The Ninja trait in Teamfight Tactics (on at exactly one or exactly four, off between), the Golden Order tools in Elden Ring that want Faith and Intelligence matched, and The Wise Oak in Path of Exile, which pays for balanced resistances.

Only the legend of Pythagoras and the blacksmith's hammers and the music of the spheres as a picture; threshold set bonuses exist, but I know no system that pays for exact ratios between counts and punishes one step past.

name: Coming Round
idea: A rule on the shared tree: when a character's owned nodes close a ring, meaning the path returns to a node already owned by a different road, that ring has come round. Every small node on a closed ring is worth double; a node on two rings is still only doubled once. With about 100 points to spend, the plan is a choice between one wide ring through distant parts of the tree and several small ones close to home.
source: A piece of change ringing ends when the bells come round, returning to the row they started from.
nearest: The passive tree in Path of Exile, where doubling back is wasted points. Differs in making closed loops the thing that is rewarded.

notes.where: The Stat Matrix in Kingdom Hearts Re:coded (chips on a completed link between two processors count double), closed features in Carcassonne and doubled loops in Tantrix, and finished constellations in Grim Dawn.
The closed summoning circle and the Ouroboros; in games, Carcassonne paying for a completed city or road. Rewarding loops on a passive tree is its own.

name: Five Lines, One Lathe
idea: An item is a cast bell worn on the body. It has a Weight and five lines, one per note, each a property rolled sharp of its true value by 0 to 6 steps. One lathe cut flattens a chosen line one step and takes 5% of the item's Weight. A line exactly on true is doubled; past true it is halved; no cut can be undone. Below 70% Weight every line halves. No tiers: an item is worth its distance from true and the Weight left to get there.
source: A founder brings a bell's five partials into tune by turning metal off on a lathe; a bell needing no tuning is called a maiden bell.
