nearest: Crafting currencies that reroll modifiers. Differs in every change being chosen, one-directional and paid from a visible budget, with no rarity classes at all.

notes.where: Forging Potential in Last Epoch (a visible budget that every craft eats), ability-stone faceting in Lost Ark, and the bust in blackjack for going one past the mark. A one-way cut toward an exact target on each line, with no rarity tiers, is not known.
Blackjack and The Price Is Right (closest to the mark without going past it), and Goldilocks's 'just right'. Gear with no tiers, tuned by one-way cuts from a weight budget, is its own.

name: Chiselled Legends
idea: An item's properties are its inscription: up to three clauses, each built as verb, object, condition, for example I BREAK, THE HEAVY, AT THE TOLL. The verb is the stat and amount, the object limits it to tagged things, the condition says when. A chisel only removes words: striking off the condition makes the clause always on at 60%; striking off the object widens it to everything at 60%. Letters are stamped by hand, so one clause in ten has a reversed letter and its condition is inverted.
source: Words pressed into a bell mould come out raised on the shoulder, and old bells often carry backward or misplaced letters.
nearest: Affix lists on Diablo-style items. Differs in properties being sentences that the player shortens word by word, trading narrowness for size.

notes.where: Baba Is You (rules are words that can be taken away), host and augment cards in Magic: The Gathering's Unstable (trigger and effect as separate halves), the Orb of Annulment in Path of Exile (crafting by removal), and conditional affixes in Diablo-style games.

The Golem's emet struck down to met, one letter removed and the meaning turned; Mjolnir's conditional inscription; Animal Farm's amended commandments; in games, Baba Is You, where rules are sentences changed by taking a word away. Subtractive wording on gear is its own.

name: Recast and Cool
idea: Two or more items can be broken up and poured into one. The new item's Weight is the sum less 10% dross. Each line comes from one parent's line in that place, heavier parents likelier. One word the player owns may be pressed into the mould and comes out as a fixed clause. It must then cool: it cannot be worn until the account has heard 6 more tolls. It may be taken early, but each toll short gives a 15% chance of a void: one line left blank.
source: A cracked bell is broken up and recast with its metal going into the new one, and a casting is cooled slowly for days.
nearest: Item fusion with inherited traits, as in Persona fusion or gear merging. Differs in weight-weighted inheritance, one chosen stamped clause, and a wait measured in tolls survived.

notes.where: Breeding in Pokemon: each stat comes from one parent's value in that place, a held Power item fixes one chosen stat, and the egg must be walked before it can be used. Also Recombinators in Path of Exile, and the alchemy pot in Dragon Quest VIII, which makes the player wait.
notes.mutation: Choose inheritance by pour order instead of rolling it: the first parent poured gives the low lines and the last the high, so the player decides every line. Let cooling tune rather than gate: the item is wearable at once, and each toll the account hears before it is first worn brings its sharpest line one step toward true.

notes.where: The reforged blade of saga (Gram and Nothung, Narsil made Anduril), Schiller's 'Song of the Bell', Persona fusion and the wait timers of mobile games. A wait counted in tolls with a risk for haste is its own.

name: A Passing Told
idea: A bell begins to tell a death: a rope appears at a marked spot 20 to 30 m off and tolls once a second. Each stroke adds one level, and 4% more loot, to an elite that will rise beside the rope. The telling stops only when the player stands at the rope for 1 s and stills it; the elite then rises at once at whatever the count has reached. Left alone, the count stops at 40. The player chooses how old to let it grow.
source: The passing bell tells a death by a count of strokes and then one stroke for each year of the life.
nearest: Shrines that summon an elite for a reward. Differs in the elite's strength being a running count that the player ends by arriving.

notes.where: Stacking neutral camps in Dota 2 (let the camp grow for a bigger payout, then clear it), Delirium and Essence monsters in Path of Exile, and the Dead Adventurer in Slay the Spire.

The stock 'stop the ritual before it finishes', where the thing called grows worse the longer the rite runs, and the cuckoo whose calls are counted as years; elite-summoning shrines in games. Choosing how long to let it grow is its own.

name: The Pour
idea: A furnace is tapped at a marked spot, and bright metal runs down a channel 15 m long to a pit, taking 12 s. Any body standing in the channel ahead of the metal stops the run, the player's own body included. If the metal reaches the pit unbroken, it leaves a gear item with all five lines. Each stop longer than 1 s leaves a cold shut: one line of the item is void. The player clears the channel just ahead of the metal without standing in it.
source: A bell must be poured in one unbroken run; an interrupted pour leaves a seam of weakness called a cold shut.
nearest: Escort and defend-the-point objectives. Differs in the thing protected being an advancing line that the player's own body also blocks.

notes.where: The payload in Team Fortress 2 and Overwatch (an advance that halts while bodies contest it), Pipe Mania and Unrailed! (stay just ahead of an advancing flow), and Escort Duty in Deep Rock Galactic.

The bell pour of Tarkovsky's Andrei Rublev and the gold channels of The Desolation of Smaug; in games, the payload of Team Fortress 2 that halts when bodies contest it. The player's own body blocking the run is its own.

name: The Answer
idea: A great bell is struck far across the water. Its note is one of the five weight classes, shown as a size mark on the toll clock 3 s before. For 10 s every body of that class in the district is in sympathy: a Stroke landing on one of them also lands at 50% on every other body of that class within 12 m. Every body of any other class moves 25% faster for the same 10 s. At most once between tolls; never a keeper's class.
source: A struck bell makes another bell tuned to the same note hum without being touched.
nearest: Shared-damage links such as Fatal Bonds in Dota. Differs as a district-wide moment announced in advance, binding one size of enemy while speeding the rest.

notes.where: Warlock's Fatal Bonds in Dota 2 (harm to one linked body is shared to the rest), Synchronoise in Pokemon, and mission mutators in Deep Rock Galactic.

Sympathy in Rothfuss's The Name of the Wind, where like bound to like shares what is done to it; the Corsican Brothers; the wax doll; Fatal Bonds in Dota. A district-wide announced moment by size is its own.

name: The Ring of the Dead
idea: The Carillon is a frame of twelve bell-pits. A dead character is recast as one bell, its weight the tolls it heard in its whole life. Bells hang in order of weight. Each gives every later character one small grant fixed by its class. A true ring gives more: each neighbouring pair whose weights differ by 10 to 30% adds a step to a ring bonus. A ring needs trebles as much as tenors, so a character that died young fills a pit a veteran cannot.
source: A ring of bells runs from the light treble to the heavy tenor, and a broken bell's metal is recast into a new one.
nearest: Lineages of fallen heroes that grant bonuses, as in Rogue Legacy. Differs in early deaths being needed as the small bells of a graded set.

notes.where: Link Skills and Legion in MapleStory (every character gives the account one grant fixed by its class), the lineage of Rogue Legacy, and Fame from dead characters in Realm of the Mad God. A graded set that needs short lives as its small pieces is not known.

The hall of ancestors and the memorial wall (Rogue Legacy's lineage, XCOM's memorial, Darkest Dungeon's graveyard) and Hearn's soul in the bell. Needing early deaths as the small bells of a graded ring is its own.

name: Told on Every Voice
idea: Echoes are earned only when a character dies or is retired. The passing bell tells it: one stroke for each character level, rung on every district bell the account has ever given back its voice by beating its keeper. Echoes earned are the strokes rung: level times voiced bells, 1 to 5. Echoes buy bell-pits in the Carillon and the words that can be stamped on the dead character's bell; each word, earned by a deed in that life, becomes a clause every later character carries.
source: The passing bell tells a death with one stroke for each year of the life, and a bell's inscription is fixed when it is cast.
nearest: Meta-currency paid on death in roguelites. Differs in the payout being multiplied by bells restored across the account, and spent on wording the dead character's own lasting grant.

notes.where: Fame in Realm of the Mad God (paid only at death, a base amount times bonuses for deeds done in that life), prestige currency in idle games (reset, multiplied by overall progress), and legacies chosen from a dead captain in Sunless Sea.
notes.mutation: Drop the banked currency: the strokes of the telling are the letters the dead character's inscription may use, level times voiced bells, spent at once on words earned in that life and never carried over. A short life affords one short word and a long life a full clause, so the payout is an epitaph to compose rather than points to save.

notes.where: The epitaph and the deed-name of saga, Wildermyth's legacy heroes, and the death currency of any roguelite. Spending it on the wording of the dead character's own grant is its own.

name: Half-muffled Tolls
idea: Twist on the tolls: they come in pairs. An odd toll is open: danger rises and the arrivals for the next 75 s are drawn fresh. The even toll after it is muffled: the same arrivals come again from the same sides in the same order at 80% strength, while rewards rise as usual. The player meets each new danger once to learn it and once to profit from it. The keeper's toll, the eighth, is muffled, so the keeper arrives with an echo of the seventh toll's horde.
source: In half-muffled ringing every second row is a faint echo of the row before it.
nearest: Repeating wave patterns in arcade games. Differs in strict learn-then-repeat pairs tied to the tolls of the vigil.

notes.where: Time-loop games such as Majora's Mask and Deathloop (the same arrivals replay, so the player learns and then profits), the fixed spawn script of Devil Daggers, and call-and-response in Rhythm Heaven.
Groundhog Day and Edge of Tomorrow, the same assault met a second time by someone who now knows it; repeating waves in arcade games. Strict learn-then-profit pairs are its own.

name: Ringing Down
idea: Twist on the gates: a character cannot step out at once. Standing in an open gate rings down: one stroke a second for six strokes. Each stroke banks one sixth of what is carried, in an order the player set beforehand, and each stroke also silences one sixth of the character's sigils. Driven off before the sixth, the character keeps what was banked, stays in the vigil, and raises the silenced sigils again at one per 2 s. Leaving is a retreat in stages, not a door.
source: Lowering a bell takes many strokes, just as raising it does.
nearest: Channelled extraction in extraction shooters. Differs in banking a share with every second and paying for it with skills falling silent.

notes.where: Extraction countdowns in Hunt: Showdown and Escape from Tarkov, handing in loot piece by piece under threat in Sea of Thieves, and the interruptible Recall of League of Legends. Paying for each banked share with a silenced skill is not known.

The diver's decompression stops and the fighting retreat of the rear guard; in games, channelled extraction (Dark and Darker, Escape from Tarkov) and the safe havens of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. Paying for each banked share with a silenced skill is its own.

name: The Row of Chimes
idea: Twist on leveling: chimes are not dealt at random. Six chimes stand in a visible row, places 1 to 6. At a level-up the player takes one from places 1 to 3, and a new one enters at place 6. After every level-up the row changes as ringing does: neighbours swap in fixed pairs, alternately 1-2, 3-4, 5-6 and then 2-3, 4-5. The player can see which chime will walk to the front in two levels and decide whether to wait for it.
source: In plain hunt each bell walks through the row one place at a time by neighbours swapping in alternating pairs.
nearest: Card rivers in board games, such as the sliding card row in Through the Ages. Differs in the row moving by ringing swaps, so offers walk forward and back on a path that can be read ahead.

notes.where: The card row of Through the Ages and the centre row of Ascension, the next-piece queue of Tetris, and locking shop items in Brotato. A row that weaves by alternating neighbour swaps is not known.
The sushi conveyor, the card row of Through the Ages and Tetris's next-piece queue. Offers that walk forward and back by ringing swaps are its own.

name: The Half-muffled Keeper
idea: Every attack of this keeper lands twice on the same ground. Phase one: the full stroke, then a 30% echo 2 s later, so struck ground stays dangerous. Phase two (at 60%): the leather is on the other side. The faint echo comes first and is the only warning; the full stroke follows 1.2 s later on the same ground. Phase three (at 25%): rung backward and fast. Three echoes are laid one after another, then their three full strokes land in reverse order, last-laid first.
source: Half-muffled ringing makes every second row a faint echo, and ringing backward was the alarm.
nearest: Delayed repeat attacks on bosses. Differs in the echo becoming the telegraph itself, and then in the order of landing being reversed from the order of warning.

notes.where: Pontiff Sulyvahn in Dark Souls III, whose phantom strikes just before he does, Grand Magistrix Elisande in World of Warcraft, whose echoes replay attacks on the same ground, and order-memory mechanics in Final Fantasy XIV.

The White Queen of Through the Looking-Glass, who screams before she pricks her finger; lightning before thunder; T. H. White's Merlyn living backward; raid telegraphs that resolve in sequence. The echo as the only warning, then reversed order, is its own.

name: The Touch of Five
idea: Twist on the one-sitting run: its five districts are a row. Each new run's district order is the last run's order with exactly one neighbouring pair swapped, and the player chooses which pair before starting. The keeper of the district rung last arrives at double strength and leaves double Echoes. Every order the account has rung is kept; an order never rung before pays 25% more. There are 120 orders, and the player walks between them one swap at a time.
source: From one row to the next a bell may only keep its place or swap with a neighbour, and a true touch never repeats a row.
nearest: Route choice between runs in roguelites. Differs in each run's order being one neighbour-swap from the previous run, with unrepeated orders paid extra.

notes.where: Choosing island order in Into the Breach (later islands scale up) and stage order in Mega Man, the clan-pair completion grid of Monster Train, and Dark Thirst in Hades for paying variety. A rule that each run must be one neighbour swap from the last is not known.

Only Mega Man's free choice of stage order and the permutations of a peal in The Nine Tailors; I know no game or story where each run's order is one neighbour-swap from the last and unrung orders pay more.

name: The Three Dues
idea: Harm is Rung (bell, knock, cry), Written (chisel, quill, notch) or Covered (earth, iron, cloth). Each risen dead was denied one rite and shows which: a gaping mouth (never rung), a blank slab on its chest (never written), no shroud (never covered). Any harm can drop it, but a body dropped by the wrong kind stands again at the next toll with 60% life; dropped by its due it is laid for good and its drop doubles. Protection is three yes-or-no states, Muffled, Blank and Shrouded, each halving one kind.
source: A decent death was owed three things: the passing bell, a name cut in stone or entered in the register, and covering earth; these dead rose for want of one.
nearest: Tabletop trolls that stay dead only if burned, and elemental weakness charts. Here the matching kind does not hit harder: it decides whether the kill is permanent, and the penalty arrives on the bell.

notes.where: Dark Souls Catacombs skeletons, which stand up again unless felled with a divine weapon; D&D trolls and hydras that only stay dead to fire or acid; laid over an ordinary three-way weakness chart (Pokemon match-ups, Destiny Match Game shields).
notes.mutation: Take the due off the killing blow: every fallen body lies unlaid until its missing rite is done to the body itself before the toll - a cast sounded within earshot for the unrung, the player standing on it for the unwritten, another body dropped on top of it for the uncovered - so permanence comes from what the player does around corpses, not from a damage tag.

notes.where: The restless dead who cannot lie until given the rite they were denied: unburied Elpenor in the Odyssey and Palinurus in the Aeneid, the Witcher 3 botchling that is laid only by a name and a burial, the Dead of Garth Nix's Sabriel who keep returning until a bell sends them on; Supernatural's salt-and-burn, without which the ghost comes back; trolls that regenerate unless burned. Three rites each answered by one kind of harm, read off the body, with the failure arriving on the bell, belongs to none of them.

name: Tale, Weight and Term
idea: Harm is counted three ways: by tale (how many blows), by weight (how heavy each), by term (how long it stays). Each of the dead answers to one. Tale-bound: it falls after a set count of blows, however light: 3 for a child, 6 for a woman, 9 for a man. Weight-bound: a flat amount comes off every blow, so only heavy ones count. Term-bound: nothing harms it until the player has stood within 5 m for a set number of seconds. The player's wards are bound the same ways.
source: The Exchequer took payment by tale (counted), by weight, or held over for a term; the death knell counted nine strokes for a man, six for a woman, three for a child.
nearest: Hit-count shields, flat armour thresholds and stand-here timers each exist separately in many games. Here they are the only three protections there are, and they replace typed damage altogether.

notes.where: Fallout: New Vegas Damage Threshold (a flat amount off every hit), hit-count objects such as League of Legends wards and Zelda enemies that die in N hits, and stand-in-the-zone gates; the many-hits, big-hits, time split also mirrors attack-speed, slam and damage-over-time builds in Path of Exile. No game I know makes these the only three protections.

Pwyll in the Mabinogion, who must strike Hafgan exactly once because a second blow would restore him (the blow-count rules of folk tale); the cat's nine lives; Smaug and Achilles, whom only the right blow gets through; hit-count bosses and flat damage thresholds in games. The knell's 3, 6 and 9 reused as a blow count, and the stand-near term, come from no story.

name: In Mourning
idea: When an elite dies, every lesser dead within 8 m goes into mourning for it. Full mourning, 6 s: it turns black, stops, faces the body and will not strike. Half mourning, the next 6 s: grey, half speed, strikes half as often. Then it is out. Harming a mourner in full mourning ends its mourning at once and it strikes 30% faster for 6 s. The player chooses: walk away through a quiet crowd, or keep fighting and wake it with skills that hit areas.
source: Mourning was worn for set terms that stepped down by grade, full black and then grey half-mourning, and ordinary business stopped while it lasted.
nearest: Pacify and daze effects that break on damage. This one is caused by an important death nearby, steps down in two grades on a clock, and punishes the player for breaking it.

notes.where: Halo Grunts breaking and panicking when their Elite dies, Shadow of Mordor grunts fleeing a dead captain, Total War morale shocks; joined to WoW-style crowd control that breaks on damage. The two timed grades and the pause facing the body are not in those.

Kill the leader and the host stops: the Keystone Army of Ender's Game, the droid army switching off in The Phantom Menace; elephants standing over their dead in nature films; daze and pacify effects that break on damage. Graded, timed mourning that punishes the player for interrupting it is its own.

name: Forfeit
idea: Falls on whatever harms the player, when a skill, vow or pick says so. If the offender was moving when it struck (a charger, a thrown or rolling thing), all of it is forfeit: it changes sides for 6 s, then falls. If it was standing still, only the part that struck is forfeit: it cannot strike for 6 s but still walks and blocks. A ground patch counts as standing and goes dark for 6 s. Forfeit things give experience only if the player lays them.
source: Under the law of deodand a thing that caused a death was forfeit: if it was in motion the whole of it, if at rest only the part that struck.
nearest: Charm and disarm effects. Which of the two happens here is decided by whether the attacker was moving when it hit, so the player can choose how to be struck.

notes.where: Retaliation effects that punish the attacker (Path of Exile 'when hit' curses and blinds, Dota 2 Blade Mail), plus ordinary charm and disarm. I know no game where the attacker being in motion or at rest decides which one it gets.

'If thy right hand offend thee, cut it off', where only the part that offended pays; the medieval trials of animals and objects behind the film The Hour of the Pig; charm and disarm effects in games. Choosing between the two by whether the attacker was moving is in no story I know.

name: Coined
idea: Two coins are laid on a dead thing's eyes. For 5 s it cannot see: it keeps walking on the heading it had, in a straight line, turning only when it bumps a wall, and it strikes whatever it walks into, the other dead included. Any Rung (sound) harm within 4 m tells it where the player is and ends the state early. When the state ends the two coins drop as a pickup; if the player lays it while it is coined, four coins drop.
source: Coins were laid on a corpse's eyes to keep them shut, and were said to be the fare for the ferryman.
nearest: Blind and confuse states. This one fixes the heading instead of scrambling it, is undone by the player's own noise, and pays the player back in coin.

notes.where: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon's Blinker status and NetHack's blinded monsters (lose the target, blunder about and hit their own side), Monster Hunter monsters flailing after a flash; bounty marks such as Dota 2 Bounty Hunter's Track for the coin payout.

Blinded Polyphemus groping after Odysseus; A Quiet Place, where any sound gives you away; Mr Magoo walking straight through trouble; Cadmus' stone that sets the dragon's-teeth warriors on each other; coins on the eyes as Charon's fare. A blindness that fixes the heading and is broken by the player's own noise is its own.

name: Felon
idea: One dead thing is cried as felon for 6 s. Every other dead thing within 6 m of it must turn and strike it instead of the player. If a pursuer lays the felon, that pursuer becomes the felon and the 6 s start again, up to 5 times; if the player lays the felon the cry ends. Things that cannot hear (Mutes, anything Muffled) never join and are never chosen. The player receives the experience and drops of every body the chase leaves.
source: When the hue and cry was raised everyone who heard it had to join the chase, and it was handed on from township to township.
nearest: Enrage and bait effects that turn enemies on one of their own, as in BioShock. This one passes to whoever makes the kill, so it travels through the crowd by itself until the player ends it.

notes.where: Dota 2 Winter Wyvern's Winter's Curse (one enemy is cursed and every ally of it nearby must attack it) and BioShock's Security Bullseye and Enrage; the hand-on to the killer is Halo's Juggernaut rule (kill the juggernaut, become the juggernaut).
notes.mutation: Hand the cry on by place, not by kill: the felon runs, pursuers must stop at each street or parish line and stand idle there while the dead on the far side take up the chase, so the player uses one cry to strip bodies out of the fight in relays along a route.

notes.where: The King of the Wood at Nemi in Frazer's The Golden Bough, 'the priest who slew the slayer, and shall himself be slain': whoever kills the marked one becomes the marked one. Halo's Juggernaut game type runs exactly that chain, everyone hunting whoever holds the mark. Cadmus' stone among the dragon's-teeth men and Shirley Jackson's The Lottery supply the crowd turning on one of its own; tag supplies 'you're it'.
notes.mutation: Hand the cry on by hearing, not by the kill: when a felon falls, the cry passes to the pursuer standing farthest from the player, so the chase always rolls outward through the crowd and away, and the player steers it by where they stand instead of the killer inheriting the mark.

name: Abjured
idea: An abjured dead thing stops fighting, takes up a cross and walks in a straight line to the nearest edge of the district, where it leaves for good and gives nothing. While it keeps to its line the player cannot harm it. If anything moves it more than 2 m off the line (a push, a pull, a body shoving it) it has strayed: it stands lost for 4 s, takes triple harm from everything, and the other dead strike at it. Laying a strayed abjurer gives triple experience.
source: A felon in sanctuary could abjure the realm: he walked barefoot with a wooden cross straight to an assigned port, and if he strayed from the road anyone might kill him.
nearest: Banish and fear effects that remove an enemy for no reward. Here the banishment is a visible straight walk that the player can spoil on purpose to turn it into a triple-value kill.

notes.where: WoW Banish and Turn Undead (enemy untouchable or fleeing for no reward), Diablo III treasure goblins escaping through a portal, tower-defence creeps walking to the exit. Knocking a banished thing off its line to cash it in I have not seen.

'Stay on the path' in Little Red Riding Hood and 'stick to the road' in An American Werewolf in London; routed units walking off the map edge in Total War; banishment effects. Spoiling a protected walk on purpose to turn it into a triple-value kill is its own.

name: Sin-laden
idea: Some dead carry sins, shown as 1 to 9 dark lumps stacked on the back. Each sin gives its carrier 5% more harm and 3% less speed. When a sin-laden thing dies its sins pass to whatever is nearest within 2 m: another dead thing, or the player. The player carries sins on the same terms and sheds them only by leaving through a gate or by letting a Dole-seeker take one pickup per sin. Lay sin-carriers from a distance, or step in on purpose to take the load.
source: A sin-eater took a dead person's sins on himself by eating bread and drinking ale passed over the corpse, and was shunned for what he carried.
nearest: Stacking buffs that jump to a nearby ally on death. This one can jump to the player, is a deliberate trade of speed for harm, and is shed by custom rather than by time.

notes.where: Path of Exile's Soul Eater (stacks gained from deaths nearby) and Headhunter belt (the player takes a dead rare's powers by killing it), WoW raid debuffs that jump to the nearest target on death, Risk of Rain 2 trade-off items such as Stone Flux Pauldron. The carry-it-or-keep-away choice at 2 m is the idea's own.

Christian's burden of sin on his back in The Pilgrim's Progress, shed only at the cross; the sin-eater who takes a corpse's sins on himself (Francine Rivers' The Last Sin Eater, Atwood's 'The Sin Eater'); the demon of Fallen (1998) that jumps to the nearest body when its host dies; Marley's chain. A visible load of harm bought with speed, passed between the dead and the player, is none of these.

name: Named
idea: A thing that has been cried three times is Named until the next toll. Its crier's skills may pick it at any distance and through walls. In return it always knows where its crier is: it ignores hiding and mourning dress and moves 20% faster toward them. The rule cuts both ways. When a dead Crier names the player, every dead thing in the district gains that hold on the player, and the player's skills may pick that Crier from anywhere on the map.
source: The town crier proclaimed a name three times with 'Oyez', after which the person named was held to have had notice wherever they were.
nearest: Marks that reveal a target, and taunts. This is one state with the same rule for both sides: between namer and named, range and hiding stop counting.

notes.where: Dota 2 Bounty Hunter's Track and Bloodseeker's Thirst (a revealed target and speed toward it), Hunter's Mark in D&D and WoW, and Dead by Daylight's Object of Obsession, where killer and survivor see each other. One state binding both sides and cancelling range for skills is the new part.

Say the name three times and it comes for you: Beetlejuice, Bloody Mary in the mirror, Candyman. The Taboo on Voldemort's name in Deathly Hallows, where speaking it lets his followers find the speaker anywhere, is the case of a dead Crier naming the player; true names that give a hold across any distance (Earthsea, Rumpelstiltskin) and the two-way link between Harry and Voldemort give the symmetry.
notes.mutation: Bind the hold to a posted bill rather than a thrice-spoken name: the crier nails a proclamation to the nearest door, range and walls stop counting between crier and named only while both are within sight of that bill, and the named thing goes to tear it down rather than run at the crier, so the bond becomes a fight over a place on the map.

name: Pole, Wick and Stone
idea: Three personal measures. Pole is the character's yardstick: skill reach and area are written in Poles (1 Pole is 1 m plus 1% per point). Wick is their clock: durations are written in Wicks (1 s plus 1% per point). Stone is their weight: harm per blow, and how much unbanked loot they carry before slowing, are written in Stones. Nothing has a minimum. Instead gear is cut to a measure, such as Pole 40: within 5 points of it the item fits and its properties gain 25%.
source: Old measures came from the trades: the pole or perch of land, the inch of candle that timed an auction, the stone of the market weigh-beam.
nearest: Area, duration and damage stats, and attribute requirements on gear. Here the attributes are the units the skill text is written in, and gear rewards matching a value exactly rather than exceeding it.

notes.where: Vampire Survivors' Area, Duration and Might, the three stats every weapon scales by, and likewise Path of Exile area, skill duration and damage; plus ordinary encumbrance. Only gear cut to an exact value has no clear precedent.
notes.mutation: Drop the percent-per-point scaling: fix a character's Pole, Wick and Stone at creation like a body's build and let all growth come from how closely gear, skills and bindings are cut to those three numbers, so the game is tailoring to a measure instead of stacking area, duration and damage.

notes.where: Procrustes' bed and Cinderella's slipper, which serve only the one they fit, and Goldilocks' 'just right'; measures taken from the body, the cubit and the foot; attribute requirements on gear in role-playing games. Attributes as the units the skill text is written in come from no story.

name: Sexton
idea: Digs the graves and rings the bell. The thumb's new verb is to stop: stand still for 2.5 s and the Sexton finishes a grave underfoot, a 2 m pit. The next 6 dead to walk into it drop in and are laid; then it closes. At most 4 graves lie open. The Sexton digs ahead of the crowd and leads it across. Starting skill, Spadeful: every 1.2 s throws grave-earth over the nearest dead within 5 m, harming it and slowing it 30% for 2 s.
source: The sexton dug the parish graves, and a grave is the one place the dead are meant to stay.
nearest: Trap-laying characters, and bonuses for standing still in some horde games. Here standing still is construction time, and what is built is a hole that fills up and closes.

notes.where: Lode Runner, Heiankyo Alien and Space Panic: dig a hole, the pursuers walk into it, it closes over them. Standing still as the price is Brotato's Soldier and stand-still items.
notes.mutation: Put the Sexton in the hole: while digging he is below ground and cannot be struck from the sides, the grave holds one body per second dug, and climbing out takes half a second per body of depth, so every grave is a bet on how deep he dares go before the crowd reaches the lip.

notes.where: The Very Deep Pit that Pooh and Piglet dig for a Heffalump, tiger pits, the spiked pits of zombie fiction; Hamlet's gravedigger and the sexton as stock churchyard furniture; trap-laying classes. Standing still to dig, and leading the crowd across a hole that fills and closes, is its own.

name: Verger
idea: Carries the verge, the rod that clears the way for a procession. While the Verger walks, a wedge 3 m long opens ahead: dead inside it are shouldered 1.5 m to either side and cannot strike for 0.5 s. The thumb drives straight through the thickest crowd instead of round it. The wedge exists only while moving and covers only the front 120 degrees, so stopping or turning back inside a crowd is fatal. Starting skill, The Verge: every 0.9 s raps the two dead nearest the wedge's edges.
source: A verger walked ahead of the procession with a rod of office to clear people and animals out of its way.
nearest: Charge and plough abilities on a cooldown. Here parting the crowd is the class's ordinary walk, and the price is that only the front is covered.

notes.where: Dynasty Warriors horseback riding through crowds, Dead Rising shopping carts and Diablo III's Steed Charge shouldering enemies aside. As a permanent passive walk with a blind rear I have not seen it as a class.

Moses lifting his rod to part the sea (The Ten Commandments), the walls closing on whoever is caught inside; the lictors and mace-bearers who cleared a road; the flying wedge. As a class's ordinary walk that covers only the front, it is its own.

name: Knocker-up
idea: Paid to wake workers by tapping bedroom windows with a long pole. When the Knocker-up passes within 4 m of a house window, the pole taps it: the house wakes for 10 s and the living inside pelt the street, harming all dead within 4 m of that wall each second. A house cannot be woken again for 20 s. The thumb hugs the walls and plans a round of house-fronts. Starting skill, Rap: strikes one dead between 1.5 and 4.5 m away, never nearer.
source: Knockers-up walked a round before dawn tapping clients' upper windows with a long pole and did not leave until the sleeper showed at the glass.
nearest: Characters who switch on turrets or shrines by passing them. Here the turrets are the district's own houses, so the class's power lies in a route along walls.

notes.where: Call of Duty Zombies wall traps and Orcs Must Die! environmental traps (fixed map hazards the player sets off, each on a cooldown); minimum-range attacks like the Clash Royale Mortar's blind spot. Turrets that are the houses themselves, set off by walking a round, are the idea's own.

Townsfolk pelting attackers from upper windows: Quasimodo pouring molten lead from Notre-Dame, the 'gardyloo' of old Edinburgh, the French castle flinging a cow in Monty Python and the Holy Grail; shrines and turrets switched on by passing in games. The knocker-up's round as a route of turrets is in no story.

name: Ferryman
idea: Takes fares. One quiet dead at a time waits at a landing stair holding up a coin. Walk through it and it climbs on the Ferryman's back: 15% slower while loaded. Carry it to the opposite stair, marked by a lamp, and it steps off for good, paying experience equal to 10 kills and one coin. Below half life the fare slips off. The thumb plays there-and-back crossings through the horde. Starting skill, Sweep: every 1.5 s the oar swings a 3 m half-circle behind the direction of travel.
source: Ferrymen carried passengers between named stairs for a fixed fare, and the coins on a corpse's eyes were called the fare for the last crossing.
nearest: Delivery and escort objectives, and couriers who walk loads across hostile ground as in Death Stranding. Here it is one class's way of levelling inside a horde fight, and the passenger is one of the dead, paid off instead of killed.

notes.where: Crazy Taxi fares (pick up, deliver to a marked stop, get paid), capture-the-flag carriers slowed while they hold it, Spiritfarer and Death Stranding for ferrying the dead. As one class's main source of experience inside a horde it is new to me.

Charon, who carries the dead across for the coin they hold (Aeneid VI, Percy Jackson), and Spiritfarer, where the player takes over his job and ferries spirits to their rest; Grim Fandango's Manny selling the dead their passage. The passenger who climbs onto your back and weighs you down is St Christopher's child and Sinbad's Old Man of the Sea.
notes.mutation: Reckon fares like a Thames waterman's rather than Charon's: each waiting dead names a landing by the number on its token and pays one coin and one kill's experience per stair passed on the way, so the Ferryman chooses short hops or long crossings over a map of numbered stairs instead of shuttling the dead to rest between two fixed banks.

name: Toll-keeper
idea: Keeps the bar at bridge and gate. One button plants the toll-post where the keeper stands. A bar then runs from post to keeper, up to 7 m long, and moves as the keeper moves. Every dead thing the bar passes over pays toll: harm equal to one blow, doubled each time the same thing pays again within 10 s. Because the dead chase the keeper, circling the post sweeps the bar through them like a clock hand. Starting skill: the bar itself.
source: A turnpike was a bar across the road beside the toll-house, swung aside for those who paid, and the charge was levied again at every passing.
nearest: Tether and beam-between-two-points weapons in arcade shooters. Here one end is fixed by the player, the charge doubles per crossing, and the play pattern is an orbit round a post.

notes.where: Lines that hurt what crosses them (Dota 2 Io's Tether, Geometry Wars gates, co-op laser tethers), rotating bars like Mario's fire bars, and Vampire Survivors' Phieraggi sweeping beams like clock hands. The player as the free end of the bar, with the charge doubling per crossing, is its own.

The swinging blade of Poe's 'The Pit and the Pendulum', the tilting quintain, the sweeper arm of Wipeout; the troll who takes toll at the bridge in The Three Billy Goats Gruff; tethered beams in arcade shooters. A bar from a planted post to the keeper, charging double on repeat passes, is its own.

name: Glazier
idea: Carries a leaded panel of coloured glass on a pole. Each district has one fixed great light: a rose window, a beacon, a low moon. The panel throws a coloured patch on the ground, 3 m wide, lying 2 to 5 m from the Glazier on the side away from that light. Only dead standing in the patch are harmed, 4 times a second. The thumb keeps the light at its back and the crowd down-light; where a building blocks the light, the patch fails. Starting skill: the patch.
source: Leaded glass is small coloured panes held in lead cames, and what it does is throw a patch of coloured light on the floor away from the window.
nearest: Fixed-offset damage zones and flashlight cones. Here the direction of the offset belongs to the district, not the character, so the class plays differently on every map and uses the game's real light.

notes.where: Weapons whose direction is fixed in the world rather than aimed (vertical shooters, Vampire Survivors' Whip and Axe) and Zelda's Mirror Shield, where a fixed light and where you stand decide what the light hits. A per-map light setting the offset, with shadowing by buildings, I have not seen.

The burning glass every child has turned on ants, Archimedes' mirrors against the Roman fleet, the Staff of Ra in Raiders of the Lost Ark throwing a spot of sunlight on the map-room floor; vampires burned by light through a window. Harm placed by the district's one light, on the far side of the bearer, is its own.

name: Organ-blower
idea: Pumps the organ's bellows. Skills never cast while the Blower moves. Walking fills the wind-chest, 1 unit per metre, up to 30; a weight on a string above the figure shows how full it is. Standing still lets the wind out: all skills cast at 3 times their rate, spending 10 units a second, and stop when the chest is empty. The thumb alternates a 30 m run with a 3 s stand. Starting skill, Stop: a pipe note harming a cone 6 m long.
source: An organ made no sound unless a blower pumped its bellows by hand, and a tell-tale weight showed how much wind was left.
nearest: Charge-by-moving items and stand-to-fire characters. Here movement is the only fuel and standing the only trigger, with the gauge hung above the figure.

notes.where: Brotato's Soldier (cannot attack while moving, stronger standing still) and League of Legends Energized items such as Statikk Shiv (charge built by distance walked, spent on the attack). The two joined so that walking is the only fuel I cannot name.
The self-winding watch, wound by its wearer's walking; Aeolus' bag of winds let out all at once; charge-by-moving items and stand-to-fire characters in games. No story has it as a rule.

name: Fossor (from Sexton)
idea: Every grave the Sexton digs now throws up a spoil bank: a wall of earth 3 m long on the far side of the grave from where the Sexton walked in. The dead cannot cross a bank and are turned round its ends, toward the pit. A bank lasts until its grave is full; then the earth goes back in and both vanish. With 4 graves open the Sexton has 4 walls to place, and each stop is chosen for the pen it completes as much as for the pit.
source: Digging a grave throws up a heap of spoil beside it, which stays there until the grave is filled in.
nearest: Wall-placing abilities and tower-defence mazing. These walls come only as the by-product of the class's own traps and are removed when the traps succeed.

notes.where: Wall skills (Dota 2 Earthshaker's Fissure, Path of Exile Frost Wall, Diablo II Bone Wall) and tower-defence mazing as in Desktop Tower Defense. Walls that exist only as spoil from the class's own traps and vanish when the trap fills are new to me.

The fortified village of Seven Samurai that lets the bandits in only where the samurai want them; buffalo-jump drive lanes; tower-defence mazing. Walls that are the spoil of the class's own graves and vanish when the graves fill are its own.

name: Sin-eater (from Sexton)
idea: A new rule about bodies. Standing on a fallen body for 0.5 s eats its sin: that body is laid for good whatever it was owed, and gives double experience. Each body eaten adds 1 Sin to the Sin-eater: 1% more harm dealt and 0.5% less speed, without limit. Sin is shed only by leaving through a gate, where each point becomes 1 Echo. The Sin-eater grows stronger and slower through a vigil until staying is no longer possible, and must judge which body is the last worth eating.
source: The sin-eater was paid to eat bread and drink ale over a corpse, taking its sins so that it would lie quiet, and pledged his own soul for it.
nearest: Stacking on-kill buffs. This one is taken body by body on purpose, costs speed with no ceiling, and turns into permanent currency only by leaving alive.

notes.where: WoW's Cannibalize (stand on a corpse to consume it), Dota 2 Pudge's Flesh Heap and League of Legends Cho'Gath's Feast (permanent stacks per kill), and extraction-game encumbrance, where what you carry slows you until you get out. Unlimited speed loss cashed only at the gate is the own part.

The sin-eater of Welsh border folklore, retold in Francine Rivers' The Last Sin Eater, the film The Order (2003) and Atwood's 'The Sin Eater': eating over the corpse lets it rest and the eater carries the sin. Geist: The Sin-Eaters makes the name a player role; corpse-consuming stacks exist in Diablo and Path of Exile. Growing stronger and slower without limit until the vigil has to end is in none of them.

name: Beadle of the Procession (from Verger)
idea: Dead parted by the Verger's wedge no longer close in behind. For 5 s they fall into two files 1.5 m apart and follow the Verger's exact path at the Verger's pace, unable to strike; the files hold up to 40. If the Verger stops, or turns more than 90 degrees within a second, the files break: everyone in them strikes at once and moves 30% faster for 3 s. A surrounding crowd becomes a column, and anything that harms along a line has something to aim down.
source: The beadle marshalled the parish procession into order behind the verger and kept it in file.
nearest: Kiting a train of enemies, which happens by accident in most horde games. Here the column is a state with rules, a size, and a penalty for breaking it.

notes.where: MMO trains and kiting (EverQuest), Snake-style followers that retrace the leader's exact path (Nimble Quest), Pikmin files. A pacified two-file column with a capacity and a break penalty is not in those.

The Pied Piper of Hamelin, a column that falls in behind its leader, follows helplessly and is led to its end in the Weser; Death leading the dancers in a line over the hill at the close of The Seventh Seal; the danse macabre. The rule that turning back breaks it is Orpheus and Lot's wife.
notes.mutation: Have the parted dead stand rather than follow: they fall into two still files facing inward along the route the Verger has just walked, unable to strike for 5 s, and both files strike inward at once if the Verger turns back into the lane, so the crowd becomes a corridor laid behind the player to aim along, not a train led like the Piper's rats.

name: Curfew-warden (from Knocker-up)
idea: A house that is awake can be covered. Passing a woken house a second time while it is still awake raps it shut: its windows go dark and every dead thing within 4 m of that wall, up to 12, lies down asleep where it stands. Sleepers cannot be harmed, give nothing and block nothing. All of them wake together at the next toll. The warden uses the street to put part of the horde off until the bell, and must then be somewhere else when it rings.
source: At the curfew bell every household had to cover its fire and put out its lights for the night.
nearest: Sleep effects that break on damage. These sleepers cannot be touched at all and wake on the district's bell, so the effect is a loan against the next toll.

notes.where: StarCraft Arbiter's Stasis Field and WoW Banish (enemies frozen, untouchable and out of the fight for a term). Setting it off from map houses and ending it on the shared bell is the idea's own.

Sleeping Beauty's castle, everyone asleep where they stood until the spell ends; 'the curfew tolls the knell of parting day' in Gray's Elegy; sleep effects that break on damage. Sleepers that cannot be touched and wake on the district bell are its own.

name: The Mute (from Knocker-up)
idea: The Knocker-up falls silent. The dead find the living by sound: any dead thing more than 6 m from the Mute no longer knows where the Mute is, and walks instead to the loudest thing it can hear, which is the nearest woken house. They crowd under the windows that are pelting them. The Mute's own Rap makes no sound. The class stops being chased and starts placing the horde, house by house; anything within 6 m still sees it and gives chase.
source: Hired mutes stood silent at the door of a house of death, and the knocker-up's whole trade was deciding who heard what.
nearest: Stealth with noise-maker decoys. Here the decoys are the houses the class already wakes, and the whole horde, not a guard or two, goes to them.

notes.where: Left 4 Dead's pipe bomb and Days Gone's attractors: the whole horde leaves the player and crowds round a noisy lure that then kills it; The Last of Us bottles and Clickers for sound-led enemies.
notes.mutation: Remove the lure: dead that cannot hear the Mute follow the nearest dead thing that can still see him, so the horde becomes chains led by the few inside 6 m and the Mute steers the whole crowd by choosing which few are allowed to see him.

notes.where: A Quiet Place, where the creatures hunt only by sound and the family draws them off with fireworks; the thumpers of Dune that call the worm away from whoever walks without rhythm; the noise-led hordes of World War Z and The Walking Dead; Tremors. A whole horde that loses the silent one and goes to the loudest thing is that premise.
notes.mutation: Let the dead gather to a house of mourning instead of to noise: each door the Mute stands at for 1 s is draped, and every dead thing beyond 6 m walks to the nearest draped door and waits there for the body to be brought out, so the class places the horde by marking houses of death, woken or not, rather than by luring it with sound.

name: Dredgerman (from Ferryman)
idea: The Ferryman may now carry a body instead of a fare. Walking over the body of an elite loads it: 25% slower. Either stair will take it. The near stair, on this bank, pays a finding fee of 5 coin. The far stair, across the district, pays three times as much, 15 coin, and adds one property to the best item that body drops. While a body is carried, the dead move 10% faster, drawn to it. Every elite laid sets the same question: near bank or far.
source: Thames dredgermen were paid a reward for each drowned body they brought in, and one bank of the river paid about three times what the other did.
nearest: Carry-the-objective modes, and carrying a corpse to be disposed of in Death Stranding. The body here is a product of ordinary play, and the same delivery has a cheap near price and a dear far one.

notes.where: Sea of Thieves loot hauling, where carrying treasure further before selling raises both the price and the risk, Hunt: Showdown bounty carriers who draw attention, Deep Rock Galactic heavy objects carried to the drop-off. Near-bank and far-bank prices on an ordinary elite's corpse are its own.

Gaffer Hexam and Rogue Riderhood fishing drowned bodies out of the Thames for what they bring in Dickens' Our Mutual Friend; the bounty hunter hauling in a corpse (For a Few Dollars More, The Mandalorian); the carried bodies of Death Stranding. The cheap near bank against the dear far bank is its own.

name: Burgess of the Bar (from Toll-keeper)
idea: A dead thing that pays at the Toll-keeper's bar three times and is still standing is made quit of toll: free of the city. It stops fighting, walks to the nearest gate and leaves, and at the gate pays 3 coin into what the keeper carries. Freed dead give no experience. The bar now has two uses, and the keeper chooses by how hard it hits: strong enough to lay the crowd for experience, or light enough that the crowd survives three payings and walks out as coin.
source: A burgess who had paid his dues was quit of toll and passed every bar in the realm free.
nearest: Effects that turn kills into gold instead of experience. Here the conversion needs the enemy to survive three hits, so the player tunes a weapon to be weak on purpose.

notes.where: Undertale's spare (gold but no experience, and some monsters must be worn down first), Pokemon's False Swipe and Monster Hunter captures, where you hold back the killing blow for a different reward.
notes.mutation: Do not let the freed dead leave: a burgess stays in the district, harmless and unharmable, and pays 1 coin into the keeper's purse at every toll it is still standing, but it still takes up room and blocks, so the keeper is choosing how much of the street to fill with paying tenants.

notes.where: Undertale, where a spared monster pays gold and no experience; weakening without fainting in order to catch, in Pokemon; spared foes who repay, from The Lion and the Mouse to the grateful dead of folk tale. Tuning the bar weak so that the crowd survives three payings is its own.

name: Clerk of the Bills (from Toll-keeper)
idea: At each toll the Clerk publishes a Bill: a count of every kind of dead laid since the last toll. The kind with the highest count is struck from the roll: none of that kind rise during the next interval. The numbers must still be made up, so every other kind rises 15% more. The Bill is shown as it fills. By steering toward one kind and leaving another alone, the player chooses which part of the horde the district will be missing for the next 75 s.
source: Parish clerks compiled the weekly Bills of Mortality from the searchers' reports: a count of the dead under each cause.
nearest: Banishing an enemy type from the pool through a menu. Here the choice is made by what the player actually lays most, is renewed at every toll, and is paid for in more of the rest.

notes.where: Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII, where a species hunted enough goes extinct, Vampire Survivors' Banish for striking an entry from a pool, and spawn directors that react to play (Left 4 Dead). A per-interval strike of the most-killed kind, paid for in more of the rest, I have not seen.

The weekly Bills of Mortality in Defoe's A Journal of the Plague Year; the Hydra, where every one cut down is made up by more; banishing an enemy type from the pool in games. Banishment chosen by what is laid most, renewed at every toll, is in no story.

name: Rose-wright (from Glazier)
idea: The second button plants the Glazier's panel in the ground, where it stands until the next toll and keeps throwing its patch from the district's fixed light; a new panel is carried at once. Up to 3 stand at a time. Planted patches harm at half force, but where patches overlap their harm adds, and a patch that falls on another panel passes through it and is thrown a second time, further on. The Rose-wright builds a window across a street and fights in the pool of colour behind it.
source: A rose window is many small panels set in one frame, each throwing its own colour onto the same floor.
nearest: Placed turrets. These have no aim of their own: where they act is fixed by the map's one light, so placing them is geometry rather than coverage.

notes.where: Beam-relay placement in The Talos Principle, Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 Prism Towers feeding one another, Zelda mirror puzzles. As combat turrets whose throw is set by the map's one light it is new to me.

Sunlight passed from mirror to mirror down a tomb in adventure films, the Staff of Ra in Raiders of the Lost Ark, the light-bending puzzles of Zelda and Tomb Raider; placed turrets. Panels whose patch is fixed by the map's one light and thrown on through one another are their own.

name: Sale by Candle
idea: Every 12 s an inch of candle is set down at the thickest group within 8 m and burns for 4 to 7 s. While it burns, every blow the player lands on dead within 4 m of it is a bid: its harm is also added to a pot. When the flame dies the whole pot falls on the one dead thing the player struck last. The flame flares for 0.5 s before it dies; the player uses that warning to step beside the target that ought to win.
source: In a sale by candle the last bid before the flame went out took the lot, and Pepys noted that the wick flares just before it dies.
nearest: Abilities that store damage and release it on one marked target. Here the store is filled by fighting a crowd, the winner is whoever was struck last, and the end is random with a short tell.

notes.where: Stored-damage release such as League of Legends Zed's Death Mark and Path of Exile Explosive Arrow, and hidden-timer games like musical chairs and Mario Party's bomb passing. A pot filled from a crowd and awarded to whoever was struck last at an uncertain moment is its own.

Hot potato and musical chairs, where whoever holds it when the music stops takes it all; Pepys' candle auctions; stored-damage skills released on one target. A pot filled by fighting a crowd and dropped on the last one struck is its own.

name: Steelyard
idea: Every 9 s the two dead nearest the player are hung on the weigh-beam for 1 s, shown as a bar joining them. The one with more remaining life loses the difference, up to 30% of its full life; the lighter one is unharmed. The skill does nothing to two fresh bodies and most when one is nearly finished and the other is a brute, so the player herds a wounded straggler alongside the thing they want cut down, and keeps both closer than anything else.
source: Market toll was charged by weight on the town's public weigh-beam, where the two sides had to be brought level.
nearest: Health-equalising spells in turn-based games. Here it is automatic, takes only the nearest pair, and the player's part is arranging who that pair is.

notes.where: Health-levelling moves: Pokemon's Pain Split, Dota 2 Terrorblade's Sunder, Hearthstone's Equality. Those involve the caster or the whole board; an automatic levelling of the nearest pair, which the player arranges by herding, is not in them.

The weighing of the heart against Maat's feather in the Book of the Dead, Zeus' golden scales sinking Hector's fate in Iliad XXII, 'weighed in the balances and found wanting' (Daniel 5); Pain Split in Pokemon, which evens two health bars. Automatic, nearest pair only, and herded by the player, it is its own.

name: Resting Stones
idea: Every 10 s a resting stone is set where the player stands; only the newest two remain. The straight line between them is a corpse road, up to 14 m long. Dead that come within 2 m of the road are taken onto it and must walk along it to the newer stone, feet first, unable to turn or strike, then stand there 1 s before they are free. The player lays the road so that it carries the crowd away, or through ground the other skills have prepared.
source: The dead were carried to the mother church along fixed corpse roads, feet first and never turning back, the bier set down only at resting stones.
nearest: Conveyor lanes in tower defence, and skills that pull enemies to a point. Here the lane is drawn by where the player last stood twice, and it only moves bodies along it.

notes.where: League of Legends Bard's Magical Journey (a one-way corridor that carries friend and foe), Orcs Must Die! push traps and tower-defence conveyor lanes, vacuum pulls like Dota 2 Dark Seer's. A lane drawn by the player's own last two standing points is new to me.

Corpse roads and spirit paths of folklore, the belief that spirits can travel only in straight lines (hence the zig-zag bridges of Chinese gardens), Irish fairy paths; the Roman soldiers seen marching their old road through the cellar of York's Treasurer's House; conveyor lanes in tower defence. A road drawn between the player's last two stops is its own.

name: Month's Mind
idea: Every dead thing the player lays is remembered. Exactly 30 s after it fell, one bell-note sounds at the spot where it died, harming everything within 3 m for 40% of what that body's full life was. The newest 40 deaths are kept. A faint ring on the ground marks each spot and closes as its time nears. The player learns to bring the crowd back, half a minute later, across the ground where the last fight was thickest.
source: A month's mind was a mass said for a dead person one month after the death: a remembrance owed at a fixed, known time.
nearest: Delayed explosions and time bombs. These are placed by the kills themselves, come due on a fixed half-minute, and scale with what died there, which sets the player a lap time.

notes.where: Diablo II's Corpse Explosion and Path of Exile's Detonate Dead: a blast at the place a body fell, sized by that body's full life; Risk of Rain 2 on-kill explosions. Only the fixed 30 s delay is added.
notes.mutation: Replace the blast with a reckoning: when the note sounds it lays outright any dead standing on the spot whose remaining life is less than the remembered body's full life and does nothing to anything bigger, so the lap is about bringing the right-sized dead back over the right-sized graves.

notes.where: The ghost that re-enacts its death at the same spot on its anniversary, the residual haunting of Nigel Kneale's The Stone Tape; Corpse Explosion in Diablo II, scaled by the corpse's full life; delayed blasts. Coming due at the death spot on a fixed half-minute, as a lap time, is its own.

name: Rap at the Grave
idea: The graves from which the next toll's dead will rise are visible as mounds during the 75 s before. Every 5 s the skill raps the nearest unopened mound within 8 m. Its occupant rises at once with 40% life and stands unready for 2 s; left alone it would rise at the toll with full life and that toll's added danger. A rapped body gives full experience. The player spends the quiet seconds touring the mounds to thin the wave before the bell brings it.
source: The knocker-up's trade was waking sleepers before the bell did, at an hour chosen in advance.
nearest: Calling the next wave early for a bonus in tower defence. Here it is done body by body, by walking to each grave, and what comes up early comes up weak.

notes.where: Calling the next wave early for a bonus in Kingdom Rush, and Plants vs. Zombies graves that will throw up zombies in the final wave unless a Grave Buster deals with them first; killing eggs before they hatch. Waking them one by one, early and weak, by walking the mounds is its own.

Buffy the Vampire Slayer's cemetery patrol, waiting at a fresh grave to stake the fledgling as it claws out weak and dazed; Van Helsing in Lucy's tomb and the daylight round of the resting places in Dracula and 'Salem's Lot, dispatching the dead before they rise at full strength; calling the next wave early in tower defence.
notes.mutation: Make the rap a booking, not an early kill: a rapped mound's occupant rises at full life exactly 20 s later instead of at the toll, and pays double experience only if the player is within 8 m to see it up, as the knocker-up waited for the sleeper at the glass, so the quiet seconds are spent drawing up a timetable of risings and keeping it.

name: Split Tally
idea: Every 6 s the skill cuts a tally against the 8 dead nearest the player; each carries its half, shown as a pale stick on its chest, for 10 s. Every point of harm the player deals to such a body is also notched on the stick. When the player passes within 1.5 m of it, the two halves are fitted and the whole notched sum is dealt again at once. A half nobody fits lapses unpaid. Wound from far off, then brush past.
source: A debt was notched on a stick that was then split lengthwise; creditor and debtor each kept half, and the debt was proved when the halves were fitted together.
nearest: Mark-and-detonate skills. Here the trigger is physical nearness, so collecting is a risk taken with the thumb, and the amount is exactly what was notched.

notes.where: League of Legends Zed's Death Mark and Kalista's Rend: a mark that builds with the harm you do to its bearer and deals it again on a trigger; Katarina's daggers for walking to the spot to cash in.
notes.mutation: Split each tally between two of the dead instead of between the dead and the player: the notched sum is paid to both only when the two carriers are brought within 1.5 m of each other, so the player wounds from afar and then herds two particular bodies together.

notes.where: The broken token of ballad and romance, lovers' halves of a ring or coin that prove each other when fitted, and the Greek symbolon; mark-and-detonate skills in games. Collecting by brushing past the marked body is its own.

name: Tellers
idea: Every 6 s the hand-bell tells the nearest dead thing within 8 m: three strokes if it is small, six if middling, nine if large, a quarter-second apart. Each stroke harms it and everything within 2 m of it. If it falls before its count is finished, the strokes left over are told on its nearest neighbour and count double. The player gets most from it by standing nearest to something large that is already close to falling, in the middle of a crowd.
source: The death knell began with tellers, three times three strokes for a man, three times two for a woman, three for a child, so that hearers could count who had died.
nearest: Burst attacks that move to a new target when the first dies. Here the length of the burst is read off the size of the victim, and unspent strokes pass on at double weight.

notes.where: Excess carrying over to the next body as in Magic: The Gathering's trample, retargeting bursts like D&D Magic Missile and WoW Arcane Missiles, chain lightning. A burst whose length is read off the victim's size, with leftovers doubled, I cannot place.

Dorothy L. Sayers' The Nine Tailors, built on the tellers of the knell ('nine tailors make a man') and ending with a man killed by the bells; Donne's 'for whom the bell tolls'; overkill that carries on to the next target in games. A burst whose length is read off the victim's size is its own.

name: Lamp and Long Shadow
idea: Every 8 s the skill lights the nearest street-lamp within 8 m for 12 s. A lit lamp makes every dead thing within 9 m of it throw a real cast shadow on the ground, pointing away from the lamp and as long as the thing's distance from it. For the player's skills that shadow counts as part of the body: whatever strikes the shadow strikes its owner. The player fights with a lamp between themselves and the crowd, so the shadows reach toward them.
source: Lamplighters walked a fixed round lighting each street-lamp with a long pole, and a low lamp makes every figure throw a long shadow behind it.
nearest: Folk tales of pinning someone by their shadow, and enlarged hit areas on marked enemies. Here the enlargement is the visible shadow drawn by the game's real light, so its direction and length are read straight off the screen.

notes.where: Lost in Shadow and Contrast, where shadows thrown by movable lights are the things you act on, and Naruto's shadow-bind in the fighting games. Real cast shadows as extra hit area for automatic skills I have not seen.

The belief Frazer records in The Golden Bough that to strike, stab or tread on a man's shadow wounds the man; Peter Pan's shadow, caught and sewn back on; Shikamaru's shadow techniques in Naruto; kage-fumi, shadow tag. A real lamp-cast shadow used as an extended body for the player's skills is its own.

name: Founder's Pit
idea: Every 20 s a casting pit 2 m across is dug where the player stands and stays open 12 s. Each dead thing that falls within 5 m of it pours into the mould, so the player must hold that ground. When the 12 s are up the bell is struck once. With 8 or more poured it rings: harm to everything within 2 m plus 0.3 m per body, equal to a quarter of the summed full life of the bodies poured. With fewer it cracks and does nothing.
source: Great bells were cast in a pit dug beside the tower they were meant for, and a short pour made a cracked bell fit only to be broken up.
nearest: Totems charged by nearby kills. This one is all or nothing at a known count, and its size is the bodies themselves.

notes.where: Kill-charged effects such as Path of Exile Vaal skills and Ritual circles, Risk of Rain 2's hold-the-zone teleporter, and corpse-life scaling from Diablo's Corpse Explosion. The all-or-nothing count of eight is its own.

Lafcadio Hearn's 'The Soul of the Great Bell': the casting fails until the founder's daughter leaps into the metal, and then the bell rings; the Emille Bell legend of a child poured into King Seongdeok's bell; the bell cast in a pit in Tarkovsky's Andrei Rublev, where everything hangs on whether it rings or cracks; builder's-sacrifice legends such as Master Manole. A bell that rings only with enough of the dead poured in is that story.
notes.mutation: Make the crack a matter of tempo, not of how many die: metal that stops flowing sets in a cold shut, so the bell rings only if bodies keep falling within 5 m with no gap over 1.5 s from first to last, and the ring grows with the length of the unbroken pour, so the player must keep the killing steady rather than merely plentiful.

name: Ledger Stones
idea: Every 4 s a ledger stone, 2 m by 1 m, is laid flat on the spot where the last dead thing fell, and stays for the whole vigil, up to 60 stones. The dead walk 25% slower on a ledger; the player walks 15% faster. Where 6 or more stones touch they make a floor: nothing can rise up through a floor, and a body that falls on one never stands again. The player paves a home ground by choosing where the killing is done.
source: Ledger stones are the inscribed slabs a mason sets flat in a church floor over graves, until the whole floor is paved with them.
nearest: Slowing ground effects. These are permanent, are placed by where kills happen, and join into a floor that denies rising, so the player is building territory.

notes.where: Splatoon ink and StarCraft Zerg creep (your ground speeds you and slows them), and Minecraft players paving with slabs so nothing can spawn there. Permanent tiles laid where kills fall, joining into a floor that seals graves, I have not seen as a skill.

Hallowed ground the dead cannot rise from: the Everlasting Rest of the Dungeons & Dragons Hallow spell, the holy ground of vampire fiction and Highlander; church floors paved with ledger stones; slowing ground effects. Territory laid down by where the kills fall is its own.

name: Hatchment
idea: Every 14 s a lozenge 7 m across is laid on the ground at the player's feet for 8 s, split down its length into a black half and a white half. Dead standing on black take 50% more harm; dead standing on white deal 50% less. The same binds the player: on black the player takes 50% more, on white deals 50% less. The split runs along the direction the player was walking when it was laid, so the thumb sets the board and then picks a side.
source: A hatchment showed the dead person's arms on a lozenge whose ground was black behind the dead spouse's half and white behind the survivor's.
nearest: Buff and debuff zones. This is one zone with two opposite halves whose rule binds the player as well, so the question is always who is standing where.

notes.where: Guild Wars nature rituals, whose rule binds friend and foe alike, and Archon's light and dark squares. One placed zone with two opposite halves that bind the caster too is its own arrangement.
The chessboard of Through the Looking-Glass and the two halves of the yin-yang; buff and debuff zones in games. One lozenge whose halves bind both sides, aligned by the player's heading, is its own.

name: Dexter and Sinister
idea: The skill is split down the line the player is walking. Whatever it strikes on the player's right hand (dexter) takes 70% more harm; whatever it strikes on the left (sinister) takes 70% less. The split turns with the thumb, lagging 0.3 s, and holds its last line when the player stands still. Cost: half the skill's field is nearly dead, so the player must keep steering to put the crowd on the right, and a skill that only acts straight ahead gains nothing.
source: On a hatchment the dexter half stood for the husband and the sinister for the wife, and the black half showed which of them was dead.
nearest: Backstab and flank bonuses tied to the enemy's facing. This is tied to the player's own heading and to left and right, which I have not seen used.

notes.where: Broadside combat in Sid Meier's Pirates! and Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, where harm depends on having the target on your beam and you steer to put it there; the right-hand peek advantage of third-person shooters. A strong right and a dead left on an ordinary skill I have not seen.

The sheep set on the right hand and the goats on the left in Matthew 25, the sinister left of superstition; flank and backstab bonuses in games. A bonus by the player's own right and left is nothing I can place.

name: Easting
idea: Blows from this skill that travel westward, pushing the dead back down onto their backs, deal double harm; blows that travel eastward deal half; north and south are unchanged, with a smooth scale between. Against risen clergy, who were buried the other way round, the rule is reversed. Cost: the skill is worth having only while the player keeps to the east of what it is aimed at. Every district's compass is fixed and can be read from which way its gravestones face.
source: Christians were buried with feet to the east so as to rise facing east, and by custom priests were laid the opposite way, to rise facing their flock.
nearest: none known; directional bonuses in games are relative to the target's facing, not to the compass of the map.

notes.where: Only distant things: wind in Worms and Scorched Earth (a map-wide direction that helps shots one way and hinders them the other), attacking out of the sun in flight sims, Animal Crossing's feng shui by compass side of the room. No game I know scales a blow by the compass direction it travels.

Burial with the feet to the east so that the dead rise facing the Second Coming, with priests laid the other way, as folk custom; the fixed wind that helps or hinders every shot in Worms; facing-based backstab bonuses. Harm by the map's compass is in no story.

name: Foil
idea: The skill keeps only half its harm, the stock. The other half is left on the target as a foil, shown as a notch, for 8 s. When a different skill of the same character next strikes that target, the halves fit: the foil is paid at double, so the pair together deal 150% of the first skill's harm. Striking again with the same skill only renews the foil. Cost: alone the skill does half its harm; it needs a partner skill that reaches the same bodies within 8 s.
source: One half of a split tally was worth nothing by itself; stock and foil proved the debt only when the two were fitted.
nearest: Supports that reward alternating two damage types. This pairs two particular skills on the same body, and a half that is never fitted is simply lost.

notes.where: Primer and detonator combos in Mass Effect 3 and Dragon Age: Inquisition, Genshin Impact reactions, Guild Wars 2 fields and finishers, Path of Exile's Trinity Support: one skill sets a state and a different skill cashes it for a bonus.
notes.mutation: Make it a matter of timing rather than sequence: the modifier is cut in two and socketed into two skills, and the tally pays only when both strike the same body within a quarter-second of each other, so the player tunes two self-casting rhythms until they coincide.

notes.where: Mass Effect's prime-and-detonate combos, where one power sets a state and a different power sets it off for extra harm; elemental combos in Divinity: Original Sin; the split token of romance. Holding back half of the first skill's own harm is its own detail.

name: Lych-wait
idea: The skill no longer casts the moment it is ready. It waits, as the bier waits under the lychgate for the priest, until at least 5 dead stand inside the place it would strike, or until 4 s have passed. For every full second it waited, its harm rises 20%. Cost: against a thin or scattered crowd the skill casts late and seldom. The player makes it work by drawing the dead into a knot and holding them there until it lets go.
source: At the lychgate the bearers set the bier down under the roof and waited for the priest to come out and meet it before going further.
nearest: Charge-up supports. Here the skill decides for itself when the shot is worth taking, by a rule the player can see and feed.

notes.where: Dragon Age: Origins tactics ('enemy clustered with at least three') and Final Fantasy XII Gambits for conditional casting, and Path of Exile's Unleash Support, which stores power while a spell is held back. A self-casting skill that waits for a knot and is paid per second of waiting is a fair new joining.
'Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes' at Bunker Hill; the bier waiting under the lychgate; charge-up supports in games. A skill that waits for a crowd by a visible count is its own.

name: Passes Free
idea: The first dead thing the skill would strike is let through untouched. The skill passes on and strikes the next thing along its path, or the next nearest to its centre, and that blow deals 60% more. If there is no second target the cast is wasted. Cost: the skill can never harm the thing nearest the player, so it must be paired with something that can. It is for reaching the keeper standing behind its crowd.
source: Some travellers passed the toll-bar free: funerals, the mail, and burgesses whose town was quit of toll.
nearest: Piercing shots that carry on after the first hit. This one skips the first body entirely, which reverses what the skill is good against.

notes.where: League of Legends Miss Fortune's Double Up (the body behind takes the heavier hit), Darkest Dungeon attacks that can only reach the back ranks, Path of Exile Far Shot and Pierce. A modifier that lets the first body go wholly untouched I have not seen.

The troll in The Three Billy Goats Gruff, letting the first goat over to wait for the bigger one behind; the Passover, the destroyer passing over the marked door to strike the next; piercing shots in games. Skipping the nearest to strike the next one harder is its own.

name: Narrowing Border
idea: At each toll the skill's area starts 80% wider than normal and its harm 40% lower. With every cast after that, the area shrinks by a tenth of normal and the harm rises by a tenth, until the area is at 50% and the harm at 190%; the next toll sets it wide again. Cost: the skill is never one thing for long: wide and weak when the toll's crowd arrives, narrow and heavy once only its strong ones are left.
source: Mourning stationery carried a black border that was made narrower at each stage of the mourning term.
nearest: Ramping buffs that reset on a timer. Here size is traded for weight step by step, and the reset is the district bell.

notes.where: Path of Exile's Intensify Support: each successive cast shrinks the area and raises the area damage up to a cap, then resets; Concentrated Effect and Increased Area are the static versions of the same trade.
notes.mutation: Let the crowd, not the cast count, set the border: the skill's area is as wide as the share of the current toll's wave still standing and its harm rises as that share falls, so the player can keep it wide by sparing stragglers or narrow it by clearing them.

notes.where: The narrowing black border of Victorian mourning paper itself; ramp-and-reset buffs in action games. Nothing in stories that I can place.

name: Indenture
idea: The cast is cut in two along a wavy line. The halves leave the player 40 degrees apart, curve, and meet again at exactly 7 m. Along their separate paths each half deals 50% of the skill's harm; at the meeting point, where the cut edges fit, they deal 300% in a circle 1.5 m across. Cost: the skill is weak at every distance but one, so the thumb must hold its target 7 m off, neither nearer nor farther.
source: An indenture was written out twice on one sheet and cut apart along a wavy line, so that the two copies proved each other when the edges were matched.
nearest: Sweet-spot weapons that hit harder at the tip. This one has two weak travelling halves and a single point where they are worth six times as much.
