notes.where: Gun convergence in WWII flight sims such as IL-2 Sturmovik and War Thunder (two streams leave apart and cross at one set range, where they bite hardest), Enter the Gungeon's Helix Bullets, Marth's tipper in Super Smash Bros.
notes.mutation: Take away the fixed 7 m: each half flies until it strikes a body, and the halves fit only if the two bodies struck stand within 1.5 m of each other, so the sweet spot is a gap between two of the dead that the player lines up, not a distance from the player.

notes.where: Crossing the streams in Ghostbusters, two beams that do something far greater where they meet; the locked wand-beams of Priori Incantatem in Goblet of Fire; tipper sweet spots in fighting games. One cast split into halves that meet at a single range is its own.

name: The Vigil Candle
idea: The pool that vows hold is the character's vigil candle, 12 inches long. One inch burns away at every toll. A vow does not use candle up; it holds inches back unburnt: with a 3-inch vow kept, only 9 inches are left to burn. When no free candle remains, every vow goes dark until wax is found (a keeper drops 3 inches). So a vow is paid for in time: three vows give a strong first six tolls and nothing after, one vow lasts the night.
source: A wake was timed by its candles, and an endowment held capital back untouched so that it could go on paying.
nearest: Reserving a share of a resource bar for lasting effects. Here the bar is also the run's clock, so the price of each vow is how long any vow lasts.

notes.where: Path of Exile mana reservation for the frame; Darkest Dungeon's torch and Candleman's ten seconds of wax for a light that is also the clock. Reserving part of the clock itself, so that vows shorten the night, I have not seen.

Grimm's Godfather Death, where every life is a candle burning down in Death's cave; Meleager's log; the enchanted rose of Beauty and the Beast shedding petals as a clock; 'out, out, brief candle'. A reserve pool that is also the run's clock is its own.

name: Full Mourning
idea: Holds 4 inches of the pool. The character wears full black, and the dead cannot make the wearer out beyond 7 m: those farther off lose them and walk to where they last saw them. But nothing bright may be taken in full mourning: coin and gear are not picked up, only experience. At every third toll the mourning lightens a grade: grey, seen at 10 m, coin allowed; then lavender, seen at 14 m. To return to black the vow must be dropped and taken again at a gate.
source: Full mourning forbade anything shiny, even jewellery other than jet, and lightened by set stages to grey and then lavender.
nearest: Stealth effects that shorten enemy sight. This one forbids loot while it holds and wears off in grades timed by the bell.

notes.where: D&D 3.5's Vow of Poverty (power for owning nothing), NetHack conducts, and the shortened aggro radius of stealth in WoW. The stepped fading by tolls is its own.

Aladdin's cave, 'touch nothing but the lamp', and the fairy-mound rule that whoever takes nothing comes out safe; Scarlett O'Hara in full black, forbidden to dance, in Gone with the Wind; stealth that shortens enemy sight. Grades that lighten on the bell are its own.

name: Tell the Bees
idea: Holds 3 inches of the pool. A hive rides on the character's back and its bees fetch every pickup within 10 m. In return the bees must be told of every important death: within 10 s of an elite or keeper falling anywhere in the district, the player must stand still for 1 s. If a death goes untold the bees leave until the next toll, taking what they were carrying. Each telling also sends the bees to drive the 5 nearest dead back 3 m.
source: Bees had to be told of a death in the household, with a knock on the hive, or they would leave or stop making honey.
nearest: Pickup-magnet companions. This one carries a duty that makes the player stand still for a second at the worst moment, just after a big kill.

notes.where: Loot-gathering pets in Diablo III and Lost Ark and Vampire Survivors' Attractorb; duties owed on a timer like Gears of War's active reload or feeding a Tamagotchi. A magnet that leaves if a death goes unannounced is new to me.

Whittier's poem 'Telling the Bees' and the custom it records; the household brownie and Melusine, helpers who leave the moment a duty or taboo is broken; pickup-magnet pets in games. A magnet whose price is a second's stillness after each big death is its own.

name: Deodand
idea: Holds 3 inches. Once every 10 s, the next thing that harms the character is declared deodand. If it was moving when it struck, it changes sides for 6 s; if it was standing, it cannot strike for 6 s; a ground patch goes dark for 6 s. The holder is paid its appraised value: coin equal to 5% of that thing's full life. Since the first harm in each 10 s is the one seized, the player can pick it, and walk into a charger on purpose.
source: The coroner's jury named the object that had caused a death, appraised it, and declared it forfeit as a deodand.
nearest: Thorns and reflect effects. This seizes the attacker instead of hurting it, pays by what the attacker was worth, and rewards choosing which blow to take.

notes.where: Thorns and on-hit retaliation with an internal cooldown (Dota 2 Blade Mail, Path of Exile 'when hit' effects), JRPG Counter abilities, bounty gold sized by the victim. It is the same rule as customs-04 held as a vow; the moving-or-standing test remains the unseen part.
The deodand itself and the medieval prosecution of animals and objects (The Hour of the Pig); thorns and reflect effects. Seizing the attacker and paying out its appraised value is its own.

name: Ring Your Own Knell
idea: The character's passing bell is rung and the dead take them for one of their own. Until the next toll nothing new rises, and the dead already standing ignore the character unless struck. But everything that should have risen in that time is only held back, and all of it rises together at the toll, on top of the toll's own wave. Taken when the player needs up to 75 quiet seconds to collect, cross the district or reach a gate, and can afford what follows.
source: The passing bell was rung for a person who was dying but not yet dead, so the parish heard of the death before it happened.
nearest: Invisibility and wave-skip pickups. Nothing is skipped here: it is postponed and delivered in one piece on the bell.

notes.where: Borrow-now-pay-later rules such as Hearthstone's Overload and Magic: The Gathering's Pacts, Vampire Survivors' Orologion freeze, and the smeared-in-guts camouflage of The Walking Dead games. A whole interval's rising postponed and delivered at once on the bell is its own.

Walking through the dead smeared in their guts in The Walking Dead's 'Guts', pretending to be zombies to cross the crowd in Shaun of the Dead; Tom Sawyer at his own funeral; wave-skip and invisibility pickups. The rule that nothing is skipped and all of it rises on the bell is its own.

name: Funeral Biscuit
idea: A biscuit wrapped in printed paper and sealed with black wax. Sealed, it does nothing. At any later level-up the player may break the seal instead of choosing: it then counts as two picks, both taken from that level-up's offers. If it is still sealed when the character leaves through a gate, it is kept as a token and adds 20% to the Echoes that vigil leaves. If the character dies with it sealed, the player's next character starts its first vigil holding it.
source: Funeral guests were given biscuits wrapped in printed paper and sealed with black wax, often kept for years as a remembrance or sent to those who could not come.
nearest: Banked rerolls and saved level-ups. This has three different ends, depending on whether it is opened, carried out, or left behind by the dead.

notes.where: Vampire Survivors' Skip and banked rerolls, Slay the Spire relics that pay later, and Sunless Sea legacies handed to the next captain when one dies. One object with three different ends I cannot place.

The gift that must not be opened, Pandora's jar and Urashima Taro's box; funeral biscuits kept for years; banked rerolls and saved level-ups. Three different ends, by whether it is opened, carried out or left behind by the dead, are its own.

name: Coins on Your Own Eyes
idea: The ferryman is paid in advance. From now on a gate opens for this character at every toll, 20 m from where they stand, for 15 s, instead of only from time to time. The fare is 2 coins out of what the character carries, taken at each toll whether the gate is used or not, and it rises by 1 each toll. The first time the fare cannot be paid the pick is lost, and no gate at all opens for the next two tolls.
source: The coins laid on a dead person's eyes were said to be the fare owed to the ferryman for the last crossing.
nearest: Extraction beacons bought in extraction games. This is a standing subscription to exits, paid from the same purse the exits exist to save.

notes.where: Paid vehicle extracts in Escape from Tarkov, and Luck Be a Landlord's rent that rises every cycle until you cannot pay. A subscription to exits paid from the purse the exits exist to save is a new joining.

Charon's fare paid in advance ('Don't pay the ferryman until he gets you to the other side'); extraction beacons bought in extraction shooters. A rising standing fare for exits, taken from the purse the exits protect, is its own.

name: Short Tally
idea: Take any one of the other picks on offer at double effect, but as a tally: the character holds the stock and the gate holds the foil. The tally must be fitted by leaving through a gate within three tolls. If the third toll passes and the character is still in the district, the tally is void: the doubled pick is removed, and so is the pick taken before it. A way to burn bright for under four minutes and then go.
source: A tally bound both parties to a day of reckoning; after that day an unmatched half was a stick of firewood.
nearest: Timed power-ups. This one is ended by the player choosing to leave, and overstaying costs an extra pick.

notes.where: Dead Cells cursed chests (power now, with a condition you must clear or suffer), Binding of Isaac devil deals, ordinary timed power-ups. A doubled pick that is kept only by leaving on time I have not seen.

Cinderella's finery that lasts only until the clock strikes twelve, so she must leave the ball in time; the Little Mermaid's three days; Faust's term; timed power-ups. A doubled pick kept only by leaving, where overstaying also costs the pick before it, is its own.

name: The Weigh-in
idea: At the next toll, the coin the character is carrying is weighed on the town beam. For every 20 coins on them at that moment they deal 2% more harm for the rest of the vigil. Until that toll the pick gives nothing, and after it carrying coin gives no more. Coin carried is coin not yet banked, and falls with the character. So the player must stay away from gates, and alive, for at most 75 s with as full a purse as they dare.
source: Market toll was reckoned on the public weigh-beam at the moment the goods crossed it, neither before nor after.
nearest: Damage-per-gold items. This is measured once, at a known moment, so it asks for one risky minute rather than permanent hoarding.

notes.where: The Binding of Isaac's Money = Power and Balatro's Bull and Bootstraps: harm scaled by the coin you are holding; carried loot at risk is the extraction-game stake.
notes.mutation: Weigh two pans, not one: the beam sets the coin carried against the bodies laid since the last toll, and the bonus is paid only if the two come within a tenth of level, so the minute before the bell is spent trimming a purse to match a count instead of simply hoarding.

notes.where: Tula bhara, a ruler weighed against gold; the weigh-in before a prizefight; Money = Power in The Binding of Isaac, harm per coin held. Measured once, at a known toll, it is its own.

name: Pall on Hire
idea: The parish pall is hired for a term of two tolls. While it covers the character, the first blow in every 3 s is turned aside. When the term ends the pall must be returned in person: a chest appears at the far side of the district, and the player has one toll to walk into it. Returned in time, the hire cost nothing and the pall may be offered again later. Not returned, the deposit is taken: the next two level-ups offer no pick.
source: Parishes owned a pall and hired it out for each funeral, to be brought back afterwards.
nearest: Temporary shields. This one is rented, and giving it back is an errand across the map with a penalty counted in future picks.

notes.where: Ravio's item rental in The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds, and periodic hit-blockers like League of Legends Banshee's Veil. Having to walk the thing back, with future picks as the deposit, is its own.

Maupassant's 'The Necklace', borrowed finery whose loss costs ten years; fairy loans that must go back by a set day; temporary shields. A return errand across the map, paid in future picks if missed, is its own.

name: Make Your Will
idea: Name one of the character's skills in a will. Nothing changes now. If this character dies in this vigil, that skill passes whole, with its bindings exactly as they stood, to another of the player's characters, chosen afterwards. If the character leaves the vigil alive the will is torn up, and in exchange its next vigil's first level-up offers one extra pick. A pick that is worth most to a character the player expects to lose.
source: Mourning rings and named goods were left by will to chosen people, and changed hands only on the death.
nearest: Insurance slots in extraction games. This insures a built skill rather than loot, and pays a small refund if it is never needed.

notes.where: Escape from Tarkov insurance, Massive Chalice relics and Infinity Blade bloodlines passing things to the next in line, ZombiU's backpack recovered from your dead survivor. Insuring one built skill, with a refund if it is never needed, I have not seen.

The Green Lantern ring that seeks a successor when its dying bearer falls, the Slayer line of Buffy, heirloom swords such as Narsil; heirs and heirlooms in Rogue Legacy and Darkest Dungeon. Insuring one built skill, with a refund if it is never needed, is its own.

name: The Coin-Eyed
idea: Properly buried, coins still on its eyes, so it cannot see. It walks in a dead straight line until it bumps a wall or a body, then turns to face the last loud sound, the player's most recent cast, and sets off straight again. It harms by walking into things, the other dead included. Read it by two bright discs on its face and a ruler-straight path. Step aside; it drops its two coins when laid, so a line of them is worth leading into a wall.
source: Coins were laid on the eyes of the dead to keep them shut and to pay the ferryman.
nearest: Blind enemies that hunt by sound in stealth games. Here blindness makes a straight-line walker inside a homing horde, and the coins are its loot.

notes.where: The straight-line charger that re-aims after hitting a wall: Zelda's Ropes, The Binding of Isaac's Chargers, Brotato's chargers, and the Goomba's walk-until-you-bump; sound-led blind enemies are The Last of Us Clickers.
notes.mutation: Make the coins the mechanism rather than the loot: one blow knocks off one coin, a one-coin body walks a wide circle toward its open eye instead of a line, and a body with no coins sees and hunts like the rest, so the player chooses between blind, half-blind and sighted for each one.

notes.where: The clickers of The Last of Us, blind and hunting by sound; Amando de Ossorio's Blind Dead, eyeless revenants who find their victims by ear; A Quiet Place; Mr Magoo walking straight into things. The ruler-straight walker that re-aims at the last cast after every bump is its own.

name: The Mute
idea: A hired mourner still at its post. It never moves: it stands in a doorway, gate or lane-mouth holding a tall wand draped in cloth, and does no harm. But within 5 m of it nothing makes a sound, so the player's skills do not cast there. Read it by the tall black pole and its perfect stillness. The cure is to walk up and jostle it: a touch knocks the wand down for 6 s, and in that time it falls to two blows.
source: Hired mutes stood silent at the door of a house of death holding wands draped in black crape.
nearest: Silence fields cast by enemy spellcasters. This one is a harmless standing figure that guards exits, and the answer is to go and bump into it.

notes.where: Warframe's Nullifier Crewman and Comba or Scrambus (a bubble in which your powers do not work, answered by walking in and dealing with the carrier by hand), Dota 2 silence auras, debuff totems in Diablo and Path of Exile.
notes.mutation: Make its silence shut out the bell as well: inside the 5 m nothing hears the toll, so bodies there do not rise, the toll's added danger does not apply and no gate opens, which makes each Mute a pocket outside the clock that the player may prefer to leave standing and fight beside.

notes.where: The Gentlemen of Buffy's 'Hush', who take every voice in town; the Silence spell that stops casting in Dungeons & Dragons and Final Fantasy, the beholder's anti-magic cone; Oliver Twist hired out as a funeral mute by Sowerberry the undertaker. A harmless door-keeper undone by a jostle is its own.

name: The Bier Party
idea: Four dead bearers carry a fifth on a bier along the district's corpse road toward the bell. They ignore the player, never leave the road, and pause 3 s at each resting stone to set the bier down. If the bier reaches the lychgate the body is received and rises as an elite at the next toll. Lay the bearers on the move and the bier is dropped: the body wakes at once. Lay them while the bier rests on a stone and it sleeps on, and can be searched.
source: Bearers carried the bier along the corpse road and might set it down only at the resting stones.
nearest: Caravans and escorts to be intercepted. Here where the player strikes matters more than whether, and the map marks the right places in advance.

notes.where: Caravan and escort interceptions (Guild Wars 2 dolyak caravans), tower-defence creeps reaching the exit, kill-the-summoner-before-the-cast-ends timing. The marked resting stones that decide whether the cargo wakes are its own.

The close of Dracula: the gypsies carry the Count's box toward his castle against the sunset, and the hunters must cut down the bearers and deal with him while he lies helpless in it before he can rise; also caravan and escort interceptions in games. A sleeping undead carried to the place where it will wake in power is that chase.
notes.mutation: Turn the stakes from the rising to the road: wherever the bearers fall and the bier touches ground off a resting stone, that spot becomes a new stone and the corpse road bends through it for the rest of the vigil, after the belief that carrying a corpse across land makes it a right of way, so where the player drops the bier redraws the path the dead walk.

name: The Mortsafe
idea: Risen with its iron cage still locked on. Caged, it shuffles toward the player and can neither strike nor be harmed. The lock has a term of 6 s, shown as six bars that vanish one by one, and every blow on the cage puts one bar back. When the last bar goes it bursts out, three times as fast and striking hard, but with little life. Skills that keep hitting it keep it harmless and waste their blows; the player must walk away, let it open, and meet it.
source: A mortsafe was an iron cage locked over a new grave for a term of weeks, then taken off once the body was past use to the anatomists.
nearest: Shielded enemies with a break window. Here hitting the shield renews it, so the answer is to stop attacking, which self-casting skills make hard.

notes.where: Stop-attacking checks such as Diablo II's Iron Maiden and WoW reflect and absorb shields, and Mario's Boo, which acts only when you are not engaging it. A timer that every blow winds back, in a game where skills fire by themselves, is a real fit and new to me.

Devil's Snare in Harry Potter, which grips harder the more you struggle; the Chinese finger trap; the Weeping Angels, held still by the player's own attention; the mortsafes of Burke-and-Hare churchyards; shielded enemies. A cage renewed by every blow, which self-casting skills keep feeding, is its own.

name: The Searcher
idea: An old woman with a white wand, risen to finish her round. She keeps 7 m from the player and levels the wand, drawn as a white line. If the line rests unbroken on the player for 3 s she reports the cause: for 15 s every dead thing in the district deals 50% more harm to that character. The line is broken by any body standing in it, so the player hides behind the horde itself. She has little life but backs away from whoever comes at her.
source: Searchers of the dead were old women who examined each body, carried a white wand so that people could keep clear of them, and reported the cause to the parish clerk.
nearest: Snipers with a visible aiming line. This one emboldens the others instead of shooting, and the cover the player uses is the enemy crowd.

notes.where: Laser-sight snipers (Half-Life 2, Borderlands 2), Darkest Dungeon's Fungal Artillery marking a hero so the Scratchers hit harder, spotters calling fire in Company of Heroes. Breaking the line with the horde's own bodies I have not seen.

The pod-person's point-and-shriek at the end of Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1978), which sets the whole town on the one marked; the Eye of Sauron; Aboriginal bone-pointing; Defoe's searchers of the dead; sniper aiming lines. A spotter whose line the horde itself breaks is its own.

name: The Link-boy
idea: A dead child with a torch, a real light. It does not chase: it runs 4 m ahead of the player in whatever direction the player is heading, and never strikes. Dead standing in its torchlight can see their way and move 40% faster. It is always lighting the ground the player is about to run onto. Read it by the small figure and the bright pool ahead. A sharp turn leaves it behind for 2 s; one blow lays it, but only skills that reach forward can catch it.
source: Link-boys carried torches ahead of people walking at night for a farthing, and some led their customers to waiting robbers.
nearest: Support enemies that carry a buff zone. This one takes its position from the player's own heading, so it punishes running in a straight line.

notes.where: Pac-Man's Pinky, who aims for the space ahead of where the player is heading, and standard-bearer or shaman enemies that carry a buff aura. The two joined as a harmless runner lighting your path is its own.

The will-o'-the-wisp, a light always just ahead that leads travellers into the mire; the link-boy who led his customer to waiting robbers, as London lore has it; buff-carrying support enemies. A light placed by the player's own heading is its own.

name: Dole-seekers
idea: The parish poor, risen for the funeral dole. They come as a slow crowd of 20 with open hands, never strike, and fall to one blow. Each takes the first experience pickup it reaches, then turns and leaves the district, saying the prayer it owes: the player gains one ward-stroke, which stops one blow, 20 at most. They turn experience into protection one for one. Laying one gives nothing and makes the others take two pickups each. Read them by pale colour and flat upturned hands.
source: The poor came to funerals for the dole of bread or pence, and owed a prayer for the dead in return.
nearest: Thief enemies that grab pickups and run. These pay for what they take, and the choice is whether to let them.

notes.where: Pickup thieves (Gauntlet's Thief, Golden Axe gnomes) and beggars who take a resource and pay back, as in The Binding of Isaac and Kingdom's vagrants. A crowd that trades experience for stored blocks, and bargains harder if you kill one, is new to me.

The beggar at the door who must be given to, from the disguised enchantress turned away in Beauty and the Beast to Perrault's 'Diamonds and Toads' and Baucis and Philemon; thief enemies that grab pickups and run. Dole taken in exchange for ward-strokes is its own.

name: The Forfeit Wheel
idea: A forfeit thing, not a body: the cartwheel, millstone or fallen clapper that once killed someone. It rolls in straight lines at twice walking pace, bouncing off walls and harming whatever it runs over, dead or living. It cannot be destroyed. Its next two bounces are drawn on the ground. If it strikes the player it is forfeit again, this time to them: for 15 s it bends its path toward the nearest dead after every bounce, then stops for good. Being hit once is how to own it.
source: A deodand was the object that had caused a death, such as a cartwheel, forfeit because it had moved to the death.
nearest: Indestructible bouncing hazards in arcade games. This one changes owner when it hurts the player, so taking the hit is a tactic.

notes.where: Indestructible bouncing hazards (Zelda blade traps and Bubbles, Vampire Survivors' Runetracer), balls that belong to whoever last touched them in Lethal League, Windjammers and Knockout City, and the kicked Koopa shell. Ownership won by being hit is the unseen part.

Wanyudo and Katawaguruma, the burning cart-wheels of Japanese folklore that roll the roads taking whoever they meet; the rolling boulder of Raiders of the Lost Ark; Christine, the object that kills; indestructible bouncing hazards in arcade games. Changing owner when it strikes the player is its own.

name: Resurrection-men
idea: Living thieves, in pairs, with sack and spade. They run against the flow of the horde to wherever bodies and pickups lie thickest, stuff up to 6 into the sack in 3 s, and make for the district's edge. They never strike, and the dead ignore them. Two blows drop one and spill the sack. They are also a free way to be rid of bodies that would stand again at the toll, so sometimes the player lets them work and guards only the coin.
source: Body-snatchers dug up the newly buried by night to sell to anatomists, which is why graves were caged and watched.
nearest: Loot goblins and pickup thieves. These take the player's uncollected leavings, and because they also remove bodies they are sometimes welcome.

notes.where: Gauntlet's Thief, Golden Axe's sack-carrying gnomes and Diablo III's Treasure Goblin: a non-fighting runner grabs loot, heads for the exit and spills it when struck.
notes.mutation: Stop them being loot carriers: they take bodies only, each sack they get out of the district strikes that many dead from the next toll's rising, and every body in a sack that is dropped wakes on the spot, so the pair is a service to guard or a hazard to trigger, never a prize to chase.

notes.where: Burke and Hare, Jerry Cruncher the 'resurrection man' of A Tale of Two Cities, Stevenson's 'The Body Snatcher' and its 1945 film; Diablo III's treasure goblins and other loot thieves. Thieves who also carry off bodies that would stand again, and so are sometimes welcome, are their own.

name: The Layer
idea: Sixteen dead from a plague pit, risen as they were laid: one flat rank four by four, white with lime, locked shoulder to shoulder. The layer moves as a single slab 4 m square, slowly, and turns no faster than 30 degrees a second. Nothing can push through it or part it, and it harms along its whole leading edge. Its members fall one by one, leaving gaps; when 8 are gone it breaks up into ordinary dead. Get round to its side, where it cannot turn in time.
source: Plague dead were tipped into pits in layers and covered with lime, without coffins or separate graves.
nearest: Shield-wall formations in strategy games. In a horde game this is one rigid slab that the player out-turns rather than outruns.

notes.where: Total War pike phalanxes (slow to turn, beaten from the flank), Space Invaders' block formation that thins into gaps, Vampire Survivors' sweeping walls of enemies. One rigid slab of sixteen with a turn rate is its own unit in this genre.
The Roman testudo of Asterix and the phalanx; the gashadokuro, a giant made of the unburied dead; Defoe's great pit at Aldgate. In a horde game, one rigid slab to be out-turned is its own.

name: Keeper of the Passing Bell
idea: Phase one, the tellers: three sets of three strokes, each a ring spreading from him to 12 m in 1.5 s with one 60-degree gap, the gap shown 1 s ahead as a pale wedge. Phase two, below 60% life, the age: one stroke for every level the character has, each a 2 m circle drawn under the player 0.8 s before it lands. Phase three, below 25%: he digs graves, outlined 1.2 s before they open; he is laid only by leading him across one of his own.
source: The death knell told the sex of the dead by sets of three strokes and then the age, one stroke for each year.
nearest: Ring-with-a-gap boss patterns are common. The barrage whose length is the player's own level, and a keeper finished by his own graves, are the parts I have not seen.

notes.where: Stock boss parts: expanding rings with a gap (Hades, Enter the Gungeon, any bullet-hell), aimed ground circles, and the boss finished by his own attack or arena (Agahnim's volley in A Link to the Past, Bowser's bridge); attacks keyed to level are Final Fantasy's Level 5 Death family.
notes.mutation: Give him a knell instead of a life bar: he must finish the count (tellers, then one stroke per level) on the character, every stroke that lands counts and the character dies when the count is complete whatever its life, and each stroke the player makes him spend on one of his own open graves is un-rung.

notes.where: 'Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein' (Proverbs 26:27), Haman hanged on his own gallows, 'hoist with his own petard'; the strokes of age in The Nine Tailors; ring-with-a-gap patterns in bullet-hell bosses. A barrage as long as the player's level is its own.

name: Keeper of the Chantry Bell
idea: He has no life, only an endowment: a chest of 600 coin beside him. Every attack is a mass that must be paid for. Phase one, trentals: lines of sound shown 0.7 s ahead, 5 coin each. Phase two, below 400, obits: a 9 m circle shown 2.5 s ahead, 60 coin. Phase three, below 150, he begs: quick cheap strokes, 2 coin each. He falls when the chest is empty. The player baits costly attacks, or robs the chest: stand on it 2 s to take 30 coin, kept.
source: A chantry was an endowment that paid a priest to sing masses for one soul for exactly as long as the money lasted.
nearest: Survive-the-timer bosses and bosses that tire. Here the timer is a visible purse that the boss spends by attacking and the player can rob.

notes.where: Final Fantasy VI enemies that die when their MP runs out, coin-cost attacks like Gil Toss and Ragnarok Online's Mammonite, The Binding of Isaac's Greed. A boss whose only life is a purse he spends by attacking and the player can rob is new to me.

Ali's rope-a-dope, letting the other man punch himself out; Bilbo carrying a cup off Smaug's hoard; Zeninage (Gil Toss) in Final Fantasy, attacks paid for in money; bosses that tire. A boss whose life is a purse it spends by attacking is its own.

name: Keeper of the Pest Bell
idea: Phase one, the search: a white line follows the player; where it rests 2 s, thickening, the searcher-general names the character's most-used skill and seals it for 10 s. Phase two, below 65% life, the Bill: the three kinds of dead this character has laid most in this vigil rise again, 30 bodies in the same proportions, from mounds shown 2 s ahead. Phase three, below 30%: the house is shut. Four walls, outlined 2 s ahead, close a 10 m square round her and the player for 20 s.
source: Searchers reported each death's cause for the weekly Bills of Mortality, and a plague house was shut up for a term with its people inside.
nearest: Bosses that summon helpers. The helpers here are a replay of the player's own kill count, so the fight differs with how the vigil was played.

notes.where: Metal Gear Solid 3's The Sorrow (the boss sends back everyone you killed, as you killed them) and Psycho Mantis reading the player's habits; skill seals from any JRPG; the closing walls are Diablo III's Waller and Jailer affixes.
notes.mutation: Turn the Bill over: she raises the kinds this character laid least or avoided all vigil, in inverse proportion, and seals the skill that has cast least, so the fight examines the hole in the build rather than replaying its strength.

notes.where: The ghosts of Richard III's victims rising before Bosworth to say 'despair and die'; Defoe's shut-up plague houses; Disable in Pokemon, sealing a move; arena lock-ins. A replay of the player's own kill count is its own.

name: Keeper of the Sanctuary Bell
idea: The floor is lit by a hearse of 15 candles. In each of three rounds, every pattern the keeper finishes (lines of sound, shown 1 s ahead) puts one candle out, and the lit ground shrinks; the player's skills pick only targets standing in light. The last candle is carried behind the altar: 4 s of dark, in which a faint glow marks the one safe spot, then the crash, harming everything elsewhere. The candle returns, all 15 relight, and the keeper kneels open to harm for 6 s.
source: At Tenebrae fifteen candles on a triangular hearse were put out one by one, the last was hidden, a crash was made in the dark, and the candle was brought back.
nearest: Shrinking-arena and find-the-safe-spot boss phases. The device here is the game's real lighting, counted down as candles in a fixed liturgical order.

notes.where: The stock raid cycle of WoW and Final Fantasy XIV: the safe floor shrinks, a wipe attack leaves one marked safe spot, then the boss kneels for a damage window; lights-out phases as in Luigi's Mansion and Alan Wake.
notes.mutation: Hand the last candle to the player: whoever carries it is the only lit thing and draws the keeper and every dead thing, and the crash spares whatever stands where the candle is set down, so the player chooses where the safe spot will be and what else it will save.

notes.where: Tenebrae itself; the figures vanishing one by one in And Then There Were None; the torch of Darkest Dungeon; shrinking-arena and safe-spot boss phases. The countdown carried in the room's real candles is its own.

name: The Shut Parish
idea: No dead come in from the edges. Every house door bears a red cross with a term: the cross fades until the door opens and 5 to 12 dead come out. Standing 2 s at a door nails it shut for one more toll, but twice as many then come out. A dead-cart circles a fixed route taking every body and pickup within 2 m. Shapes: box houses, crosses of two thin boxes, a cart of one box and two cylinders. Colours: lime white, ox-blood, tar, straw, pewter.
source: A plague house was shut up for a set term with a red cross on the door, and the dead-cart made its round for the bodies.
nearest: Spawner doors in arcade shooters. Here every door shows its timer and can be put off at a price.

notes.where: Killing Floor's welded doors and Call of Duty Zombies' boarded windows (stand at an opening to hold it shut while more pile up behind it), plus Gauntlet's monster generators for doors as spawners.
notes.mutation: Make shutting a true quarantine: nailing a door also locks inside whatever stands within 3 m of it, up to the house's count, and all of it comes out together when the term ends, so doors become rooms the player fills with horde instead of timers the player postpones.

notes.where: 'Bring out your dead!' and the plague cart of Monty Python and the Holy Grail; Defoe's houses shut up under a red cross; the marked doors of the Passover; spawner doors in arcade games. Doors whose timers can be put off at a price are their own.

name: The Close
idea: Three rings lie round the cathedral door, marked by crosses at 30 m, 15 m and 4 m. The dead deal 20% less harm in the outer ring, 40% less in the middle, 70% less at the door. But sanctuary is granted for a term: each character has 40 s of each ring per vigil, counted while standing in it. A spent ring is ordinary ground. Shapes: flagstone slabs, crosses of two boxes on steps, a west front of tapered boxes. Colours: limestone, lead grey, verdigris, candle gold, window blue.
source: Beverley's sanctuary lay in rings marked by crosses, the penalty for seizing a fugitive rising toward the centre, and sanctuary lasted a fixed number of days.
nearest: Safe zones and defensive ground. These are graded, and each is a personal ration of seconds that the player spends across the vigil.

notes.where: Graded defensive terrain such as Fire Emblem forts and thrones, safe rooms, base and fountain zones in MOBAs. A personal ration of seconds per ring, spent across the vigil, I have not seen.

Quasimodo's 'Sanctuary!' in The Hunchback of Notre Dame, the holy ground of Highlander and vampire fiction; the Beverley frith stool and its crosses; safe zones in games. Graded rings rationed in seconds are their own.

name: The Tron
idea: A market square of 30 stalls round a weigh-beam. Nothing may be sold before the bell: for 15 s after every toll the stalls open, and walking into one buys what it shows for carried coin, with no pause. The same toll raises the danger, so every bell is a dash to a stall. A stall the dead are pushed into overturns and is shut for the vigil. Shapes: box stalls with tapered striped awnings, a post-and-beam scale, a stepped cross. Colours: awning red, cream, cobble grey, brass, wet wood.
source: Markets opened on the market bell, and dealing before it rang was punished as forestalling.
nearest: Mid-run shops. These are physical, open only in the dangerous seconds after each bell, and can be destroyed by the fight.

notes.where: Killing Floor's Trader, open only for a countdown tied to the wave clock so every wave ends in a dash to the shop; buying in real time under attack as in Risk of Rain 2 and Call of Duty Zombies wall buys; Spelunky's wreckable shops.
notes.mutation: Let the fighting decide what opens: at each toll only stalls with no body laid within 5 m of them since the last toll put up their shutters, so the player spends every interval keeping one corner of the square clean for the bell.

notes.where: The Floating Market of Gaiman's Neverwhere, open only at its set times; Rossetti's 'Goblin Market'; Brigadoon; the cabbage merchant whose stall is wrecked in every chase in Avatar: The Last Airbender; mid-run shops. Stalls open only in the dangerous seconds after each bell are their own.

name: Beating the Bounds
idea: The tree is drawn as a map of parishes. Points are not spent on the nodes inside a parish but on the boundary marks round it, 5 to 8 to a parish. When every mark of a parish has been taken, all the nodes inside are granted at once. Neighbouring parishes share the marks on their common border, so one point can count toward two or three parishes. Planning is choosing a block of parishes with the most shared border, and deciding which unfinished boundary is worth closing next.
source: A parish was defined by walking its boundary each year and striking every mark, and neighbouring parishes shared the marks between them.
nearest: Dots and Boxes on paper, and bonuses for filling a cluster of nodes. As the whole shape of a passive tree, paying for edges and being given areas is new to me.

notes.where: Dots and Boxes and Qix (close a boundary, take what is inside), Grim Dawn constellations completed for their bonus, Path of Exile's Thread of Hope ring. A passive tree where points buy edges and areas are granted is new to me.
Dots and Boxes, territory in Go, completed cities in Carcassonne; the beating of the bounds itself. Nothing in stories; as the whole shape of a passive tree it is its own.

name: Lapsing Tolls
idea: The tree's regions are divided by the river and the walls, and every bridge and gate between regions charges a toll of 1 to 4 extra points to cross. Each class is quit of toll at the gates of its home region. Every toll was granted for a term: printed on each crossing is the character level at which it lapses and becomes free. A planner chooses between paying 3 points to cross at level 12 and working round the home region until the bridge falls free at level 25.
source: Pontage and murage were tolls granted for a fixed term of years to repair a bridge or a wall, and certain burgesses were quit of them.
nearest: Travel nodes that cost a point and give little. Here the cost sits on the crossing itself, differs by class, and expires at a known level.

notes.where: Path of Exile travel nodes and class starts on a shared tree, level-gated talent tiers in WoW and Diablo IV, Last Epoch's limits on other masteries' trees. A crossing fee that differs by class and expires at a printed level I have not seen.

The troll who takes toll at the bridge in The Three Billy Goats Gruff, the Bridge of Death and 'none shall pass' in Monty Python and the Holy Grail; travel nodes in passive trees. A crossing charge that lapses at a printed level is its own.

name: The Ossuary Rule
idea: Each road of the tree has room for six fresh graves. The six nodes most recently taken on a road work in full. When a seventh is taken, the oldest is lifted to the ossuary: it stays owned and keeps the path joined, but gives half. A deep road has six full nodes at its tip and a tail of halved ones, while five short roads have everything in full. The planner weighs depth against breadth, and the order of taking matters because order decides what is lifted.
source: Graves were reused after a term: the old bones were lifted and stacked in the ossuary to make room for the new dead.
nearest: Diminishing returns on stacking one stat. This works by age along a path, is visible node by node, and makes the order of purchase matter.

notes.where: Slay the Spire's orb slots (a new one pushes the oldest out), diminishing returns on stacked stats, the three active trait lines of Guild Wars 2. Halving by age along a road, so that order of purchase matters, I cannot place in any tree.
The ossuaries of Sedlec and Hallstatt; summon caps where the oldest minion is replaced; diminishing returns. Nothing in stories.

name: Masons' Marks
idea: Every character cuts its mark on each node it takes, and the marks stay on the shared tree after that character dies. A node bearing the marks of 3 dead characters is worn: it costs nothing to the next character who reaches it, though it must still be reached. Marks of the living do not count. Over many lives the roads the player's dead walked most become free ground, and each new character can spend its points further out than the last.
source: Each mason cut his personal mark on every stone he dressed so that his work could be counted and paid for.
nearest: Permanent unlocks bought with a meta-currency. Nothing is bought here: the discount is laid down by where dead characters actually spent their points.

notes.where: Death Stranding paths worn in by repeated walking, NetHack bones left by dead characters, Dead Cells unlocks paid off across many runs, Rogue Legacy's permanent purchases. A discount laid down by where dead characters spent their points is its own.

The bloodstains and messages Dark Souls leaves where others died, the trails worn by many players' footsteps in Death Stranding, pilgrim steps worn hollow; meta-currency unlocks. A discount laid down by where the player's own dead spent their points is its own.

name: Split Nodes
idea: Forty nodes on the tree are half-tallies. Each stock has one foil somewhere far off, usually in another class's region, with the same pattern of notches drawn on both. A half alone gives a small effect. A character holding both halves fits the tally and gains a large named effect that neither half reveals beforehand. The tree draws a thin line between the halves of every tally the player has fitted on any character, living or dead, so knowledge of the pairs is inherited.
source: The two halves of a split tally were kept by different parties and proved their bargain only when brought together.
nearest: Set bonuses, and keystones with two distant requirements. These are pairs hidden in the tree, found by matching notch patterns, and the discovery outlives the character.

notes.where: Vampire Survivors' evolutions (a weapon and one particular passive held together make a new named weapon, unknown until first made and then recorded) and Hades' Duo Boons; set bonuses generally.
notes.mutation: Do not author the pairs: give every half-node a notch pattern and let any two halves fit to the degree their notches coincide, the effect being built from the notches they share, so there are hundreds of partial fits to find rather than forty recipes to look up.

notes.where: The urSkeks of The Dark Crystal, split into Skeksis and Mystics far apart and whole again only when rejoined; the split medallion that proves a lost heir; the Triforce; set bonuses. Pairs hidden in the tree by notch pattern are their own.

name: Bequests
idea: Every item is something left by will. It carries 2 to 5 legacies, each a rolled property with a named heir: 'to my sexton', 'to one who keeps two vows'. A legacy works only while its wearer answers the description. There are no tiers: an item is as good as the fit between its heirs and its wearer. To change one, contest the will before the scrivener: strike the heir out of one legacy so that it works for anyone, and one other legacy, of the scrivener's choosing, is voided.
source: Goods and mourning rings passed by will to named persons, and contesting a will could win one claimant a legacy at another's cost.
nearest: Conditional affixes and class-restricted items. Here every property has its own condition, and crafting trades the number of properties for their freedom, one legacy at a time.

notes.where: Diablo II class-only skill affixes, Path of Exile conditional mods ('while holding a shield'), Diablo III class legendaries; Path of Exile Annulment and Vaal crafting for trading one property against another. Every property having its own named heir, with no tiers, is its own system.

Jarndyce and Jarndyce in Bleak House, where contesting a will eats the estate; the conditional inheritance of Brewster's Millions; Mjolnir's inscription, power only 'if he be worthy'; conditional affixes and class items. Every property with its own heir is its own.

name: Halves
idea: Items drop as halves. A half is a notched stick: each notch is one property and its width is its size. A half can be worn alone at face value. Two halves whose notches fall in the same places (the same properties in the same order, at any widths) can be fitted into one whole item, with the widths added and one new notch cut where they join. To change a half, have one notch recut wider; each recut shortens the stick, and a stick has three recuts in it.
source: Exchequer tallies recorded sums as notches of set widths, and a stock fitted only its own foil.
nearest: Fusing duplicate items, and two-piece sets. This is a search for a matching pattern rather than a matching name, with a hard limit on rework.

notes.where: Minecraft's anvil (two like items combined, matching enchantments stepping up, with a hard cap on rework), Path of Exile's Recombinators, Last Epoch forging potential, duplicate fusion in gacha games and auto-battlers.
notes.mutation: Give each half exactly one true foil: when a half drops, its twin is put in the hands of a named dead thing that rises at a later toll in the same vigil, and only that twin fits, so the craft is deciding whether to stay long enough to meet the carrier.

notes.where: The Exchequer tally and the broken token of romance; fusing duplicate items in games. Matching by notch pattern, with a hard limit on rework, is its own.

name: Appraisal
idea: An item is found blank, with four empty lines. The first four different kinds of elite it helps to lay each write one line: a property drawn at random from that kind's own short list (a Mute's is about silence, a Bier Party's about roads) with a rolled size. The player shapes an item by choosing what it is used on first. To change it, forfeit a line to the Crown: the line is struck out, a little coin is paid, and the space waits for the next new kind.
source: A coroner's jury appraised the thing that had caused a death, and it was the death that gave the object its standing in law.
nearest: Weapons that earn traits from tracked kills. Here the kills decide which pool each random property is drawn from, in the order they happen.

notes.where: Vagrant Story, where a weapon's affinities grow toward whatever classes of enemy it is used on, and Path of Exile Bestiary and Essence crafting, where the monster decides the property; Shadow of War gear from captains.
notes.mutation: Have the line appraised by a jury: its size is set by how many lesser dead stand within 6 m when the elite falls, up to twelve, so an elite picked off alone in a corner writes a thin line and one laid in the thick of the crowd writes a fat one.

notes.where: Elric's Stormbringer drinking the souls of the slain, Sigurd tasting Fafnir's heart; Mega Man taking a weapon from each boss he beats; weapons that earn traits from kills. The order of first kills deciding which pool each property comes from is its own.

name: Terms of Mourning
idea: Every item is found in full mourning, with one property showing and three veiled. Wearing it advances its term, counted in tolls stood while it is worn. At 8 tolls it lightens to grey and the second property shows; at 24, lavender and the third; at 60 it is out of mourning and the fourth shows at 150% of its roll. To change an item, send it to the dyer: it goes back to black, every property not yet shown is rolled afresh, and the count starts again.
source: Mourning was worn for fixed terms and lightened by stages, and cloth was sent back to the dyer to be made black again.
nearest: Unidentified items, and gear that levels with use. This reveals itself by time worn at risk, and a reroll costs the time already put in.

notes.where: Destiny 1 weapons whose perk columns unlock as the gun is used, Torchlight II items that gain stats after a set number of kills, Path of Exile veiled modifiers, Warframe's Forma resetting a weapon to rank 0.
notes.mutation: Advance the term only by abstaining: a toll counts toward an item's mourning only if its wearer picked up no coin during that interval, so bringing gear out of mourning is a discipline kept at a cost, not time served.

notes.where: Unidentified items and gear that levels with use in role-playing games; Victorian mourning grades. Nothing in stories.

name: Bier-right
idea: A murdered body lies on a bier in the open. Three elite dead, the suspects, arrive and hunt the player. Custom says a corpse bleeds when its murderer comes near: each time a suspect passes within 2 m of the bier, the bier either stays pale or runs red. Lead them past it one at a time to find the guilty one. Lay the guilty one first and the body gives up an item with an extra property; lay an innocent first and the body rises as a fourth elite.
source: By bier-right, suspects were made to approach or touch the corpse, which was believed to bleed afresh at its murderer.
nearest: Pick-the-right-target puzzles. The test here is carried out by steering hostile elites past a spot on the ground in the middle of the fight.

notes.where: Find-the-real-one fights against clone bosses, Phasmophobia's evidence gathering while hunted, the blood tests of The Thing game. Steering hostile elites past a spot one at a time as the test is its own.

Cruentation as a story device: Siegfried's wounds bleed afresh when Hagen comes to the bier in the Nibelungenlied, dead Henry's bleed at Richard's approach in Richard III, and Scott's The Fair Maid of Perth turns on an ordeal of bier-right in which the suspects of a murder are summoned to pass the corpse. Leading the suspects past the bier to find the guilty one is that ordeal.
notes.mutation: Let the bier read degrees rather than name one culprit: each suspect carries a hidden share of the guilt, the bier runs redder the larger the share of whoever passes, and the reward depends on laying them in order of guilt, so the player compares three readings taken under pressure instead of sorting one murderer from two innocents.

name: Sanctuary
idea: Each district's church door has a knocker. Once per vigil the player may grasp it by standing at it 1 s. For a term of 40 s no dead thing may touch the character, the character's skills fall silent, and the whole build is open to change: bindings moved, points spent, vows swapped. The bell does not wait: every dead thing that arrives stands in a ring 3 m off. When the term ends, or the player lets go, the character must break out through whatever has gathered.
source: A fugitive who grasped the sanctuary knocker could not be seized for a set number of days, while his pursuers kept watch outside.
nearest: Safe rooms and rest points. This one is taken in the middle of the fight, runs on a clock, and collects a siege round itself as its price.

notes.where: League of Legends Zhonya's Hourglass (untouchable and unable to act while the enemy gathers round and waits), and rest points that allow rebuilding such as Hollow Knight's benches. A long, once-only stasis that buys a rebuild at the price of a siege is a new joining.

Quasimodo crying 'Sanctuary!' from Notre-Dame while the mob waits below; the chalk circle the dead cannot cross in Gogol's Viy and the protective circle held all night in The Devil Rides Out, with the things gathering outside it; the farmhouse ringed by the dead in Night of the Living Dead. Safety on a clock while the horde masses round, then breaking out, is that stock scene.
notes.mutation: Do not ring the character: the dead that arrive during the term go to keep watch on the district's gates instead, a watch building at each gate in turn, so the character steps out into a clear street with every exit watched and must choose which watch to break, rather than cutting out of a ring like a besieged magic circle.

name: The Candle Lot
idea: A lot is set on a block in the open: one item, shown. Beside it an inch of candle burns for an unknown time between 15 and 30 s, flaring for its last second. When the flame dies, the lot goes to whoever is standing on the block, living or dead. If that is the player, the item is theirs. If it is one of the dead, that body puts the item on and becomes an elite with its properties; lay it to take the item back.
source: At a sale by candle the lot fell to the last bidder standing when the flame went out, and nobody knew when that would be.
nearest: King-of-the-hill and capture points. Here only the unknown final instant counts, and losing creates an enemy that wears the prize.

notes.where: King-of-the-hill points, hidden-timer games like musical chairs and Mario Party's bomb passing, and enemies that pick up and use loot in NetHack and Breath of the Wild. Only the last instant counting, and the loser wearing the prize, is its own.
Musical chairs and king of the hill; the candle auction; NetHack's monsters picking up and wielding what they find. A prize that, when lost, walks off on an elite wearing it is its own.

name: Hue and Cry
idea: A living body-snatcher breaks cover with a sack and runs for the far edge of the district, 60 m away. The cry goes up, and all who hear must join: for as long as he runs, every dead thing within 20 m of him chases him instead of the player. If the dead catch him, the stolen body in the sack wakes among them as an elite. If the player touches him first he drops the sack (an item and 10 coin), the cry ends, and the horde turns back.
source: Raising the hue and cry obliged everyone within hearing to leave what they were doing and pursue the felon.
nearest: Chase-the-loot-carrier events. In this one the horde is chasing him too, so it is a race against the enemies and a rest from them at once.

notes.where: Diablo III's Treasure Goblin chase, and fights where enemies turn on a third party (Doom infighting, Halo's Flood against the Covenant). A runner the horde is racing you for I have not seen.

Aladdin's 'One Jump Ahead', the thief chased by the whole market; Ealing's Hue and Cry (1947); the runner who draws the dead off the others in zombie films; loot-carrier events. A race against the horde for the same quarry is its own.

name: Rogation
idea: Seven bound-stones stand round the district's edge, where the dead come in. Passing within 2 m of a stone strikes it with the willow wand and it is remembered, lit, for two tolls. For each remembered stone the player's skills reach 4% further. If all seven are lit at once the bounds are beaten: until the next toll nothing rises inside them, and the district's danger steps back one toll. The circuit is some 300 m of the most dangerous ground on the map, so it is a plan.
source: Each year the parish walked its boundary and struck every mark with willow wands so that the bounds would be remembered.
nearest: Shrine and beacon circuits. This one is laid along the edge the enemies enter by, fades stone by stone, and pays in full only while the whole ring is held together.

notes.where: The stock light-them-all-before-the-first-goes-out objective: Zelda's timed torches and switches, and Domination-style hold-every-point modes.
notes.mutation: Make the stretches count, not the stones: any two neighbouring stones lit together close the edge between them so nothing enters there, which lets the player choose which side of the district to wall, with the full ring only the limit of the same rule.

notes.where: The beacons of Gondor lit across the hills; warding stones and the beating of the bounds; light-every-brazier puzzles in games. A ring along the spawning edge that pays in full only while whole is its own.

name: The Pavement
idea: The permanent tree is not designed in advance: it is a church floor that the player paves. Every character that dies becomes one ledger stone, laid by the player on any free square beside an existing stone. Its inscription is its effect, drawn from that life: class decides the kind of effect, the district of death its condition, the toll reached its size. Echoes do not buy nodes; they cut an inscription deeper, up to three times. A stone gains 10% for each neighbouring stone of a different class.
source: Ledger stones were laid in the church floor over the dead, one by one, until the floor was made of them.
nearest: Family trees and graveyards of past characters, which are usually decoration. Here each death is a placed, upgradable node, and the layout is the player's own.

notes.where: Dungeonmans' academy built up by each fallen hero, Realm of the Mad God's graveyard and death fame, Rogue Legacy's lineage, Cult of the Lamb graves; adjacency placement as in Civilization VI districts. Each death as a placed, upgradable node of the permanent tree is its own.

The past Avatars whose strength the living one draws on in Avatar: The Last Airbender; Inscryption's death cards, made from a dead run's cards and dealt into later runs; Rogue Legacy's family tree. A floor of the player's dead, laid by hand and valued by its neighbours, is its own.

name: Hung in the Hall
idea: Whatever kills a character is forfeit to the household. The kind of dead, or the keeper, that dealt the last blow is hung in the hall as a deodand, appraised at the dead character's level. Every later character deals 1% more harm to that kind per 5 levels of appraisal and sees its attacks marked 0.2 s sooner. A kind is replaced only by a higher appraisal. Echoes are paid on top, 10 for each level appraised. Dying to something new is the richest way to lose a character.
source: The thing that had caused a death was appraised by the coroner's jury and forfeited, its value put to pious use.
nearest: Bestiary bonuses earned by kills, and nemesis systems that promote whoever killed you. Here the reward comes from being killed, once per kind, and is sized by what was lost.

notes.where: Shadow of Mordor's Nemesis system and Total War: Warhammer's Book of Grudges (whoever beat you is remembered), bestiary bonuses earned per monster kind in Tibia. A bonus earned by being killed, once per kind and sized by what was lost, I have not seen.

Inigo Montoya, who spends his life training against the six-fingered man who killed his father in The Princess Bride; Ahab's whale; trophies hung in the hall (Gaston's antlers); the nemesis system of Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor. A bonus sized by what was lost, once per kind, is its own.

name: The Household in Mourning
idea: When a standing character dies, every other standing character goes into mourning for it, for a term set by the dead one's level: one vigil per 10 levels, at least one. Full mourning is the first half of the term: the mourner earns 50% more Echoes and may not pick up coin. Half mourning is the second half: 25% more Echoes, coin allowed. A second death during the term extends it and does not stack. The death of a high character changes how the whole household plays for several vigils.
source: The length and grade of mourning depended on who had died, and the whole household wore it together.
nearest: Rested-experience bonuses. This is triggered by a death, scaled by what died, and comes with a rule about what may be picked up.

notes.where: WoW rested experience and comeback bonuses; grief states on survivors in The Sims, Darkest Dungeon and Crusader Kings. A roster-wide term set by the dead one's level, with a pickup rule, is its own.
Victorian household mourning, as in Scarlett O'Hara's scandal at dancing in black in Gone with the Wind; rested-experience bonuses. A bonus set off by a death and barred from coin is its own.

name: Told Out
idea: When a vigil ends, the bell tells the character out, and every stroke heard is one Echo. Tellers first: nine strokes if the character died, three if it left by a gate. Then one stroke for each character level, and one for each toll stood in that vigil. A death therefore pays six strokes more than an escape with the same record, and the death of a high character rings for a long time. The count is played in full, stroke by stroke, and can be listened to or skipped.
source: The death knell rang the tellers and then one stroke for each year of the dead person's age.
nearest: End-of-run currency tallies. This one is played as sound in the game's own code of strokes, and pays a fixed premium for dying.

notes.where: The stock end-of-run conversion of level reached and time survived into meta-currency, found across roguelites and survivors-likes, and Realm of the Mad God's fame, which is reckoned and paid out when the character dies; count-up tallies with sound go back to arcade score screens.
notes.mutation: Ring the count over the next vigil instead of on a results screen: each stroke owed sounds a second apart in the heir's first district and lays the dead nearest the new character, so a high character's death is a long protected opening that is played, not a number.

notes.where: The tellers and the strokes of age in Sayers' The Nine Tailors; Donne's bell; end-of-run tallies. Paying in strokes, with a fixed premium for dying, is its own.

name: Arrears
idea: A twist on one life and the tolls. Harm does not come off life when it lands. It is chalked on a slate as arrears. At each toll the slate is presented: life falls by the arrears and the slate is wiped. A character dies only at a toll, or at the instant arrears reach twice its remaining life. Between tolls arrears can be worked off: every experience pickup collected pays 1 point. The seconds before each bell are spent going back into the killing ground to pay.
source: A toll is both the stroke of a bell and a sum owed at a fixed point, and debts chalked on a slate fell due on a set day.
nearest: Delayed-damage pools cleared by a button, and regaining lost health by striking back quickly. Here one shared clock, the district bell, does all the collecting.

notes.where: WoW Brewmaster's Stagger (harm held in a pool that falls due later and can be cleared), with Bloodborne's rally and Dead Cells' recovery for winning lost life back by acting quickly; Street Fighter grey life.
notes.mutation: Chalk every mark to a creditor: arrears are owed to the particular dead thing that dealt them, laying it wipes its marks, and at the toll only creditors still standing collect, so the player pays by hunting down exactly what hurt them.

notes.where: Shylock's bond, falling due on a fixed day and paid in flesh; Dorian Gray, whose harm is held off and arrives all at once; the Brewmaster's Stagger in World of Warcraft and the rally of Bloodborne. One district bell that collects everything is its own.

name: Abjuration
idea: A twist on one life. At no life a standing character need not die. Once in each district it may abjure: it is given a cross, its skills fall silent, and it has 40 s to walk the straight marked road to the nearest gate. The dead may jostle but not harm it; pushed or stepping more than 3 m off the road, it dies. Reaching the gate saves the character, but all it carries is forfeit and that district is closed to it for good.
source: A felon in sanctuary could save his life by abjuring the realm: walking straight to an assigned port with a cross, losing his goods and never returning.
nearest: Second-wind and last-stand rules. This buys the life with a permanent loss of territory, five times at most, and it has to be walked.

notes.where: Borderlands' Fight For Your Life and other last-stand rules, WoW's ghost corpse run, Realm of the Mad God's escape to the Nexus to save a permadeath character. A walked, shove-able escape paid for with a district closed for good is its own.

Orpheus leading Eurydice out of death, saved only if he never looks back, and Lot's wife; 'stick to the road' in An American Werewolf in London; last-stand and second-wind rules. A life bought with a district closed for good is its own.

name: Tally at the Gate
idea: A twist on the gates. A gate offers two choices. Leave, banking everything as usual. Or split a tally and stay: half of what the character carries is banked now and is safe whatever happens; the gate keeps the stock and the character the foil. If the character later leaves alive by any gate in the same vigil, the halves are fitted and the half banked earlier is doubled. Only one tally can be open at a time. Dying with the foil loses the doubling, not the half.
source: With a split tally each party held half the record, and the bargain was completed when the halves were brought back together.
nearest: Safe-haven thresholds in quiz shows, and partial extraction. This adds a doubling that is paid only if the player also finishes alive.

notes.where: Push-your-luck banking in Incan Gold and Deep Sea Adventure, Loop Hero's retreat-or-die payout, quiz-show safe havens, Tarkov's secure container. The doubling of the earlier half on a later live exit is its own clause.
The safe havens of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, double or nothing; partial extraction. A doubling paid only on finishing alive is its own.

name: A Wake for Your Dead
idea: A twist on the two ways to play. The one-sitting run through five districts is always a wake held for one of the player's dead standing characters, chosen at the start. The new character begins as that one's class with its first three picks already taken. Each district completed is one watch of the night. If all five are kept, the dead character's name goes on the bede-roll and whatever it left in the permanent tree gives double from then on. A broken wake may be held again.
source: A body was watched through the night before burial, and the names of the dead were entered on a bede-roll to be read aloud.
nearest: Run modes that revisit a past character's grave or ghost. Here the short mode exists to complete the long mode's deaths, and inherits their opening choices.

notes.where: Wizardry rescue parties and corpse runs in Dark Souls and ZombiU (a new outing made for the sake of a dead character), Rogue Legacy heirs inheriting traits. A short mode that exists to complete the long mode's deaths is new to me.

The vigil over the dead in Gogol's Viy, three nights of reading over the witch's body; Finnegan's Wake; ghost runs against a past self; heirs in Rogue Legacy. A short mode held as a wake to complete a dead character is its own.

name: The Bell Tells What Comes
idea: A twist on the tolls. Each toll is not one stroke but a count. First the tellers: nine strokes if the coming 75 s will bring mostly large dead, six for middling, three for small and many. Then, after a pause, one quick stroke for each elite that will rise, and a single low stroke if a gate will open. A player who counts knows the next interval; one who does not is surprised by it. An option draws the count as marks, for play without sound.
source: Hearers of the death knell counted the tellers and the strokes of age to learn who had died before any news reached them.
nearest: Wave previews shown as icons. This puts the preview only in the synthesized bell, as a code the player learns to count.

notes.where: Left 4 Dead's audio stings announcing each special and the horde, tower-defence next-wave previews, Deep Rock Galactic swarm callouts. A counted code that states size, elites and gate in strokes I have not seen.

'One if by land, and two if by sea' in Longfellow's 'Paul Revere's Ride'; the tellers of the knell and the bell-ringing cipher of The Nine Tailors; bells rung backwards as an alarm; wave previews. The forecast carried only in a count of strokes is its own.

name: Posture harm: Blow, Drag, Knell
idea: Three kinds of harm, each blunted by a posture. Blows (single hits) are cut by Brace, in full only after 0.4 s standing still. Drag (harm per second inside a crowd or zone) is cut by Stride, in full only above 70% of top speed. Knells (announced area strikes) ignore stats; only an obstacle between source and target stops them. Enemies obey the same rules: runners are open to Blows, standers to Drag. Anything that turned over 90 degrees in the last 0.5 s is Wrong-footed and takes 50% more.
source: One thumb has three clean states in a crowd (stopped, walking, hidden behind something), so each kind of harm asks for a different one.
nearest: Stance systems in duelling games (Nioh, For Honor) swap stats by chosen stance; here there is no stance button, protection follows what the feet are already doing, and it applies to enemies too.

notes.where: Path of Exile's Arctic Armour (less harm from hits while stationary) and its 'while moving' defences; BattleTech's Brace against evasion earned by moving; hiding behind pillars from raid-boss blasts in World of Warcraft. No game found that maps three kinds of harm to three foot postures for both sides.

Three kinds of harm each with its own counter is stock (bludgeoning, piercing, slashing in D&D); 'only the pillar saves you from the dragon's breath' is the stock line-of-sight beat of film and raid; chosen stances in Nioh. Protection that simply follows what the feet are doing, for enemies too, I cannot place.

name: Depth of harm: Graze, Strike, Knell
idea: Harm has three depths, set by how long the attack was shown first. Graze (no warning) is cut by a flat Thickness per hit and returns at 8% of life per second after 3 s untouched. Strike (shown 0.4 to 1.5 s) is stopped only by Guards, charges that each swallow one Strike; Strike life and Guards return at the toll. Knell (shown over 1.5 s) meets no protection and mends only at a gate. If unreturned Graze exceeds 30% of life, further Grazes land as Strikes.
source: A one-life player wants to say exactly why they died, so the harm that lasts is always the harm that was shown longest.
nearest: Regenerating shield over health in shooters, and recoverable grey health in fighting games; here depth is set by warning time and the healers are the game's own toll and gate.

notes.where: Warhammer 40,000: Darktide's toughness, health and corruption (one layer regenerates, one does not, one is healed only at a station); trauma in Back 4 Blood; Halo shields; one-hit block charges. Setting the layer by how long the attack was shown is in none of them.

World of Darkness tabletop horror (Vampire: The Masquerade, Chronicles of Darkness): bashing, lethal and aggravated damage - three depths that heal at three speeds, are soaked less the deeper they go, and overflowing bashing is upgraded to lethal. Also the recharging shield over health of Halo.
notes.mutation: Drop the three-rung ladder and its overflow rule: let every wound keep the exact warning time it was shown for, and mend only when the player has stood still that many seconds on the spot where it landed, so harm is a debt in seconds owed to a place and not a tier.

name: In Procession
idea: An enemy that has chased the player for 5 s unbroken, staying within 2.5 m of the player's wake (the path of the last 4 s), is In Procession. It moves 15% faster, takes 30% more harm and drops 25% more experience. It ends when the enemy touches the player, is pushed, or strays more than 3 m off the wake. The count of processing enemies (cap 40) is a stat other effects can read.
source: A thumb leading a crowd in a train is the central act of the genre, and the train's length is cheap to count against a short list of past positions.
nearest: Aggro or threat stacks in online games; this one is earned only by being followed along a path and makes the follower both riper and faster.

notes.where: The ghost train in Pac-Man Championship Edition DX (enemies fall in behind you and the train's length is the prize); 'training' monsters in EverQuest. A follower status that makes the enemy faster, riper and countable is its own.

The Pied Piper's train; leading the herd down the road in The Walking Dead; MMO players 'training' monsters (EverQuest's 'train to zone'). A condition earned only by being followed along the wake, which makes the follower riper and faster, is in none of them.

name: Sounded
idea: Keep one warden, keeper or other large enemy between 4 m and 6 m away for 2 s without a break and it becomes Sounded for 6 s. Every range of harm against a Sounded enemy rolls its top value, and its attacks are shown 0.3 s earlier. Leaving the band for more than 0.5 s ends it; holding the band refreshes it. The band is drawn as two thin rings around the enemy.
source: Holding an exact distance from one enemy is a hard thing for a thumb, and a leadsman sounds depth by holding a marked line taut.
nearest: Sweet-spot spacing such as the tip of a sword in Smash Bros; here the spacing is held over time and pays in earlier warnings, not in one bigger hit.

notes.where: Critical distance for bows and bowguns in Monster Hunter (a range band where harm is best); the tipper sweet spot in Smash Bros; Close and Distant enemy states in Diablo 4. None asks for the band to be held over time or pays in earlier warnings.

Keeping measure (ma-ai) in fencing and samurai duels, where two fighters hold one distance and read each other; sweet-spot ranges such as the tip of Marth's sword. Spacing held over time that buys earlier warnings is its own.

name: Wound
idea: The game sums the signed angle the player travels around each warden, keeper or rooted enemy within 6 m. Each full sunwise circuit adds one Turn (max 3): the enemy's attacks come 12% slower per Turn. One full widdershins circuit spends all Turns at once; each deals a hit equal to 150% of the player's strongest sigil hit. Turns lapse 10 s after the last circuit. Turns show as coils around the enemy's base.
source: A thumb circles naturally and can circle either way, a free two-way choice; walking sunwise to bind and widdershins to undo is an old real custom.
nearest: Build-and-spend combo points (rogue classes in online games); here the building and the spending are the two directions of walking a circle round the target.

notes.where: The tow cable in Star Wars: Rogue Squadron (circle the walker several times to bind it); capture loops in Pokemon Ranger; combo points built and spent on one target. Winding one way and unwinding the other is not in them.

Folk circumambulation: thrice sunwise (deasil) to bless or bind, widdershins to undo or curse - Burd Ellen taken for running widdershins round the church in Childe Rowland, 'weave a circle round him thrice' in Kubla Khan; Joshua circling Jericho before the blow. The fiction is the old rite itself; the build-and-spend rule laid on it is new.

name: Clung
idea: Applied by small clingers that leap from 1.5 m. Each one riding the player adds a stack (max 5): 8% slower and 2 Drag harm per second per stack. Stacks never time out. Passing within 0.8 m of any obstacle at over 70% speed scrapes every clinger off and kills them; standing still lets one more climb on every 2 s. Clingers show as small boxes stuck to the figure.
source: Hugging an obstacle is something one thumb can do with precision, and things that cling are scraped off against stone.
nearest: Grab enemies shaken off by waggling the stick (Zelda's ReDeads); here the cure is a place and a pace, not a waggle.

notes.where: Zombie Highway (zombies leap onto your car, each one weighs it down, none lets go, and you scrape them off by sideswiping roadside wrecks at speed); the same in Mad Max and State of Decay; Micro-Goombas that cling to Mario and slow him.
notes.mutation: Let clingers be passed on, not scraped off: brushing within 0.8 m of a warden, keeper or other large enemy at speed moves every clinger onto it, where they drag and bite it instead. Stone does nothing; the cure is a dangerous neighbour.

notes.where: The Old Man of the Sea riding Sinbad's shoulders; the stock chase beat of scraping a clinging attacker off against a wall or a low branch; Zelda's Morths (The Wind Waker) and Poison Mites (Twilight Princess), which cling and slow until shaken off. A cure that is a place and a pace is its own.

name: Knotted
idea: When the player's path crosses their own wake laid in the last 5 s, every enemy within 2.5 m of the crossing point (up to 12) is Knotted for 3 s. Knotted enemies move 70% slower and each passes 20% of any harm it takes to every other member of the same knot. A knot ends early if fewer than two members remain. A knot is drawn as a loop on the ground.
source: Cutting back across the train you lead is a crisp thumb act, and a line crossed over itself is a knot.
nearest: Light-cycle trails in Tron, where crossing a trail kills; here crossing your own trail ties up whatever was following it.

notes.where: Warlock's Fatal Bonds in Dota 2 (linked enemies each take a share of harm dealt to any one of them) and Domino in Dishonored 2. The trigger, crossing your own wake, is new, but the condition it applies is that link plus a slow.
notes.mutation: Make the knot a rope, not a harm-share: knotted enemies are tied to the crossing point in the order they followed and can move only round it at rope's length; shoving or felling one jerks the next into it.

notes.where: Snowspeeders winding tow-cable round the AT-AT's legs in The Empire Strikes Back; the cartoon chase in which pursuers following a looping runner end up tied in a knot; Pokemon Ranger's drawn loops; soul-link curses that share harm. Crossing your own wake as the act that ties is its own.

name: Knee, Heel, Hand, Ear
idea: Four attributes, each tied to one thing the body does. Knee governs standing still: +1% to effects tagged Still per point, and life. Heel governs moving: +1% to effects tagged Moving, and less speed lost in a sharp turn. Hand governs nearness: +1% to effects on targets within 3 m, and pickup reach.
