Ear governs timing: +1% to effects tagged Timed, and every 10 points shows enemy warnings 0.05 s sooner. Sigils and gear each name one attribute and a number needed to use them.
source: The thumb can only stop, go, close in or wait for a moment, so the character sheet measures those four acts.
nearest: Strength, dexterity and intelligence triads; these are not kinds of person but kinds of moment, and each is switched on by what the player is doing.

notes.where: Approaches in Fate Accelerated and action ratings in Blades in the Dark (stats that are ways of acting, not kinds of person); attribute requirements on gear in Diablo 2 and Path of Exile, with their 'while stationary' and 'while moving' tags. Stats named for stop, go, near and wait are its own.

Body-named stat sets in tabletop games (head, heart and hands triads); one percent per point and a stat needed to use gear are the stock Diablo attribute. Attributes that measure kinds of moment (still, moving, near, timed) I cannot place in any story or game.

name: Ropewalker
idea: A maker of bell-ropes. Walking within 10 degrees of one heading pays out rope from where the straight began. Turning more than 35 degrees, or reaching 14 m, pegs it as a taut line for 5 s (three lines at most). Starting sigil, Standing Line: enemies crossing a line take harm multiplied by its length over 4 m and are slowed 40% for 1 s. The thumb draws long straights and sharp corners.
source: Ropemakers really walked backwards down a long straight ropewalk paying out fibre, and a straight line is the plainest thing a thumb can hold.
nearest: Trail weapons such as the Tron light-cycle wall; here only a straight walk makes a line, its length is its strength, and the turn is what sets it.

notes.where: Light-cycle walls in Tron; Blaze in Diablo 2 and Singed's poison trail in League of Legends (harm laid by walking); laser fences between posts in Command & Conquer. A line whose strength is the length of an unbroken straight walk is not in them.

Tron's light cycles (the 1982 film and every game since): long straights and sharp corners that leave walls punishing whatever crosses them. Also the rope stretched across the road to unhorse riders (Sleepy Hollow, the Ewoks' trip-lines). Length-as-strength and the turn that pegs are the fresh part.
notes.mutation: Make it a rope and not a wall: a pegged line lies slack and harmless, and only the next straight walked directly away from its peg hauls it taut for as long as that walk lasts, so harm comes from pulling a line laid earlier instead of from leaving a trail.

name: Mute
idea: A hired mourner who stands silent at doors. Class rule: the Mute becomes Unheard after 0.6 s still instead of 1 s, even with enemies as near as 1 m. Starting sigil, Last Word: on the first step out of stillness, everything within 4 m that is facing away from the Mute is hit, harm growing 50% per second held still (cap 3 s). The thumb freezes in the crowd's path, lets it pass, then moves.
source: Victorian funerals hired mutes to stand motionless at the door, and standing still as the crowd arrives is the hardest thing to ask of a player's nerves.
nearest: Stand-still damage bonuses in survivor games; here stillness is the dodge itself and the hit lands only on backs that have walked past.

notes.where: The Spy with the Cloak and Dagger in Team Fortress 2 (stand still unseen while enemies walk past, then stab their backs); the stealth-then-backstab opener of rogues in World of Warcraft; Brotato's Soldier, who attacks only while still.
notes.mutation: Drop the bonus on backs. Let Last Word run down the file of enemies in the order they walked past the Mute, each stroke stronger than the one before, so the Mute wants a long single-file stream and not merely turned backs.

notes.where: The thief's backstab from hiding (the D&D rogue, Ambush in World of Warcraft) joined to stand-still invisibility that pays a bonus when broken - Teemo's passive in League of Legends, the Spy's Cloak and Dagger in Team Fortress 2. The funeral mute as a figure is in Oliver Twist (Oliver walks as Sowerberry's mute), though not as a fighter.
notes.mutation: Drop the back-stab test: Last Word strikes everything that crossed an unseen threshold line through the Mute's shoulders while it stood, growing per crosser and not per second, so the class counts who came through the door it kept instead of whose back is turned.

name: Lamplighter
idea: Walks a round of lamps. Six lamp posts stand in each district. Passing within 2 m lights one for 45 s; every toll puts all out. Each lit lamp raises sigil cast rate 10% and shows warnings inside its 5 m light 0.4 s sooner. Starting sigil, Taper: every 2 s each lit lamp throws a spark at the enemy nearest to it. The thumb plans a circuit and keeps it against the clock.
source: Lamplighters walked a fixed round to light every lamp before dark, which is reaching places before a deadline, over and over.
nearest: Totem or turret upkeep classes; here the posts are fixed places in the district, so the class is a route and a timetable, not a placement.

notes.where: Timed light-every-torch puzzles in Zelda; totem upkeep classes and EverQuest bards twisting short songs; perk machines at fixed places in Call of Duty Zombies. A class that is a round of fixed posts kept against the wave clock is its own.

The lamplighter of The Little Prince, bound to relight a lamp that a relentless clock keeps putting out; the leeries of Mary Poppins Returns; Stevenson's 'The Lamplighter'. Timed light-all-the-torches puzzles in Zelda and capture-point upkeep in shooters. A class that is a route and a timetable round fixed posts is its own.

name: Bierman
idea: Carries the plank a coffin rides on, held in front. Blows arriving within the 120-degree arc ahead of the heading are cut 60%; blows from behind land 40% harder. Starting sigil, Shoulder: every 1.2 s strikes a box 3 m long and 2 m wide straight ahead and shoves what it hits 1.5 m. The thumb walks toward what it wants hurt and chooses which crowd gets its back.
source: With one thumb, facing and heading are the same thing, so choosing which of two crowds to face is a real decision only if the back is weak.
nearest: Shield-bearing enemies and directional blocking in action games; here the player carries it in a horde, with no block button, and pays for it behind.

notes.where: Mars's Bulwark in Dota 2 (a passive shield that cuts harm arriving in the front arc by facing alone, with no button) and Bristleback's armoured rear; the shield-bash tank class generally.
notes.mutation: Give the plank weight: it keeps the heading of one second ago and swings round after the turn, so a quick turn leaves the new front bare and the old side covered, and every corner is planned around where the bier still points.

notes.where: The stock shield-bearer: big shield in front, bare back, shield bash - hoplites and riot shields in fiction, Reinhardt in Overwatch, Mars's Bulwark in Dota 2 (harm cut by facing), lance and greatshield play in Monster Hunter and Dark Souls. Only the coffin plank is new.
notes.mutation: Fix the guarded arc to the compass bearing walked at the last toll instead of to the facing: for that whole toll period the bier guards one side of the world, drawn on the ground, and the player must keep the crowd on that side until the bell lets them choose again.

name: Leadsman
idea: Sounds the flooded streets with a weighted line. Starting sigil, Lead Line: a weight circles at 5 m and hits only enemies between 4.3 m and 5.7 m from the player; anything nearer is untouched. Class rule: the Sounded condition needs 1 s in the band instead of 2 s. The thumb keeps the crowd at exactly arm's length and steps back whenever it closes inside the swing.
source: A leadsman swings a weighted line to a known mark, and holding an exact distance is a distinct skill of the steering thumb.
nearest: Orbiting weapons in survivor games, which protect the body; this one leaves the body bare and works only at one distance.

notes.where: The original Aurelion Sol in League of Legends (stars orbit at a fixed radius, hit only at that radius, and enemies inside the orbit are untouched); King Bible and Unholy Vespers in Vampire Survivors; Darius's outer-ring blade.
notes.mutation: Pay for the empty middle, not the orbit: each swing's harm is multiplied by the enemies in the band and divided by those inside it, so a clean interior is the weapon and one enemy let inside spoils the stroke.

notes.where: Meteor-hammer and chain-weapon duels in which the swung weight kills at its arc and is useless inside it (Gogo Yubari in Kill Bill); the 'get inside the reach' rule of every spear and whip fight; Mark Twain's leadsman for the figure; orbiting weapons in Vampire Survivors. An orbit with a bare middle as a whole class is its own.

name: Verger
idea: Walks ahead of processions with a rod. Starting sigil, Turn About: fires only when the heading reverses by 150 degrees or more within 0.3 s; a wave runs 12 m back along the wake, hitting each enemy for base harm plus 3% per enemy In Procession (cap 40). It recharges in 2 s. The thumb leads a long tidy train, growing greedier, then flicks back through it.
source: A verger really walks at the head of a procession to clear its way, and a thumb's reversal is a sharper event than any turn.
nearest: Kiting a pack and turning to strike it, done in every action game; here the reversal itself is the trigger and the train's length is the multiplier.

notes.where: Pac-Man Championship Edition DX: lead an ever longer train of ghosts, grow greedy, then turn back and run down the whole train for a prize that rises with its length. Only the trigger differs, a U-turn in place of a pellet.
notes.mutation: Do not harm the train: turn it. The wave about-faces each enemy In Procession and marches it back down the wake for 3 s, trampling whatever comes behind; harm is done by the turned bodies and counted by how many were turned.

notes.where: The feigned retreat that wheels on strung-out pursuers: Livy's last Horatius turning on the three Curiatii, the Parthian shot, the Normans at Hastings; the Pied Piper's train. Maugham's 'The Verger' has the figure only. A reversal as the trigger with the train's length as the multiplier is its own.

name: Mudlark
idea: Scavenges the drowned foreshore. Starting sigil, Pocketful: every pickup collected throws one stone at the nearest enemy; five pickups within 1 s throw a sixth that pierces. Class rule: each unbanked item carried adds 3% harm. The thumb steers through fields of dropped shards while they still lie among enemies, instead of circling and sweeping up afterwards.
source: Mudlarks picked a living out of river mud, and fear grows with what is carried, so this class is strongest when it has most to lose.
nearest: On-pickup effects in survivor games (heal on gem); here collecting is the only way the class attacks at all.

notes.where: Brotato's Lucky character and Baby Elephant item (picking up a material deals harm to a random enemy); Money = Power in The Binding of Isaac (harm per coin held).
notes.mutation: Let each pickup fire from where it lay back along the straight line to the previous pickup, piercing everything on that segment, so the order in which the shards are gathered draws the attack.

notes.where: Mudlarks in Mayhew and Dickens (the river scavengers of Our Mutual Friend), Pratchett's Dodger; the hoard that makes its keeper stronger (Smaug's jewelled belly); greed-scaling items such as Money = Power in The Binding of Isaac. Attacking only by picking things up is its own.

name: Winder
idea: Winds the tower clocks. The game sums how far the heading rotates. Each full sunwise circle walked stores one Turn (max 3). Starting sigil, Mainspring: a full widdershins circle releases a ring from the centre of that circle, radius 3 m plus 2 m per Turn, harm doubled per Turn. Turns lapse 12 s after the last circle. The thumb draws loops around a clump one way, then once the other way.
source: A thumb draws circles without thought and can tell the two directions apart perfectly, and tower clocks were wound by turning a crank.
nearest: Full-circle stick motions for command grabs in fighting games; here the circle is walked on the ground, its centre is where the release lands, and direction carries the meaning.

notes.where: Capture loops in Pokemon Ranger; winding up Bowser by rotating the stick in Super Mario 64; Zangief's full-circle motion; spinning one way or the other to choose Alcremie's form in Pokemon Sword and Shield. A walked circle stored one way and released the other is its own.

Joshua's circuits of Jericho before the walls fall; the cartoon wind-up punch; Hugo Cabret winding the station clocks for the figure; full-circle stick motions in fighting games and drawn circles in Pokemon Ranger. Walked loops whose direction means wind or release are its own.

name: Rigger (Ropewalker)
idea: New rule: three pegged lines that close a triangle make a Fold. For 4 s the lines are walls to the enemies inside, who cannot leave, and every sigil hit landing inside the Fold strikes twice. The lines forming a Fold expire together. Folds larger than 60 square metres do not form. The thumb now walks three straights to pen a crowd rather than one to trip it.
source: Tracing a shape is within a thumb's reach if the shape is three straight walks and two corners.
nearest: Area-claiming by closed loops in Qix; here the shape is made of at most three straight segments, each of which had to be walked through the crowd.

notes.where: Qix and Libble Rabble (close a shape to claim what is inside); Disruptor's Kinetic Field in Dota 2 (a ring enemies cannot leave). A pen made of three walked straight lines is not in them.

The closed warding figure that holds spirits inside it: the Triangle of Art of the Goetia, the devil's trap of Supernatural, the chalk or salt circle of every exorcism story. In games, capture by enclosure in Qix and Pokemon Ranger.
notes.mutation: Make the closed triangle a drawstring and not a ward: its three lines slide inward for 4 s, dragging what is inside toward the centre, and one hit lands when they meet, scaled by how much ground was drawn shut.

name: Chief Mourner (Mute)
idea: New rule: every enemy that passes within 1.5 m of the Mute while the Mute is Unheard is Passed for 5 s, shown by a bowed head. A Passed enemy takes 60% more from the Mute's next hit on it and, if that hit kills it, falls without noise, so the crowd does not turn. The reward is for standing exactly where the stream is thickest.
source: Threading a gap can be done by not moving at all, if the player has the nerve to let the gap come to them.
nearest: Graze scoring in bullet-hell shooters, which pays for near misses while dodging; this pays for near misses while standing still.

notes.where: Sneak-attack rules in Skyrim and Dishonored (an unaware enemy takes a multiplied hit and dies without alerting the rest); hiding-spot kills in Assassin's Creed as guards pass within reach.
notes.mutation: Let Passed change where they go, not how hard they are hit: a Passed enemy has paid its respects and will not turn back for 5 s whatever the Mute then does, so standing in the stream sorts the crowd into gone and still coming.

notes.where: Standing still while the procession of the dead goes by (the Wild Hunt, Galicia's Santa Compana); silent takedowns that do not alert the pack in stealth fiction (Assassin's Creed, Dishonored); graze scoring in Touhou. Being paid for being brushed past while motionless is its own.

name: Snuffer (Lamplighter)
idea: New rule: passing a lit lamp a second time snuffs it. Snuffing hits everything in its 5 m light for harm equal to the seconds it burned times a base value, and enemies caught lose the player for 3 s, holding their last heading. The Lamplighter now chooses at every post between keeping the upkeep bonus and cashing it in.
source: A round of fixed posts gives a decision at each one only if returning to a post can mean two different things.
nearest: Detonating your own placed traps or mines; here the thing spent is a standing bonus on a clock, and its age is its payout.

notes.where: Templar Assassin's Psionic Trap in Dota 2 (stronger the longer it has sat before you set it off); a paladin's Seal spent by Judgement in World of Warcraft. Snuffing a fixed post you were keeping lit, for its age, is its own.

Grimm's 'Godfather Death', where a life is a candle and death is its snuffing; the stock 'kill the lights and slip away' escape; detonating your own totems or traps in action role-playing games. Cashing in a standing bonus by its age at a fixed post is its own.

name: Lychwarden (Bierman)
idea: New rule: enemies killed inside the front arc while walking forward are laid on the bier, up to 6. Standing still for 1 s sets the bier down as an obstacle 3 m wide for 6 s plus 1 s per body. It blocks enemies and counts as shelter from Knells. Walking into it picks it up again. The Bierman builds a wall where one is wanted.
source: A bier was set down at the lychgate while the bearers waited, and a thumb that can hug an obstacle would like to bring one along.
nearest: Deployable cover in shooters; here the cover is paid for in kills made while advancing and is placed by the act of stopping.

notes.where: The Meat Wagon in Warcraft 3 (gathers up to eight corpses to carry); Bone Wall in Diablo 2; deployable cover in Gears of War. A wall paid for in kills made while advancing and set down by stopping is its own.

The Spartans' wall of Persian dead in 300 and the corpse barricades of zombie films; the necromancer's Bone Wall in Diablo II and Magic's Wall of Corpses; pick-up-again deployable shields in Rainbow Six Siege; the bier rested at the lychgate. A wall carried along, paid for in kills and set down by stopping is its own.

name: Deep-caller (Leadsman)
idea: New rule: standing still for 1 s resets the swing radius of every Leadsman sigil to the distance of the nearest enemy at that moment, anywhere between 2 m and 8 m, drawn as a chalk ring. The band stays that size until the next deliberate stop. The player tunes reach to the fight by choosing how close to let something come before stopping.
source: Stopping for a set time and holding a distance are two thumb acts that can be joined: the stop measures, the walk keeps.
nearest: none known; range is normally a stat on the weapon, not something the player measures off by letting an enemy approach.

notes.where: Io's Spirits In and Out in Dota 2 and Aurelion Sol's expanding stars (an orbit whose radius the player changes); zeroing a scope to a ranged target in Arma. Setting the radius by letting an enemy come close and then stopping is not in them.

Distant only: a sniper zeroing the scope to a ranged target, naval ranging shots before firing for effect, the leadsman calling the mark in Mark Twain. I know nothing in which an approaching enemy sets the weapon's reach.

name: Marshal (Verger)
idea: New rule: when the Verger stands still, enemies In Procession halt where they are for as long as the Verger stays still, up to 4 s, and cannot be halted again for 6 s. Enemies not In Procession keep coming. A halted train counts as standing for every rule that asks, so the Verger chooses when followers are runners and when they are standers.
source: A real procession stops when the one leading it stops, and it gives the lifted thumb a second meaning.
nearest: Crowd-freeze skills on a cooldown; this one stops only those the player has been leading and leaves the flanks alive.

notes.where: SUPERHOT (the world moves only when you move); Goriyas in Zelda: A Link to the Past, which move only when Link moves. Halting only those who were led, to switch them from runner to stander, is its own.

Follow-the-leader and Grandmother's Footsteps; a drill column halting on its leader; the Pied Piper's children; SUPERHOT, where the world moves only when you move. Halting only those the player has been leading, flanks left alive, is its own.

name: Jackdaw (Mudlark)
idea: New rule: one extra button throws the newest unbanked item 6 m ahead. It bursts in 3 m for harm equal to 200% of the strongest sigil hit for each notch on the item, and the item is destroyed. Banked items cannot be thrown. Every find becomes a question: carry it to a gate, or spend it now to live.
source: Whether to spend something that does not come back is one of the few weighty decisions a run offers.
nearest: Coin-firing weapons such as Terraria's Coin Gun; here the ammunition is the unbanked reward of this very run, one piece at a time.

notes.where: The Throw command in Final Fantasy (hurl a weapon from the pack for harm set by its quality; it is used up) and Fling in Pokemon; Tediore reload-throws in Borderlands 2; the Coin Gun in Terraria.
notes.mutation: Throw the history, not the object: the thrown item bursts once per notch and is left lying blank where it fell, to be picked up and notched again, so what is spent is the tolls it was carried through.

notes.where: Final Fantasy's Throw command (the Ninja hurls weapons out of the pack, consumed, harm by the item's worth) and Gil Toss; Pokemon's Fling; Terraria's Coin Gun. In story, Hippomenes throwing away the golden apples to win the race with Atalanta.
notes.mutation: Do not burn the find for one burst: cast it down as a standing charge that bursts and loses one notch each time the player's path re-crosses it, and that can be picked up again with whatever notches are left, so the item is whittled and not spent.

name: Regulator (Winder)
idea: New rule: sunwise circles walked around an open gate or the district's bell-post wind that object instead of the Winder. Each Turn holds a gate open 4 s longer (max 12 s) or delays the next toll by 3 s (max 9 s). Each widdershins circle around the bell-post brings the toll 3 s nearer. The Winder edits the public clock by walking.
source: The toll is a public clock the player plans around, and a class that winds clocks should be able to move its hands a little.
nearest: Time-extension pickups in arcade racers; here the clock is moved both ways, by a walked gesture, around a place that has to be reached and held.

notes.where: The Inverted Song of Time and Song of Double Time in Majora's Mask (the player slows or hastens the doom clock); Chronostasis in Lightning Returns; walking a capstan round in Sea of Thieves. Winding the wave clock by walked circles is its own.

The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask, where the player slows or hurries the bell-tower town's public doom clock (Inverted Song of Time, Song of Double Time); Superman circling the Earth backwards to wind time back; Hermione's Time-Turner counted in turns; time-extension pickups in arcade racers.
notes.mutation: Do not move the clock's hands, move its aim: circles walked round the bell-post step the next surge's entry door one radial stone sunwise or widdershins, and circles round a gate move that gate, so the Regulator edits where the bell strikes and never when.

name: Plumb
idea: Marks the last spot where the player stood still for 0.5 s or more; the mark moves only at the next such stop. Every 3 s a weight drops on the mark, radius 2.5 m. Harm rises 10% for each second the mark has stayed put (cap 100%). The player stops once in a well-chosen place, then leads the crowd back across it.
source: Returning to where you were is a thumb act that needs the game to remember one place, and a stop is the cheapest way to name it.
nearest: Placed turrets and traps; this has no placing action or count, only the memory of the last deliberate stop.

notes.where: Turrets dropped at the player's feet on a timer in Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor; Brands in Path of Exile; the ramping Inferno Tower in Clash of Clans. A mark that is simply the last deliberate stop is not in them.

Wile E. Coyote's X-marked spot under the falling anvil, to which the quarry must be led back; ramping turrets and traps left in place in action role-playing games; the plumb line of Amos for the image. A mark set only by the last deliberate stop is its own.

name: Hitch
idea: Casts whenever the player's path crosses their own wake laid in the last 5 s; recharge 1.5 s. At the crossing point every enemy within 2.5 m takes base harm multiplied by the number of enemies caught (cap 12) and becomes Knotted. It works better with a long train and a tight cut back across it; a figure of eight ties two knots per lap.
source: Leading a crowd in a train and cutting back across it is the most skilful thing a thumb does in this genre and no game pays for the crossing itself.
nearest: Loop-closing captures in Pokemon Ranger; here no loop need close, only the path must cross itself, and the crossing point is the whole effect.

notes.where: Pokemon Ranger (a loop is made when the line crosses itself, and pays on what is inside); loop closing in Paper.io. Paying at the crossing point itself, for the train caught there, was not found.

The tow-cable round the AT-AT's legs in The Empire Strikes Back; the lasso, and the Looney Tunes chase tied in a knot; closing loops in Pokemon Ranger and Qix. A strike on the crossing point itself, with no loop needed, is its own.

name: Long Draw
idea: Every 1 s fires one shot straight ahead and one straight behind. The rear shot gains 10% harm and 0.5 m width for each second the heading has stayed within 15 degrees (cap 10 s); any sharper turn resets it. It picks no target: it acts along the line of travel. The player holds a straight line through danger for as long as nerve allows.
source: Walking a straight line is easy for a thumb and frightening in a crowd, which makes it worth paying for by the second.
nearest: Forward-and-back firing weapons in survivor games; here the rear shot is a meter of how long the player refused to turn.

notes.where: Whip and Knife in Vampire Survivors (fire along the facing, front and back); tail guns in Gradius; the Lance charge in Monster Hunter that builds while running straight. A rear shot that meters seconds without turning is its own.

The Parthian shot loosed backwards from a straight gallop; 'Stay on target' in the Death Star trench, the reward for refusing to swerve; fore-and-aft weapons in Vampire Survivors. The rear shot as a meter of unturned seconds is its own.

name: Needle's Eye
idea: Casts when the player passes between two enemies that are less than 2.5 m apart and on opposite sides (bearings over 120 degrees apart) without being hit in that half second; recharge 0.8 s. A stitch runs through both enemies and 6 m beyond each, piercing everything on the line. The player hunts gaps in the crowd instead of avoiding the crowd.
source: Threading a gap is a precise, repeatable thumb act and the two enemies that made the gap give the shot its line for free.
nearest: Graze bonuses in bullet-hell shooters; here the near miss must be between a pair, and the pair defines where the attack goes.

notes.where: Pacifism gates in Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved 2 (fly between two posts to set off a blast); graze in Touhou and near-miss boost in Burnout. A gap made by two enemies, who then give the shot its line, was not found.

Scylla and Charybdis and the Clashing Rocks, the passage between two dangers; the stock fight gag of slipping between two attackers so that they strike each other; graze bonuses in Touhou. A near miss that must be between a pair, who then give the shot its line, is its own.

name: Held Breath
idea: Charges while the player stands still, up to 3 s, shown as a ring closing on the feet. On the first step it fires a cone in the direction of that step: 4 m long plus 2 m per second held, 60 degrees wide. Waiting past 3 s loses nothing. The first movement after a stop is the aim, so the escape route is also the shot.
source: With no hover and one thumb, the first step after a stop is the only pure pointing gesture the player has.
nearest: Charge shots released by letting go of a button; here the charge is stillness and the release is a direction walked.

notes.where: Archero (stand still to attack, move to stop); Shadow Pinion in Vampire Survivors (builds while moving, fires on stopping); pull-and-release aiming in Monster Strike. Stillness as the charge and the first step as the aim is its own.

The iaido showdown of samurai film: long stillness, then one step and one cut (Sanjuro's last duel, Zatoichi); the dragon's drawn breath before the flame; hold-and-release charge shots (Mega Man). Stillness as the charge and the first step as the aim is its own.

name: Quarters
idea: Strikes around the player at each quarter of the toll interval: at 18.75 s, 37.5 s, 56.25 s and on the toll itself. Radius is 3, 4, 5 and 6 m; harm doubles each time (1, 2, 4 and 8 times base). A shrinking ring shows the last 2 s before each. The player arranges to be inside the thickest crowd exactly as the bell rings, when the new surge also arrives.
source: The toll is a clock everyone can see, and old tower clocks had jack figures that struck the quarters before the hour.
nearest: Periodic pulse weapons in survivor games; this one keeps the district's public time, so its biggest stroke always coincides with the moment danger rises.

notes.where: Periodic pulses in Vampire Survivors (Pentagram, La Borra); the fourth-beat finisher in Hi-Fi Rush; effects that fire on the day tick in Loop Hero. A weapon that keeps the quarters of the wave clock is its own.

The Westminster Quarters, whose chime grows longer each quarter until the hour; clock jacks striking the quarters (Jack Blandiver at Wells); Poe's ebony clock in 'The Masque of the Red Death'; periodic pulse weapons in survivor games. A pulse that keeps the run's public time is its own.

name: Counterweight
idea: Every 1.5 s counts the enemies within 6 m on the left and on the right of the heading. It strikes the side with fewer, hitting each enemy there for base harm times the ratio of the larger count to the smaller (cap 4). With one side empty it does nothing. The player walks the seam between a big crowd and a small one and keeps both alive.
source: Choosing which of two crowds to face becomes richer if the crowd you spare is doing work for you.
nearest: none known; skills that grow with nearby enemy count exist, but not one that spends one crowd's size on the other.

notes.where: Skills that grow with the count of enemies near (Legion Commander's Overwhelming Odds in Dota 2; harm per nearby enemy in Path of Exile). Distant: nothing found that weighs the crowd on one hand against the crowd on the other and strikes the lighter side.

Distant only: the scales of judgement (Anubis weighing the heart, 'weighed in the balances and found wanting'); balance meters such as the Eclipse druid in World of Warcraft. I know nothing that spends the size of one crowd on the other.

name: Knock-up
idea: Every 2 s raps the nearest obstacle within 2 m of the player. A ring leaves the obstacle, radius 5 m. Enemies on the far side of the obstacle from the player take double harm. With no obstacle in reach it does not cast. The player fights from behind pillars and posts, keeping stone between body and crowd, and moves from one to the next.
source: Knockers-up were paid to rap on windows with a pole, and hugging an obstacle is a thumb act that deserves a sigil of its own.
nearest: Ricochet shots off walls; here the obstacle is the origin of the attack and the player's side of it is the weak side.

notes.where: Hoodwink's Bushwhack and Windranger's Shackleshot in Dota 2 (skills that work only with a tree in reach); Geomancy in Final Fantasy Tactics; fighting from cover in Gears of War. An attack that starts at the obstacle and favours its far side is its own.

Knocking spirits in the rock (Cornish knockers, King's The Tommyknockers); the knocker-up with her pole (the picture book Mary Smith); earthbenders striking stone so the blow comes out of the far side (Avatar: The Last Airbender); totem-origin spells and bank shots. The obstacle as origin with a weak near side is its own.

name: Bell-rope
idea: Every 8 s pins a rope's end where the player stands; for 5 s a taut rope joins that pin to the player. Enemies touching the rope take harm four times a second. Past 9 m the rope snaps and the cast ends. It picks no target: the player sweeps the rope like a clock hand by walking an arc around the pin.
source: Circling a point is natural to a thumb, and a line from a fixed point to a moving body turns that circle into a sweep.
nearest: Tether beams between two co-op players; here one end is where you stood, and the single player swings the other.

notes.where: Searing Bond in Path of Exile: a planted totem joined to the player by a burning beam that harms whatever touches it, swept by walking. Io's Tether in Dota 2 is the same line between two bodies.
notes.mutation: Make the rope rake, not burn: enemies it meets are carried along its sweep, and when it goes slack each one takes harm for every metre it was dragged, so the arc walked gathers a heap and then pays for it.

notes.where: The steel cable strung between two cars to scythe a herd of walkers in The Walking Dead; a chain between two riders; the maypole and tetherball sweep; tether beams between co-op partners. One end pinned where you stood and the other swung by walking is its own.

name: Appointment
idea: Every 12 s marks a spot 9 m ahead along the current heading with a ring that closes over 4 s. If the player is within 2 m of the spot when it closes, a strike of 5 m radius lands there and spares the player; if not, a strike of 2 m radius lands at a third of the harm. The heading at marking time chooses the place.
source: Reaching a place before a deadline is a complete small drama for one thumb, repeatable every few seconds.
nearest: Stand-in-the-circle buffs in action role-playing games; here the player's arrival is the key that turns a weak strike into a strong one.

notes.where: Tower markers in Final Fantasy XIV raids (be inside the ring when it resolves or the result is worse); a mage's Rune of Power in World of Warcraft; delayed air-strike markers. A self-set rendezvous that upgrades the player's own strike is its own.

'The Appointment in Samarra' (Maugham's retelling): a meeting kept at a fixed place and hour; raid 'soak' circles that must be stood in as they close (World of Warcraft, Final Fantasy XIV); stand-in-the-circle shrines. A strike that is weak unless the player keeps the appointment is its own.

name: Bounds
idea: Tracks the most northerly, southerly, easterly and westerly points the player has reached since its last cast. Every 15 s it strikes every enemy inside that rectangle, drawn beforehand as four corner stakes. Harm is base times 100 divided by the rectangle's area in square metres (cap 4 times). Small tight bounds hit hard; a wide walk hits many lightly.
source: Parishes really walked their boundary once a year to fix it in memory, and the extent of a walk is four numbers.
nearest: none known; territory games fill enclosed loops, but this takes only the extremes of where the feet have been.

notes.where: Drag-select rectangles in strategy games; area claimed by closed lines in Qix; Concentrated Effect in Path of Exile (less area, more harm). All distant: nothing found that strikes the bounding box of where the feet have been.

Tolstoy's 'How Much Land Does a Man Need?', where the land is whatever you can walk round and greed for wide bounds is the danger; Dido's oxhide; the Rogationtide beating of the bounds; territory by path in Qix. Taking only the four extremes of a walk as the strike box is its own.

name: Dead Stop
idea: Casts at the instant the player stops after moving for at least 2 s; recharge 1.5 s. A stamp hits around the feet, radius 3 m plus 1 m per 2 s of unbroken movement before the stop (cap 6 m), and pushes enemies 1 m out. Lifting the thumb is the trigger, so the player chooses the moment and the place of every cast.
source: Lifting the thumb off the glass is a distinct physical event with exact timing, and no game treats it as a trigger.
nearest: Ground-pound on landing in platformers; here the trigger is the end of a walk, in a game where everything else fires by itself.

notes.where: Shadow Pinion in Vampire Survivors (builds while you move, strikes when you stop) and Archero, whose whole control is lift the thumb to attack. The claim that no game treats the lifted thumb as a trigger is wrong.
notes.mutation: Make it a brake-check: the stamp waits 0.6 s after the stop and its harm is multiplied by the followers that run into the player's back in that time, so the train piling up, not the length of the run, is the stroke.

notes.where: The Road Runner's dead stop that sends the chaser sailing past; momentum-then-release effects (the Momentum support in Path of Exile) and ground-pounds on landing. The lifted thumb as the only trigger is its own.

name: Slip-knot
idea: The bound sigil no longer casts on its timer. It stores up to 3 casts and lets all of them go at the instant the player stops moving. Cost: casts beyond the third are lost, and the sigil's recharge runs 20% slower. The player decides when and where every cast happens by choosing when to lift the thumb.
source: The release of the thumb is an exact event the player controls, so it can stand in for a fire button without adding one.
nearest: Trigger supports in Path of Exile that cast on a condition; this condition is the player's own stop, not a hit or a kill.

notes.where: Unleash Support in Path of Exile (stores up to three repeats of the spell and lets them all go at once), with Archero's stop-to-fire as the release.
notes.mutation: Keep the stop as the trigger but let the walk place the targets: each stored cast is tied to one sharp corner turned since the last release and lands on that corner, so the path sets the marks and the stop only fires them.

notes.where: 'Hold... hold... now!' - the held volley of every film battle (Braveheart); trigger and charge-storing supports in Path of Exile. The player's own stop as the trigger is its own.

name: Back-splice
idea: The bound sigil acts from the point where the player stood 2 s ago, drawn as a faint standing figure, and chooses its targets from there. Cost: 15% slower casting, and the sigil cannot see enemies nearer than 2 m to the player's present position. A led train is always on top of the place the player just left.
source: The common dead arrive where the player was, not where the player is, so the past position is the best-placed caster on the field.
nearest: Afterimage or echo casters such as Mirage Archer in Path of Exile; here the origin is strictly the player's own position two seconds back.

notes.where: Options in Gradius: helpers that sit exactly where the ship was a moment ago along its path and fire its weapons from there. Ekko's trailing afterimage in League of Legends marks the same past position.
notes.mutation: Make it a rear-guard that is dropped and held: the figure stays at the spot 2 s back until no enemy is left within 3 m of it, and only then jumps to the new spot, so it finishes a clump before it follows.

notes.where: Ekko's trailing afterimage of where he stood seconds ago (League of Legends, Arcane); Peter Pan's shadow acting apart from him; Dragon Ball's afterimages; Mirage Archer in Path of Exile; the Cosmic Clones of Super Mario Galaxy 2. A past self as caster, blind around the present self, is its own.

name: Running Line
idea: While the heading has changed less than 15 degrees over the last second, the bound sigil casts 60% faster. Cost: any sharper turn stops the sigil entirely for 0.7 s. It makes any sigil a straight-line sigil and makes each corner a small silence that the player must place with care.
source: A straight heading is the easiest thing for a thumb to hold and the first thing fear makes it give up.
nearest: Bonuses while moving in survivor games; this pays only for not turning, and charges for the turn.

notes.where: 'While moving' and 'while stationary' conditions on supports and gear in Path of Exile; Hermes' boons in Hades that pay for speed; momentum upgrades in survivor games. A bonus for not turning, with a silence charged for each corner, is its own.

'Stay on target' and the steady bombing run (Star Wars, The Dam Busters); a broadside that needs a held course; while-moving bonuses in survivor games. Paying for not turning and charging a silence for each corner is its own.

name: Stone's Answer
idea: Each cast of the bound sigil is repeated 0.3 s later from the nearest obstacle within 6 m of the player, aimed from the obstacle's position. Cost: the repeat deals 60% harm, and with no obstacle in reach the sigil's own cast is 20% weaker. Ground with pillars doubles the sigil; open ground weakens it.
source: Hugging an obstacle should change what a build can do, so that where to fight is a choice made before the fight.
nearest: Repeat-cast supports such as Spell Echo; here the second cast comes from a fixed thing in the world that the player must stay near.

notes.where: Spell Echo and spell totems in Path of Exile (a repeat, or a cast from another origin); Qiyana in League of Legends drawing power from the nearest wall. A repeat that comes from the nearest piece of the map is its own.

The nymph Echo answering from the rocks; 'the stone shall cry out of the wall' (Habakkuk 2:11); Spell Echo and Spell Totem in Path of Exile. A repeat thrown back from whatever stone stands nearest is its own.

name: Pawned
idea: Each cast of the bound sigil spends 1 unbanked coin carried and deals 50% more harm. Cost: the coin is gone; with none carried, the sigil casts at half harm. The count on the pack falls visibly with every cast, so staying to fight eats what the gate would have banked.
source: Fear grows with what is carried, and a sigil that burns the carried sum turns that fear into a running meter.
nearest: Money-as-ammunition items in The Binding of Isaac; here the money is the unbanked take of a one-life vigil, lost for good.

notes.where: Gil Toss in Final Fantasy (spend money for harm); the Microtransaction Gun in Enter the Gungeon and the Coin Gun in Terraria (currency as ammunition); Money = Power in The Binding of Isaac.
notes.mutation: Pawn it, do not burn it: each cast leaves one carried coin lying where the cast landed for 10 s; walking back over it redeems it, and unredeemed coins sink. The price of the bonus is a journey into where you just struck.

notes.where: Money as ammunition: Final Fantasy's Gil Toss, Terraria's Coin Gun, the Microtransaction Gun in Enter the Gungeon, coin-fed items in The Binding of Isaac. In story it is the mercenary's and the ferryman's bargain, a coin for every stroke.
notes.mutation: Do not burn the coin: each cast flings one carried coin out with the hit, so it lies where the sigil struck among the dead and sinks at the next toll unless walked back for; harm is bought with reach and a return trip, not with a purchase.

name: Hair's Breadth
idea: The bound sigil gains one free cast each time an enemy attack that was shown beforehand lands within 0.7 m of the player without hitting (up to 4 stored; they fire 0.2 s apart). Cost: its ordinary recharge is 30% slower. Standing just outside a marked strike becomes a way to load the sigil.
source: Every dangerous attack in this game is shown before it lands, so the edge of the shown shape is a place the player can choose to stand.
nearest: Graze meters in bullet-hell shooters and perfect-dodge rewards; here no dodge input exists, only the choice of how near the edge to wait.

notes.where: Buzz in Psyvariar and the Tension system in Shikigami no Shiro (near misses charge the weapon); graze in Touhou. Standing at the edge of a shown strike is the same near miss without a dodge.
notes.mutation: Let the near miss lend its shape, not a free cast: the sigil's next cast takes the outline and size of the strike that just missed (ring, wedge or line), so the player chooses which enemy attack to stand beside in order to borrow it.

notes.where: Graze systems that load the weapon on near misses: Psyvariar's Buzz, the tension shot of Shikigami no Shiro, graze in Touhou; perfect-dodge rewards such as Witch Time in Bayonetta. In story it is the bullet that parts the hero's hair.
notes.mutation: Count the miss by whom it hit instead: the sigil gains a cast for each other enemy caught inside a shown strike that missed the player, so the player stands where a keeper's blow will fall on its own dead.

name: Quartered
idea: The bound sigil stops casting by itself. Every cast it would have made is saved (cap 20) and all are released together at each quarter of the toll interval, every 18.75 s, 0.1 s apart, from wherever the player then stands. Cost: nothing between quarters. The player lives through each quiet stretch and chooses a place for the release.
source: The toll gives a certain moment to count toward, and a sigil bound to it makes the counting matter between tolls as well.
nearest: Damage-storing detonation skills; here the detonator is the district's public clock, which the player cannot hurry.

notes.where: Unleash Support in Path of Exile (stored casts let go together); pooling everything for the two-minute burst window in Final Fantasy XIV raids. Release on a public wave clock the player cannot hurry is its own.

Clock figures that stand idle and all strike together on the quarter; Poe's revellers stopped by each chime; stored-damage detonation skills. A release the player cannot hurry because the district's clock holds the trigger is its own.

name: Heed, and the Vow of Stability
idea: Vows reserve Heed, a pool spent on nothing else: unreserved Heed shows every enemy attack up to 1.0 s earlier than its base warning. Vow of Stability holds 30% of Heed. Promise: stay within 12 m of the spot stood on at the last toll, drawn as a ring. Kept: 25% more harm and one extra Guard. Stepping out breaks it; it returns at the next toll.
source: What a one-life player wants most is to see danger early, so that is the only currency worth reserving; stability is a real monastic vow to stay in one place.
nearest: Auras that reserve mana in Path of Exile; here the pool is warning time, and each vow is also a promise the thumb can break.

notes.where: Mana reserved by auras in Path of Exile; opt-in burdens such as the Demon Bell in Sekiro and the Pact of Punishment in Hades; the holdout ring in Risk of Rain 2. A reserved pool that is warning time, held by breakable promises, is its own.

The Benedictine vow of stability and the anchorite's cell; power kept by a promise and lost by breaking it - the Irish geas, the paladin's oath, Nen 'vows and limitations' in Hunter x Hunter, binding vows in Jujutsu Kaisen, the Vows of Hades II; mana reservation in Path of Exile. Warning time as the pool that is reserved is its own.

name: Vow of Poverty
idea: Holds 25% of Heed. Promise: carry no more than 3 unbanked items; a fourth cannot be picked up while the vow stands and lies where it fell. Kept: experience from kills is 20% higher and gates need 1 s less standing. The vow can be dropped at any moment by standing on an item for 2 s, and returns at the next toll.
source: Fear grows with what is carried, so a vow that caps the load buys calm and sells greed, and the moment of breaking it is a decision.
nearest: Voluntary conducts in NetHack; this is a kept-or-broken state inside each vigil with a visible price lying on the ground.

notes.where: The Vow of Poverty feat in Dungeons & Dragons 3.5 (Book of Exalted Deeds): own almost nothing and receive standing bonuses, under the same name. Also Hollow Palm Technique in Path of Exile and conducts in NetHack.
notes.mutation: Pay for refusals made within reach: the vow counts each item the character comes within 2 m of and leaves lying until it sinks, and the bonus grows with that count, so poverty is earned by walking past things, not by a cap.

notes.where: The Vow of Poverty of Dungeons & Dragons 3.5 (Book of Exalted Deeds) and the monk vows of Pathfinder: own next to nothing, gain standing bonuses, lose them the moment the vow is broken - the same name and the same bargain; the mendicant friar behind them; NetHack's conducts.
notes.mutation: Make it a vow of alms and not of lack: the promise is to leave the first find of each toll period lying where it fell; each find left stands as a small cairn that pays the bonus while unclaimed, and walking back to take one breaks the vow.

name: Vow of the Unbroken Round
idea: Holds 35% of Heed. Promise: touch the district's bell-post at least once between every pair of tolls. Each toll period in which the promise is kept adds 5% to all harm and 2% to speed, stacking to 8 periods. A missed period empties the stack. The post is the middle of the district, where the surge is thickest.
source: Returning to one place before a recurring deadline is a habit the thumb can keep or lose, and losing it should cost everything saved.
nearest: Streak bonuses that reset on a miss in rhythm games; here the beat is 75 s long and each beat is a journey to a place.

notes.where: Rolling upkeep buffs that fall off if not refreshed in time (Lifebloom stacks in World of Warcraft); lap streaks in racing games; passing the campfire each loop in Loop Hero. A stack kept by one visit to a place per wave period is its own.

The hatch button of LOST, pressed every 108 minutes or else; the night-watchman's tell-tale clock rounds; the Angelus rung without fail; streak bonuses that reset on a miss. A streak whose beat is a journey to the district's bell-post is its own.

name: Tithe
idea: At every toll, 10% of the coin carried drops in one heap where the player stands. If the player comes back and picks the heap up between 6 s and 12 s after the toll, it is doubled; earlier it is merely returned, later it has sunk. The surge arrives 4 s after the toll, on that spot or elsewhere.
source: Returning to where you were is only a decision if something of yours is waiting there and something dangerous is too.
nearest: Corpse runs to recover dropped currency in Dark Souls; here the drop is voluntary, small, timed to the bell, and pays double for good timing.

notes.where: Bloodstains in Dark Souls (your currency waits where you were); the money tree in Animal Crossing (bury coin, come back for more); the well-done window on the spit in Monster Hunter. A small bell-timed heap that doubles in a 6 s window is its own.

'Cast thy bread upon the waters, for thou shalt find it after many days' and the tithe returned a hundredfold; the parable of the talents; Dark Souls bloodstains and Shovel Knight's dropped gold bags. A small bell-timed drop that pays double for a well-timed return is its own.

name: Standing Offer
idea: After each toll a ring 3 m wide appears at the place where the next toll's surge will enter. Standing inside it for 3 s without leaving grants one free chime; the ring then moves on. It shows where danger will come from a minute ahead, and pays the player for standing in exactly that place.
source: The player wants to see danger coming early and is also asked whether to stand in a dangerous place for a reward; one object can do both.
nearest: Shrines charged by standing in a circle; this circle is also a forecast of the next surge's door.

notes.where: Wave flags in Kingdom Rush (they show where the next wave enters and pay a bonus for acting on them); emergence tiles in Into the Breach; shrines charged by standing in a ring. One ring that is both forecast and offer is its own.

Wave-entrance markers in tower defence (the skull flags of Kingdom Rush); stand-in-the-circle shrines and the teleporter zone of Risk of Rain; the omen that shows where the blow will fall. One ring that is both forecast and dare is its own.

name: Rest Beat
idea: A ring closes on the player's feet over 1 s whenever they stand still. Stepping off between 0.9 s and 1.3 s after stopping doubles the next cast of every sigil. Leaving early does nothing; staying longer wastes it, and the ring reopens only after 2 s of movement. The reward is for a pause of exactly one breath amid the crowd.
source: Stopping for a set time is something a thumb can learn to do by feel, and a closing ring shows it without sound or text.
nearest: Active reload in Gears of War; the input here is the length of a stillness, not a button press.

notes.where: Active reload in Gears of War; the Aim Ring in Lost Odyssey (a closing ring and a timed release); the rocket start in Mario Kart. A timing window measured as the length of a stillness is its own.
Active reload in Gears of War; the rocket start timed on the lights in Mario Kart; a counted rest in music. A timing window measured in stillness is its own.

name: Pass the Gate
idea: Each time a gate opens and closes without the player leaving through it, experience gained rises 8% and enemy speed rises 4% for the rest of the vigil. The stacks show as notches on every later gate's arch. Taken early, this chime makes each later gate a sharper offer: the refusal is paid, and so is the price.
source: When to leave through a gate is the weightiest rare decision, and it gains weight if saying no is recorded.
nearest: Cash-out-or-continue in push-your-luck board games; here each refusal changes the run mechanically and visibly.

notes.where: Curse in Vampire Survivors (faster enemies for more reward); the Shrine of the Mountain in Risk of Rain 2; each loop not retreated from in Loop Hero. Stacks earned by refusing an open exit, and shown on the next one, are its own.

Refusing the banker in Deal or No Deal; 'one more room' push-your-luck delving; choosing to loop rather than leave in Risk of Rain; in story, the offer three times refused. A refusal recorded as a notch on every later gate is its own.

name: Kept Ground
idea: The spot where the player stands at each later level-up becomes Kept Ground: a 4 m circle lasting until the vigil ends (the oldest of 6 fades). Inside any Kept Ground, lost Graze life returns twice as fast and warnings show 0.2 s sooner. The player builds a private map of shelters out of the places where they chose to level.
source: Level-ups come often, so tying each one to the ground underfoot turns a menu event into a choice of place.
nearest: Consecrated-ground skills in action role-playing games; these are not cast but left behind by levelling, and they accumulate into a map.

notes.where: The Warbanner in Risk of Rain and Risk of Rain 2: on every level-up a banner is planted where the player stands and strengthens anyone inside its ring for the rest of the stage.
notes.mutation: Mark what was refused, not where the level came: the chimes not taken leave rings on the ground that hold a weak form of what they offered while stood in, so the map of shelters is made of the choices turned down.

notes.where: Hallowed ground the dead cannot profane (vampire lore, the holy-ground rule of Highlander); 'home base' in tag; Consecration in Diablo and bonfires in Dark Souls. Shelters left behind wherever a level was taken is its own.

name: Countermarch
idea: After reversing the heading by 150 degrees or more, the player passes through common dead without contact for 0.6 s, and each one passed through is turned to face the wrong way for 1 s. It works once per 4 s. Cutting back across the train stops being a gamble and becomes the plan.
source: A reversal is the sharpest gesture a thumb makes and the most dangerous one in a crowd.
nearest: Dash moves with invulnerable frames; here there is no dash and no button, only the U-turn, and it turns the crowd as well.

notes.where: Dashes with invulnerable frames in Hades; Phasing in Path of Exile (pass through enemies); the quick turn in Resident Evil. A pass-through earned by the U-turn itself, which also turns the crowd, was not found.

The marching-band countermarch, files reversing back through their own ranks; the matador's pass that turns the bull; Red Rover; dodge-roll invulnerability frames. A U-turn as the dodge that also turns the crowd is its own.

name: Wake-walkers
idea: The common dead do not steer at the player but at the place the player stood 1.2 s ago. They are the bulk of every surge: a slumped tapered box, slow, harming by contact. Because they follow the wake, a moving player draws them into a train on the exact path walked, a cut back meets them side-on, and a player who stops is found in 1.2 s.
source: Leading a train and cutting across it only works reliably if the crowd follows the path and not the body.
nearest: Pac-Man's ghosts, which each aim at an offset from the player; these aim at the player's own past position, which makes the thumb's path the thing they obey.

notes.where: The ghost train in Pac-Man Championship Edition DX (enemies follow the path behind you in a line); Cosmic Clones in Super Mario Galaxy 2 and Badeline in Celeste; monsters following scent in Brogue. As the steering rule of a whole horde it is its own.

Romero's shuffling dead and the herds of The Walking Dead arriving where you were; lag pursuit; Celeste's Badeline chasers and the Cosmic Clones of Super Mario Galaxy 2, which trail your past self; Pac-Man's offset targeting. A whole horde aimed 1.2 s behind the body is its own.

name: Wake-hound
idea: A low wedge that runs the player's actual path, point by point, at 1.3 times the player's speed, ignoring where the player now is. Contact is a Strike. Where the path crosses itself it loses the trail and casts about on the spot for 3 s, taking double harm. It is read by its nose-down run along the trail and must be shaken by doubling back.
source: Hares really break a scent trail by doubling back across their own track, which is a thing a thumb can do.
nearest: Pursuers that replay your route, like the shadow clones in Mario Galaxy; this one can be thrown off, and the way to do it is a crossing.

notes.where: Cosmic Clones in Super Mario Galaxy 2 and Badeline in Celeste (pursuers that run your exact path); tracker dogs in Metal Gear Solid 3. A trail-runner that is thrown off where the path crosses itself was not found.

The tracking hound thrown off by a quarry that doubles back across its own trail: fox-hunting lore, Rainsford's looped trail in 'The Most Dangerous Game', the bloodhounds of Cool Hand Luke. In games, pursuers that replay your path (Cosmic Clones, Celeste's Badeline).
notes.mutation: Make it a trail-eater and not a trail-follower: it consumes the player's wake as it runs it, so nothing behind it counts for In Procession, Knotted or Hitch, and where the path crosses itself it swallows the knot and chokes for 3 s.

name: Left-turner
idea: A planted figure with one long arm, built lopsided: arm on the left or on the right. It can turn to face the player only toward its arm side, at 60 degrees per second, and strikes a 4 m wedge in front every 2 s. Circling it against its turning keeps the player behind it for good; circling with it keeps the player in front.
source: A thumb circling a point picks a direction without thinking; this enemy makes the direction the whole question and shows the answer in its shape.
nearest: Shielded enemies that must be struck from behind; here which way you walk round matters, and each one is built left- or right-handed.

notes.where: Beamos statues in Zelda (an eye that sweeps one way, approached from behind its turn); slow-turning tank destroyers circled in World of Tanks; strafing to an enemy's shield side in Dark Souls. Left- and right-built variants shown in the shape are its own.

Zoolander, who 'can't turn left'; the fiddler crab's one great claw; the one-armed Fachan of Highland lore; the slow-turning brute you circle-strafe (Zelda's Iron Knuckle, every Dark Souls backstab). An enemy built left or right that makes the direction of the circle the whole question is its own.

name: Linkmen
idea: A marching row of 6 to 9 figures 2.5 m apart, alternate pairs joined by a held chain drawn as a thin box. Chains are Strikes to touch; unjoined gaps are safe. The row advances at walking pace across the whole fight and does not turn. Killing a figure drops both of its chains. The player threads an open gap or makes one.
source: Threading a gap needs an enemy that is a row of gaps and non-gaps readable at a glance.
nearest: Beam-linked enemy pairs in action role-playing games; here the links form one advancing line and the fight is about the holes in it.

notes.where: Laser barriers strung between emitter pairs in shoot-em-ups such as Gradius; gates in Geometry Wars; the marching wall swarms that cross the field in Vampire Survivors. One advancing line read as gaps and non-gaps is its own.

Red Rover's hand-linked line; the Danse Macabre chain of the dead (the last shot of The Seventh Seal); Marley's ghost and the chain gang; link-boys for the name; laser fences between pylons, beam-linked elites in Diablo III, bullet-hell walls with gaps. One advancing row of chains and holes is its own.

name: Early Ringer
idea: A broad slow figure dragging a rope. It ignores the player and walks from the district's edge to the bell-post, taking about 30 s. If it arrives, the next toll rings 15 s early. It has the life of forty common dead. A thin line on the ground shows its route. The player leaves the safe circuit to stop it or accepts the lost time.
source: The toll is the one thing the player counts on, so the sharpest threat is one that moves the count.
nearest: Runners that leak past in tower defence; here the thing it reaches is the run's public clock.

notes.where: The alarm-runner: guards who run to ring the alarm bell in Assassin's Creed, orcs who run to sound the horn in Shadow of Mordor, the Screamer in 7 Days to Die; leakers in tower defence. Stop him or the next wave comes early.
notes.mutation: Make him the toll, not a threat to it: one ringer walks to the post every period and the bell rings when he arrives, early if his way is clear and late if crowd, stone or the player stand in it; killing him loses that toll's reward too.

notes.where: The guard who must be stopped before he reaches the alarm bell: the bell-ringers of Assassin's Creed, the sentry running for the gong or horn in every infiltration film; runners that leak past in tower defence.
notes.mutation: Let it steal the hour instead of ringing it: it drags the bell's clapper from the post toward the district's edge, each 10 m shortening every later toll interval by 2 s, until the player kills it and walks the clapper back to the post.

name: Spotter
idea: A thin figure on a post-like cylinder that stands 15 m off and points at the player with one long arm. While it stands, common dead within 20 m of it steer at the player's present position, not the place 1.2 s behind: trains break up and cut corners. It never attacks. The player reads the pointing arm and goes out to it.
source: Going toward the noise or away from it is a real choice when the noisy thing changes how the whole crowd answers the thumb.
nearest: Buffing shaman enemies in action role-playing games; this one changes no numbers, only how well the crowd is aimed.

notes.where: Elites leading Grunts in Halo (kill the leader and the crowd behaves differently); artillery spotters in Company of Heroes; the Screamer in 7 Days to Die. An enemy that only improves how the crowd is aimed is its own.

The pod person who points and shrieks to bring the others in Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1978); the screamer zombie that calls the horde (State of Decay, 7 Days to Die); the artillery spotter and the pointer dog.
notes.mutation: Have its arm point not at the player but 1.2 s ahead along the player's heading, with the dead steering at that point: the player beats it by feinting so the arm points wrong, not by walking out to kill it.

name: Jacks
idea: Squat hammer-figures that walk slowly and strike the ground around them (3 m) on a fixed beat of 2.5 s: arm up for 1.5 s, down, up again. Every Jack in the district strikes at the same instant, so the whole field pulses together. The raised arms are the warning. The player crosses Jack ground in the off-beat and stands clear on the stroke.
source: Moving in time with a beat must be readable with the sound off, and a field of arms rising and falling together is a beat for the eyes.
nearest: Timed crushers in platform games, each on its own cycle; these share one phase across the district, so the player learns one pulse.

notes.where: Hazards on one shared beat: Beat Blocks in Super Mario Galaxy 2, every enemy acting on the beat in Crypt of the NecroDancer and Hi-Fi Rush. Platform crushers are often synced across a level, so the shared phase is not new.
notes.mutation: Do not strike together: let the stroke travel outward from the bell-post at walking pace, each Jack striking as it reaches him, so the field shows a moving wave to walk with or cut through, and a killed Jack leaves a hole in it.

notes.where: Clock jacks (Jack Blandiver at Wells, Jack the Smiter at Southwold); the marching hammers of Pink Floyd's The Wall; Wagner's Nibelheim anvils; beat blocks in Super Mario 3D World and the shared beat of Crypt of the NecroDancer. One pulse shared by every Jack in the district is its own.

name: Tidewaiter
idea: Rises inside any gate that opens while the player carries 4 or more unbanked items, and never leaves the gate ring. Its life is that of ten common dead per item carried. Every 2.5 s it sweeps one half of the ring, left then right, each shown 1 s ahead. A laden player who wants to leave must stay in the ring, stepping from half to half.
source: Tide waiters were real customs officers who met ships on the tide, and fear at the gate should grow with the cargo.
nearest: Guards at extraction points in extraction shooters; this one exists only because of what you carry and is as strong as your load.

notes.where: Ambushes drawn to extraction points in The Division's Dark Zone; shopkeepers and guards waiting at the exit in Spelunky and Shiren the Wanderer; half-room sweeps in Final Fantasy XIV. A gate guard that exists only because of the load, and is as strong as it, is its own.

The threshold guardian and toll-taker: the bridge troll of the Billy Goats Gruff, Charon wanting his obol, the customs man; the hoard-dragon roused by one stolen cup (Beowulf, Smaug); Spelunky's shopkeepers waiting at the exit. A guard that exists only because of the load, and is as strong as the load, is its own.

name: The Perambulator
idea: Keeper who walks the bounds. Phase 1: it walks a square circuit of 16 m sides around the player, dragging a visible line; when the loop closes, everything inside takes a Knell. Crossing the line is a Strike except at four corner stakes, which can be broken to open it. Phase 2: two nested loops walked in opposite directions. Phase 3: the line spirals inward and the keeper can be harmed only at its leading end.
source: Tracing a shape is something the thumb does to enemies elsewhere in this game; here a keeper does it to the player, and the drawn line is its own warning.
nearest: Qix turned inside out, with the boss as the line-drawer; the player's job is to be outside, or at a broken corner, when the shape closes.

notes.where: Paper.io and Slither.io (a rival closes a loop round you and what is inside dies); Qix; Moldorm in Zelda, hurt only at one end. A keeper built wholly on walking the bounds round the player is its own.

The nation-wide circle closed around its victims in Fullmetal Alchemist; the encircling coil of slither.io and the serpent boss hurt only at one end (Zelda's Moldorm); Qix inside out; beating the bounds. A keeper that perambulates the player, with corner stakes to break, is its own.

name: The Conductor
idea: Keeper with eight shapes hung in a row above it, one per attack. It performs them left to right, each shape lifting 1 s before its attack. After every full row two neighbouring shapes swap places, hopping visibly. Phase 2: it reads the row from both ends at once, two attacks together. Phase 3: 1.5 times faster, and each toll reverses the row. The player learns the row, not the reflex.
source: Knowing a keeper's attacks matters more than power, so this keeper publishes its order and changes it by one small visible step at a time, as ringers change the order of bells.
nearest: Enemy intent icons in Slay the Spire; here the whole queue is public, in real time, and its changes follow a rule the player can run ahead of.

notes.where: Enemy intents in Slay the Spire; turn-order bars in Grandia and Final Fantasy X; boss-timer bars in raid add-ons; Simon-says bosses. A public row that changes by one neighbour swap each pass, as bell-ringers change, was not found.

Change ringing as told in Sayers' The Nine Tailors, neighbouring bells swapping each row; Simon-style pattern bosses; enemy intents in Slay the Spire; numbered-order raid mechanics in Final Fantasy XIV. A published real-time queue that changes by one visible swap is its own.

name: The Ferry-keeper
idea: Keeper carrying a lantern. Beyond 6 m from it the whole district deals Drag; its pole sweeps everything within 2.5 m every 3 s, shown 0.8 s ahead. Phase 1: hold the band between. Phase 2: the band narrows to between 3 m and 5 m and it dashes along a line shown 1 s before. Phase 3: it throws the lantern in a shown arc; the old light dies in 2.5 s and the player must reach the new one.
source: Holding a distance from a moving enemy is the thumb's hardest sustained act, so one keeper is made of nothing else.
nearest: Safe-bubble phases in raid bosses; here the bubble is the boss for the whole fight and has a deadly middle.

notes.where: The Warpriest's aura in Destiny's King's Fall raid (stand in the bearer's ring or die); the closing circle of battle royales; darkness that kills outside the light in Don't Starve. A keeper who is the moving safe band, with a deadly middle, is its own.

Charon, ferryman of the dead with pole and lantern (Dante's beats with his oar any soul that lags; the lantern-bearing Ferryman of Sea of Thieves), joined to the stock 'stay in the light or the dark takes you' of Pitch Black, Doctor Who's Vashta Nerada, A Plague Tale and Ori. The safe band with a deadly middle is the fresh part.
notes.mutation: Lose the ferryman: make the keeper a diving bell lowered on a chain into the flooded street, with air only in a ring under its rim; the band is the air, the deadly middle is the clapper's swing, and in phase 3 the bell is hauled across the district with the player walking under it.

name: The Ropewalk
idea: Parallel lanes 6 m wide and 60 m long between long box sheds, joined by cross-alleys every 20 m, with rope-rack posts down each lane. Colours: tar black, hemp tan, wet slate, rust red, lamp yellow. Crowds can arrive only from the two ends of a lane, so every moment is a choice of which end to face, and at each toll two cross-alleys shut and two open.
source: Choosing which of two crowds to face is clearest in a place where there are only ever two directions.
nearest: Corridor levels in arena shooters; here the corridors are the whole district and the bell rearranges their joints.

notes.where: The Inlaid Library and Gallo Tower in Vampire Survivors (corridor stages where the horde comes only from the two ends); mazes with doors that change in Lady Bug. A grid of such lanes whose joints the wave clock rearranges is its own.

Dark City, whose streets are rearranged at each midnight, and the nightly shifting walls of The Maze Runner; the Hot Gates and the Oldboy corridor, where foes can only come from the ends; real ropewalks (Chatham's ropery, Longfellow's 'The Ropewalk'). A district of two-ended lanes rejoined by the bell is its own.

name: The Dial
idea: A round plaza 70 m across with the bell-post at the centre and eight radial stones. A 90-degree wedge of shadow sweeps sunwise once per toll interval; the toll rings as its edge crosses the north stone, so the clock is read from the ground. In shadow, enemies move 40% faster and warnings show 0.3 s later. Colours: chalk, noon gold, slate violet, bronze, moss. A whole vigil is one slow circling.
source: On a small screen with the sound off, the public clock should be a moving shape on the ground that the thumb can walk with.
nearest: Day and night cycles that strengthen enemies; here day and night are places a few metres apart and the boundary is the clock's hand.

notes.where: Moving shade in V Rising (day and night are places, and the boundary moves with the sun); sweeping clock-hand hazards in clock-tower boss rooms; lighthouse beams. A district that is the wave clock drawn on the ground is its own.

The sundial plaza; 'stay out of the shadows' (Doctor Who's Vashta Nerada, Pitch Black); clock-face arenas with a sweeping hand (Castlevania's clock tower); the prison-yard searchlight turned inside out. Night as a wedge a few metres away whose edge is the clock's hand is its own.

name: The Undercroft
idea: A flooded hall of round pillars on a 5 m grid under a roof drawn as darkness. Colours: bone white, verdigris, black water, candle amber, lead grey. Shelter from Knells is everywhere and sight lines are short. A pillar struck by any sigil rings for 2 s, and common dead within 8 m of it steer at the pillar instead of the player. The player pulls crowds by choosing which stone to strike.
source: Hugging an obstacle and going toward or away from noise are both thumb decisions that need a place dense with obstacles.
nearest: Noise lures in stealth games; here the lure is whichever pillar your automatic attacks happen to hit, so positioning aims it.

notes.where: The pipe bomb in Left 4 Dead and Decoy Totem in Path of Exile (the horde goes to the noise); pillar halls such as Anor Londo's in Dark Souls. A lure that is whichever pillar the automatic attacks strike is its own.

The flooded pillared cistern or crypt of gothic fiction and games (Istanbul's Basilica Cistern in From Russia with Love and Dan Brown's Inferno, Moria's pillared halls) plus the noise lure of every stealth story: slinging stones at metal to draw guards in A Plague Tale, Pippin's stone down the well.
notes.mutation: Let the ring travel: a struck pillar rings, then passes its ring to the next pillar along the grid line away from the face that was struck, four pillars in turn, drawing the dead down that aisle, so the player sends a crowd along a chosen colonnade by choosing which face to strike.

name: One Route
idea: The tree is a street plan, and a character's points lay one unbranching walk through it from the class's door. A point may only extend the head of the walk to a neighbouring node. Points are taken back only from the head, in reverse order. The route may step onto a node it already holds: that costs a point and doubles the node, once.
source: A thumb traces one line, never a branching one, so the character's growth is one line with a head that must choose its next street.
nearest: The Sphere Grid in Final Fantasy X, where a token travels a board; here the whole build is a single path with no side branches, and crossing itself is a deliberate purchase.

notes.where: The Sphere Grid in Final Fantasy X and the Crystarium in Final Fantasy XIII (growth as travel along a board); the Stat Matrix in Kingdom Hearts Re:coded. One unbranching line, undone only from its head, that may cross itself, was not found.

Ariadne's single thread, paid out and followed back; the one-path labyrinth set in the floor at Chartres; the Sphere Grid walk of Final Fantasy X; the one-line puzzles of The Witness. A whole build as one unbranching walk, taken back only from its head, is its own.

name: Beaten Bounds
idea: When the route returns to a node it already holds, closing a loop, every node lying inside the loop is granted at half strength without costing a point. A loop may enclose at most 12 nodes. Planning becomes a question of which cluster is worth fencing and how few steps the fence can take.
source: Returning to where you were closes a shape, and the pleasure of a shape is what it holds.
nearest: Radius jewels in Path of Exile that affect nodes in a circle; here the player draws the fence node by node with the route itself.

notes.where: The Lilium Orb in Tales of Xillia (activate the nodes round a cell and the skill inside is granted); Intuitive Leap and Thread of Hope in Path of Exile; Go and Dots and Boxes. A free-form fence drawn by the route is its own.

Dido's oxhide, the most ground the least fence can hold; territory by enclosure in Go and Qix; the Thread of Hope ring in Path of Exile; beating the parish bounds. Fencing a cluster of nodes with the route itself is its own.

name: Toll Rings
idea: The tree is drawn as eight rings around the centre. A node on ring N has no effect until the Nth toll of a vigil has rung, and counts in full from then to the vigil's end. Outer rings hold the strongest nodes. A route kept near the centre is strong from the first toll; a route driven outward is weak early and pays only those who stay.
source: The vigil has no fixed end and the player stays as long as they dare, so a build should say how long its owner means to stay.
nearest: Late-scaling items in action role-playing games; here the lateness is a stated toll number on the map, shared with the run's public clock.

notes.where: The mana curve in Hearthstone and Magic (a cost-N card comes into play from turn N); turn-numbered relics in Slay the Spire; neutral item tiers that unlock by game time in Dota 2. A tree whose rings switch on by wave count is its own.

A tree's yearly rings and Dante's circles for the picture; time-gated power such as the Gathering Storm rune in League of Legends; late-scaling items. Rings that switch on at a stated toll of the run's public clock are its own.

name: Straight Mile
idea: A special node. It counts the unbroken run of held nodes lying in one straight street through it, and its effect grows 25% for each node in that run beyond the fourth (cap 10 nodes). Streets on the plan are long and few of them cross the best clusters, so a straight route gives up variety for one strong line.
source: Walking a straight line is the thumb's simplest discipline, and the tree can ask for the same discipline in planning.
nearest: Adjacency bonuses in city-building games; this one counts only a straight unbroken line through one node.

notes.where: Paragon glyphs in Diablo 4 and radius jewels in Path of Exile (a socket that counts what is allocated around it); adjacency bonuses in Backpack Battles and Luck be a Landlord. Counting only an unbroken straight line through the node is its own.

Ley lines (Watkins' The Old Straight Track), power running along straight alignments; five-in-a-row; row and column bonuses in Backpack Hero and adjacency in city builders. Counting one unbroken straight street through a node is its own.

name: Notched gear
idea: An item is found blank. Each toll the character survives while carrying it unbanked cuts one notch in it and writes one line of properties (max 8). Leaving by a gate fixes it; death loses it. There are no tiers: an item's worth is the count of tolls someone dared to carry it through, and its shape shows the notches.
source: Fear grows with what is carried, so the item's quality is made to be exactly how long its carrier withstood that fear.
nearest: Unidentified items that resolve when you leave the dungeon; these are not hidden but unwritten, and staying longer writes more.

notes.where: Familiarity in Nioh and the Evolver in Enter the Gungeon (an item that grows as it is used); veiled Riven mods in Warframe; found-in-raid status in Escape from Tarkov. Worth counted in waves carried through unbanked, with no tiers, is its own.
