The gunfighter's notched grip and the Exchequer tally stick; legacy items that grow with their bearer (Earthdawn thread items, Weapons of Legacy in D&D); Hades keepsakes ranking up with encounters carried; the found-in-raid rule of Escape from Tarkov. Worth counted purely in tolls dared is its own.

name: Written by posture
idea: The line written at each toll comes from what the carrier did most in that toll period: standing still, moving straight, turning, staying within 3 m of enemies, staying beside obstacles, or carrying a heavy load. Each has its own table of lines; the amount rolls in a band that rises with the toll number. A line works only while the body is in the posture that wrote it.
source: The game can measure what the thumb did for 75 s cheaply, and a player who is asked how they played will start playing on purpose.
nearest: Skills that grow with use in The Elder Scrolls; here use writes a property onto one object, one toll at a time, and the property is conditional on the same act.

notes.where: Hero weapons in Fable III (they change by how you played); weapon affinities in Vagrant Story (grown by what the weapon was used on); skills by use in The Elder Scrolls; 'while stationary' modifiers in Path of Exile. A line written by a posture and working only in it is its own.

Raising a Digimon or a Chao, where what you did most decides what it becomes; Dwarf Fortress artifacts engraved with their own history; Riven challenges in Warframe; the wand that 'learns from its wielder' in Harry Potter; use-based skills in The Elder Scrolls. A line that works only in the posture that wrote it is its own.

name: Re-walking
idea: To change a banked item, carry it into a vigil in the Open Hand slot with one of its lines struck out. The first toll survived writes a new line there by the posture rule; leaving by a gate keeps it. Dying loses the whole item. Alternatively a line may be cut away for good, raising every remaining line 10%. Nothing else alters an item.
source: Whether to spend or risk something that does not come back is the right price for changing a precious thing.
nearest: Re-rolling one affix at a crafting bench; here the bench is a vigil, the cost is the risk of the whole item, and the result is steered by how you walk.

notes.where: Shiren the Wanderer (carry your best gear into the dungeon to improve it, lose it all on death); the one-property reroll at the Mystic in Diablo 3; destroy-on-failure enchanting in Lineage. A reroll steered by how you walk the next wave is its own.

Shiren the Wanderer and the Mystery Dungeon line: stored gear is bettered only by carrying it back into a run, and is lost whole on death; gamble-upgrades that can destroy the item (the Vaal Orb in Path of Exile, enhancement in Korean online games). In story, the blade that must go back to the fire that made it.
notes.mutation: Stake lines and not the item: dying in the re-walk erases the struck line and its two neighbours for good and leaves the rest, so the order in which an item was written decides what each rewrite puts at risk.

name: The Silence
idea: Announced 3 s ahead by the screen edge dimming. For 8 s every enemy halts. If the player also stands still for the whole 8 s, the silence is kept and the next toll raises rewards without raising danger. Moving or casting breaks it for that purpose, though the enemies stay halted and may be killed freely. Restraint and harvest cannot both be had.
source: Stopping for a set time is hard for the nerves precisely when everything else has stopped and could be killed.
nearest: Freeze-all pickups in survivor games; here the freeze is free and the real choice is whether to use it or honour it.

notes.where: The Orologion in Vampire Survivors (all enemies frozen); restraint rewarded by mercy in Undertale and by Pacifism in Geometry Wars. A free freeze that pays more for not using it is its own.

The two-minute Armistice silence and the Christmas truce of 1914; Poe's 'Masque of the Red Death', where all stand still while the clock chimes; the fairy-tale test of leaving the helpless feast untouched (Pan's Labyrinth); harvest-or-rescue in BioShock; the Orologion freeze of Vampire Survivors. A free freeze that pays only if honoured is its own.

name: The Cortege
idea: A line of twelve bearers 30 m long crosses the district in a straight line at half the player's speed, harming nothing. Enemies will not pass through it; the player can, between bearers. Walking inside the line, matching its heading within 15 degrees and its pace within 10% for 6 s, grants a notch on one carried item. Half-speed walking is done with the thumb held halfway.
source: A thumb can hold a half push as well as a full one, and nothing in these games ever asks it to.
nearest: Escort and follow missions that fail if you stray; this is optional, brief, and the skill tested is matching a pace with the thumb.

notes.where: Blending with a walking group of scholars in Assassin's Creed (keep their slow pace inside the group); tiptoeing by half tilt in Super Mario 64; tailing missions. A procession that is also a wall to the horde is its own.

The phantom funeral that sweeps the walker along: the Welsh toili, Galicia's Santa Compana, Hawaii's Night Marchers, Japan's Hyakki Yagyo; the rule never to cut through a cortege; blending into a walking group of scholars in Assassin's Creed. Matching a half pace with the thumb for a reward is its own.

name: The Narrow Gate
idea: When a gate opens there is a one in three chance that a second, narrow gate opens at the same moment at least 25 m away on the far side of the thickest crowd. Its ring is 1 m wide instead of 2 m and it shuts 5 s sooner. Leaving through it banks everything carried plus half again in Echoes.
source: When to leave is the weightiest decision, and it is heavier still if there are two ways out and the better one is through the crowd.
nearest: Risky bonus exits in roguelikes; here both doors are open at once on the same short clock and differ only in what the thumb must get through.

notes.where: Timed doors in Dead Cells and the Boss Rush door in The Binding of Isaac; paid or conditional extracts in Escape from Tarkov; the top of the flagpole in Super Mario Bros. Two exits open at once, the better one through the crowd, is its own.

'Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way' (Matthew 7:14) and Bunyan's Wicket Gate; timed doors in Dead Cells, Erebus gates in Hades, high-risk exits in extraction shooters. Two doors open on one short clock, the better one beyond the crowd, is its own in arrangement only.

name: The Lych Arch
idea: Two posts 4 m apart with a beam across rise somewhere in the district for 30 s. After the player walks between them, every enemy that passes under the beam within the next 4 s is laid to rest at once and yields 150% experience. The arch then falls. The reward is the size of the train the player dares to gather first.
source: Leading a train and threading a gap can be one act if the gap is fixed and the train must follow through it.
nearest: Luring enemies into an environmental trap; here the trap fires once, only behind the player, and pays by the length of what follows.

notes.where: Pacifism mode in Geometry Wars: Retro Evolved 2: lead a train of pursuers through a gate and the gate destroys what follows you, the bigger the train the better. The arch is that gate.
notes.mutation: Make it count, not kill: those passing under are bowed and held in the order they come, forming a file; when the arch falls one blow runs down the file and grows with each body. A mob arriving abreast jams it.

notes.where: The Red Sea closing on Pharaoh's host once the pursued are through; the portcullis dropped on the pursuers; Rome's beaten armies 'passing under the yoke'; the lychgate custom; kill-gates in trap games (Orcs Must Die). A trap that fires once, only behind the player, and pays by the train's length is its own.

name: The Knocker
idea: After a toll, a ring-shaped knocker shows on a wall at least 20 m away for 20 s. Reaching it and standing against it for 2 s grants sanctuary for 37 s: no enemy can touch the player and the player's sigils do not cast. Pickups can still be gathered. The toll clock keeps running, and sanctuary ends early if a gate is entered.
source: Durham's cathedral knocker really gave fugitives 37 days of sanctuary, and reaching a place before a deadline is a full drama for one thumb.
nearest: Invulnerability power-ups; this one must be reached and held, silences the player too, and spends half a toll period.

notes.where: Untouchable-but-harmless states: Ghost Scepter in Dota 2, Wraith's phase in Apex Legends, Ice Block in World of Warcraft, Zhonya's Hourglass in League of Legends; granted here by a stand-on-it shrine as in Diablo.
notes.mutation: Make sanctuary a place held, not a state carried: safety lasts only within arm's reach of the knocker, the dead mass at the edge and wait, and every unused second of the 37 is paid out, so the question is when to let go and walk out.

notes.where: Church sanctuary as every reader knows it: Quasimodo's 'Sanctuary!' at Notre-Dame and the Durham knocker itself; 'home base' in tag; safe rooms where nothing can follow (Resident Evil, Left 4 Dead); the invulnerable but pacified bubble of World of Warcraft.
notes.mutation: Give the real sequel to sanctuary, abjuration: the knock assigns a far gate and draws a straight road to it; nothing may touch the player while on that road, stepping off ends the protection, and the road leads out of the vigil, so sanctuary is a guarded way out and not a pause.

name: Bills of Mortality
idea: Each death writes a Bill: the enemy and attack that killed, the depth of harm, the toll number. A cause not yet on the account's Bills pays 40 Echoes times the toll number; a repeated cause pays a tenth. Each attack that has killed one of the player's characters is shown 0.15 s earlier to all later characters, up to three deaths per attack.
source: The player wants to say exactly why they died, and London once paid searchers to record every cause of death in weekly bills.
nearest: Bestiary entries unlocked by encounters; here the entry is written by dying, pays once, and permanently lengthens the warning of the very attack that did it.

notes.where: God Mode in Hades (each death adds lasting resistance); Reventure (each new way to die is a reward); the Morgue in Don't Starve and morgue files in Dungeon Crawl. A death that lengthens the warning of the very attack that caused it is its own.

Defoe's A Journal of the Plague Year, which quotes the Bills; Edge of Tomorrow and Re:Zero, where each death teaches the blow that dealt it; the Morgue of Don't Starve and the graveyard of Darkest Dungeon; Dark Souls bloodstains. A death that permanently lengthens the warning of its own cause is its own.

name: The dead are hung as bells
idea: Every dead character becomes a bell in the Carillon, sized by the tolls it heard in its last vigil. Each bell holds one boon drawn from the posture that character used most. A new character rings up to 8 bells of the player's choosing. Echoes are spent to open ringing places and to recast a bell's boon. The tree is built of the player's own dead.
source: A long-lived character is precious, so its loss should leave an object the player keeps choosing to use.
nearest: Ancestor traits in Rogue Legacy and memorial halls in Darkest Dungeon; here each dead character is itself a selectable node whose boon records how it was played.

notes.where: Legacy heroes in Wildermyth; relics of dead heroes in Massive Chalice; constellations made from how a hero was played in Moon Hunters; the graveyard and fame bonuses in Realm of the Mad God. A permanent tree whose nodes are your own dead is its own.

Hearn's 'The Soul of the Great Bell', the girl cast into the bronze who becomes its voice; Donne's passing bell and Sayers' Nine Tailors tolling a life; ancestors as traits in Rogue Legacy, fallen heroes' relics in Massive Chalice, legacy boons in State of Decay 2. A carillon in which each bell is one dead character and how it was played is its own.

name: Echoes are tolls heard
idea: Echoes are paid at the instant a toll rings, not at the end of a vigil: the Nth toll of a vigil pays N Echoes, doubled at the eighth. Nothing can remove them, so a death, a closed app or an incoming call costs no Echoes. Banking through a gate adds a share for the notches carried out.
source: Phone sessions are short and often cut off, so the permanent currency should be safe the moment it is earned.
nearest: Meta-currency awarded on the results screen of roguelites; this is awarded on the public clock, mid-run, and cannot be lost.

notes.where: Lunar Coins in Risk of Rain 2 (saved the moment they are picked up, kept through death or quitting); Darkness in Hades; survival-time milestone rewards in Survivor.io. A meta-currency safe at once and paid by time survived is standard.
notes.mutation: Pay by where the toll was heard: the Nth toll pays N Echoes times the number of different landmarks of the district the character has stood beside at a toll this vigil, still credited at once, so each bell asks for a new place.

notes.where: Per-wave rewards that are permanent the moment the wave is passed and survive defeat or quitting: round experience in Bloons TD 6 and Call of Duty Zombies, time-survived payouts in mobile survivor games, gold kept on death in Vampire Survivors. In story, the watchman paid by the hour struck.
notes.mutation: Pay each toll's Echoes into the bell that rang, not to the account: they hang in that district's bell, safe at once, and are collected by the next character who hears the same numbered toll there, so the currency is always inherited by a later life.

name: Level-ups are walked into
idea: Levelling does not pause the game. The three chimes rise from the ground 4 m from the player, 120 degrees apart, each a distinct solid shape, and the player takes one by walking into it. They sink after 8 s; an untaken level waits and adds a fourth shape to the next offer. Where a chime stands among the enemies is part of its price.
source: A phone has no hover and one thumb, so the plainest way to choose among three things is to walk to one.
nearest: Choose-one item pedestals in The Binding of Isaac; here it replaces the pause menu of every level-up, runs on a timer, and happens inside the horde.

notes.where: Choose-one item pedestals in The Binding of Isaac and perk altars in Noita; the carousel in Teamfight Tactics (walk into your pick against a timer); perk machines reached mid-horde in Call of Duty Zombies. As the replacement for every level-up pause it is its own.

The three caskets of The Merchant of Venice and 'choose wisely' in the Grail chamber; choose-one pedestals in The Binding of Isaac; unpaused item picks in Risk of Rain 2 (Artifact of Command); reward doors in Hades. Every level-up as a timed walk inside the horde is its own.

name: The gate asks you to stand
idea: Leaving through a gate needs the player to stay inside its 2 m ring for 1 s plus 0.5 s for every unbanked item carried, up to 8 s, drawn as an arch filling stone by stone. Stepping out empties it. Enemies do not stop. The more a character carries, the longer it must hold its ground in the open to keep it.
source: Fear grows with what is carried, and the exit is where that fear should be collected in full.
nearest: Extraction timers in extraction shooters; here the timer is the size of your own load.

notes.where: Extraction timers in Escape from Tarkov and Hunt: Showdown (stand in the exit zone while the count runs; leave it and the count resets); deposit time that grows with the amount carried in Deep Rock Galactic.
notes.mutation: Hand the load through piece by piece: one carried item is banked every half second in an order the player sets, the character goes last, and stepping out keeps what has already gone through, so a pressed player can bank part and run.

notes.where: The teleporter charge of Risk of Rain and the exit countdown of Escape from Tarkov; the looter too laden to get out before the door shuts (Beni in The Mummy, the Cave of Wonders, Chaucer's Pardoner's Tale); encumbrance rules. An exit timer sized by the load is its own.

name: Keeping the stroke
idea: A ring closes on the whole screen over the 3 s before each toll. If the player is standing still at the instant it closes, the toll is kept: the reward rise applies and lost Strike life returns. If moving, only the danger rises. The one certain event of the clock asks for stillness at the moment the surge is announced.
source: The toll is a public clock the player counts toward, and the cheapest way to make the count matter is to ask for one exact act on the stroke.
nearest: Musical statues; here the music stops on a known 75 s schedule and the prize is the whole reward step of the run.

notes.where: Acceleration Bomb in Final Fantasy XIV (be motionless at the instant the countdown ends); musical statues; freeze-on-the-signal minigames in Mario Party. The rule is the same, with a reward in place of a penalty.
notes.mutation: Ask for a self-set rite, not stillness: whatever the body was doing at the first toll (standing, walking one heading, circling one way) must be done again at each later stroke to keep it, with the crowd arranged differently every time.

notes.where: Millet's 'The Angelus', where work stops and all stand still at the bell; the minute's silence; musical statues; Poe's revellers frozen by the chime; on-the-beat bonuses in rhythm-action games. One exact act of stillness on a 75 s stroke is its own.

name: Tolled-for
idea: At zero life the character does not die at once. It is Tolled-for: sigils stop, speed rises 20%, and it dies when the next toll rings unless it leaves through a gate first; one gate opens at the farthest edge. A character saved this way keeps its life and loses everything carried. A fall just after a toll leaves over a minute; a fall just before leaves none.
source: One life makes the last seconds the most felt of the run, and the public clock can decide how many of them there are.
nearest: Fight For Your Life in Borderlands; here the reprieve is a run to a place, its length is whatever the bell has left, and the price is the whole haul.

notes.where: Death's Door in Darkest Dungeon; Fight For Your Life in Borderlands; the escape pod in EVE Online (lose ship and cargo, keep the pilot); the Doom countdown in Final Fantasy. A reprieve whose length is whatever the wave clock has left is its own.

Marlowe's Faustus counting the hour until the clock strikes; Cinderella's midnight; Albrecht saved by the dawn bell in Giselle; the Doom countdown of Final Fantasy; Fight For Your Life in Borderlands; the End Game Collapse of Dead by Daylight. A reprieve as long as whatever the bell has left, paid for with the haul, is its own.

name: Buttons take away
idea: Both extra buttons give something up. Cast Away throws the newest unbanked item 6 m ahead; common dead within 10 m crowd it for 5 s and it is destroyed. Hush is held for up to 3 s: the player's sigils fall silent and store up to 3 casts each, the player counts as Unheard while walking at half speed, and release fires the stored casts.
source: The second thumb is free only some of the time, so its buttons should be rare, weighty and about giving something up.
nearest: Bombs in shoot-em-ups as the panic button; these cost the player's own loot or the player's own attacks, never a stocked charge.

notes.where: Throw Money in Assassin's Creed II (the crowd gathers on what you threw) and the Alluring Skull in Dark Souls; hold-to-charge releases; Unleash Support in Path of Exile. Two buttons that both cost the player's own loot or own attacks is its own.

A sop thrown to Cerberus, Atalanta's golden apples, the sledge passengers thrown to the wolves in My Antonia; the Monkey Bomb of Call of Duty Zombies and the pipe bomb of Left 4 Dead; the stealth-game crouch-walk and the held volley. Each half is familiar; buttons that only take away is the part that is its own.

name: The class finds you
idea: In the one-sitting run the character starts with no class. Over the first two tolls the game totals seconds spent standing still, walking straight, circling, staying within 3 m of enemies and staying beside obstacles. At the second toll it offers the two classes whose act the player did most. The subclass is offered the same way in the second district, from that district's totals.
source: Classes here differ by what the thumb does, so the thumb's own habits are the fairest way to pick one.
nearest: The class suggestion at the end of Oblivion's tutorial; here it is measured, not judged by a character, and is the only way a class is given in this mode.

notes.where: Spore (each stage totals how you played and hands you the archetype and power that fit); Digimon evolving by how they were raised; the class suggested from tutorial behaviour in Oblivion.
notes.mutation: Let the classes come and watch: each guild figure stands in the district where its act is easiest and counts only what is done within its sight; the one that saw most steps forward, so a player can court a class by performing where its master can see.

notes.where: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, where the tutorial watches how you fought and proposes a class; Dungeon Siege naming your class from what you used; the Sorting Hat, and the Ceremony of Twelve in The Giver, where the elders assign a calling from observed habits; the virtue questions of Ultima IV.
notes.mutation: Let the refusal matter: the two measured classes rise as two of the district's dead tradespeople where the player did those acts most; the class is taken by standing in one's place for 2 s, and the one refused walks the district as a rival using its starting sigil against the player.

name: Press, Scour, Salt
idea: Three harms, each sized by the water at the victim's feet. Press is multiplied by depth: x0.5 dry, x1 in shallows, x2 in deep water. Scour is multiplied by the speed of water past the victim (its velocity minus the current's): x0 drifting with the flow, up to x2 standing against a race. Salt is stored on a wet victim and lands all at once when it steps onto dry ground. Wax is the one protection: a waxed body takes no Salt but 50% more Press, because wax traps air.
source: Pressure doubles with depth in a diving bell, silt is scoured only where water runs past an obstacle, and salt bursts stone only as it dries.
nearest: Weather and terrain boosting move types in Pokemon. Here the multiplier is the water under the victim, which the player controls by where the thumb leads the crowd, and Salt waits for a change of ground.

notes.where: Divinity: Original Sin 2 and Magicka, where a wet target takes more from some elements, Pokemon weather boosting move types, and Noita's stains. Harm sized by depth and by water speed past the victim, and a hit held until the ground dries, are in none of them.

Avatar: The Last Airbender's waterbenders, stronger the more water stands around them; Pokemon weather and terrain boosts; salt as the bane of slugs and the unquiet dead in folklore. The deferred Salt echoes the bends in diving thrillers, where the harm lands on leaving the water.

name: Candles of Grave Wax
idea: Every risen body is grave wax with a lit wick whose flame wastes 1% of its life each second. Break removes life at once. Draught makes a body waste four times faster for 4 seconds. Snuff puts it out: it stands inert and harmless until a lit body passes within 1 metre and relights it. Every hit is multiplied by wick length, which grows 10% per second unhit (to x3) and is trimmed to nothing by any hit. A horn lantern blocks Draught and Snuff until Break shatters it.
source: Bodies in wet airless ground turn to adipocere, a firm wax; an untrimmed wick grows long, and a draught makes a candle gutter and run away.
nearest: Enemies that get up again unless finished, as in the Dark Souls catacombs. Here only another walking flame relights the fallen, every body is on its own clock, and slow heavy hits are paid for their patience by the wick rule.

notes.where: Fallen raised by their Shaman in Diablo II, the Darklings of Slay the Spire and the catacomb skeletons of Dark Souls for the relight; the wick multiplier is near bonuses against untouched enemies (Crowbar in Risk of Rain 2, wake-up hits in Monster Hunter). The three verbs together are its own.

Grimm's Godfather Death, where every life is a candle burning down in Death's cave (retold by the Candle Maker in The Book of Life); Litwick in Pokemon, a candle ghost whose flame burns life; the lantern-bearing necromancers who raise the skeletons again in the Dark Souls catacombs. The life-candle image is stock; the wick-length and relight rules are not.

name: Girth, Wick, Bands
idea: Three measures of the character's vigil candle. Girth: 6 life per point. Wick: +1% casting rate and +4 cm of light per point. Bands: +1% duration of everything the character applies and +1 pool per point. Nothing is locked: a skill or item names the Wick or Girth it wants and works at yours divided by wanted, capped at 100%. Wick more than 25% above Girth gutters: each cast costs 1 life. Wick more than 25% below Girth tunnels: light radius is halved.
source: A candle's wick must be matched to its width: too thick a wick gutters and smokes, too thin a wick drowns in its own pool.
nearest: Attribute requirements on gear in Diablo II and Path of Exile. Here nothing is gated, a shortfall only scales the thing down, and two of the attributes are tied by a mismatch penalty in both directions.

notes.where: Dark Souls and Elden Ring, where a weapon below its stat requirement still works at reduced effect, and attribute requirements in Diablo II. Equip-load ratios punish one mismatch; a two-way penalty between a pair of attributes is not in them.

The life-as-candle of Godfather Death and 'burning the candle at both ends'; weapons that still work, poorly, below their stat requirement in Dark Souls. No story or creature has the wick-to-girth mismatch rule.

name: Ballast, Freeboard, Line
idea: Three attributes read off the character like marks on a hull. Ballast: 1% less distance moved by any push or current per point. Freeboard: the depth of water that counts as deep for this character rises 1 cm per point, from 1 metre. Line: +3 cm reach and pickup radius per point. Gear and skills have Lading in place of requirements: total Lading above Ballast is subtracted point for point from Freeboard, so an overloaded character works in full but is in deep water sooner.
source: A hull's load line shows how much freeboard is left as cargo is added, and it rides lower still in fresh water than in salt.
nearest: Equip load in Dark Souls. Here overload never slows or forbids; it lowers the depth at which the water turns against the character, so the price is paid in where the player may stand.

notes.where: Equip load in Dark Souls and the weight stat that resists knockback in Super Smash Bros.; pickup-radius stats in every horde game. Overload paid as a lower personal deep-water line is its own.

Equip load and encumbrance in Dark Souls and tabletop role-playing games; the folk-tale miser dragged under by the gold in his pockets. A price paid in depth rather than in speed is not something I can place.

name: Dead Water
idea: Applied to any body that crosses a seam where fresh water lies over salt, or by skills. For 9 seconds its speed runs on a 3-second beat: 2 seconds at 30%, then 1 second at 160%. All bodies marked by the same cast share one beat, so a crowd closes up into ranks that surge together. Anything moored, or walking the bottom in deep water, is immune. It ends early on dry ground.
source: In dead water a boat on fresh water lying over salt is held nearly still and then surges, because its push goes into waves on the hidden boundary between the layers.
nearest: Slowing effects in any action game. This one alternates held and surging on a shared beat, so its use is bunching a crowd into ranks for one blow, not escaping it.

notes.where: Space Invaders, whose whole horde steps on one shared beat, beat-locked movement in Crypt of the NecroDancer, and Zilean's Time Warp, which slows or speeds. A status that makes a crowd pulse into ranks is its own.

Pliny's remora holding a ship fast, and the becalmed ship of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner that then lurches half her length; Red Light, Green Light in Squid Game for a crowd that halts and surges on one beat; ordinary slowing effects otherwise.

name: Brined
idea: Each brine hit adds 1 stack to a wet victim, to a maximum of 20; a dry victim cannot be brined. Stacks do nothing in water. The moment the victim stands on dry ground every stack lands at once, 4% of the victim's full life each (1% on keepers, 2% on the player), and it is Crusted for 3 seconds, unable to take new stacks. Standing 1 second in fresh water (a font, a cistern, a rain pool) rinses every stack off harmlessly.
source: Salt does stone no harm while it stays wet and bursts it from inside as it dries; fresh water washes salt out.
nearest: Marks that a second skill detonates. Here nothing sets it off but the victim's own step out of the water, or the ebb leaving it dry, so the trigger is ground and tide.

notes.where: Blastblight in Monster Hunter (a pending burst the victim can clean off, faster in water), Tristana's Explosive Charge and Explosive Arrow stacks in Path of Exile; wet-then-punished in Magicka. A burst set off only by the victim's step onto dry ground is its own.

Oisin home from Tir na nOg, on whom three hundred years land the instant he touches Irish soil, and King Herla's riders who crumble on dismounting; the bends in diving stories; Bloodseeker's Rupture in Dota 2, harm that waits on the victim's own movement; marks detonated by a second skill.

name: Smoking
idea: Anything lit that is put out by a blow or a splash (a votive, a lantern, a lit body, the player's own flame) trails smoke for 2 seconds. In that time any flame within 1.5 metres relights it at once, from a distance, at no cost. After 2 seconds it is Cold, and relighting needs 1 second of touch. A snuffer, or water over the wick, skips Smoking and leaves it Cold immediately.
source: A candle just blown out can be relit through its trail of smoke without touching the wick; a snuffer leaves no smoke to light.
nearest: Revive windows on downed allies in cooperative shooters. This applies to every flame on both sides, works at range through the smoke, and how a flame is put out decides whether the window exists at all.

notes.where: Down-but-not-out in Gears of War: a felled fighter on either side has a short window in which a nearby ally brings it back, and a headshot or execution skips the window. Left 4 Dead and Apex Legends revives have the same two tiers; burnt bodies in Resident Evil and divine weapons in Dark Souls are the kill that denies the rising.
notes.mutation: Give the smoke a direction: a plume 2 metres long that leans the way the water is running, and only a flame the plume itself touches relights the wick. Whether a snuffed thing comes back then depends on which side of the other flames it was put out, upstream or down, not on a radius and a revive timer.

notes.where: 'Mostly dead' against 'all dead' in The Princess Bride; downed-but-not-out windows in Gears of War and co-operative shooters, where an execution closes the window; the parlour trick of relighting a candle through its smoke.

name: Silted
idea: In silty water any body moving slower than 1 metre per second gains 1 stack per second, to 10; each stack takes 5% off its speed, so slow things grow slower. No hit applies it. Moving faster than 3 metres per second for 1 second, or entering a current faster than 2 metres per second, scours every stack off at once. At 10 stacks the body is Mired: currents, pushes and hauls no longer move it at all.
source: Silt drops wherever the flow slows and is scoured away wherever it speeds up.
nearest: Chill that stacks toward a freeze. This is laid by the victim's own slowness and stripped by its own speed, no attack applies it, and its end state stops displacement, not action.

notes.where: Hodir's Biting Cold in World of Warcraft (stacks while you stand still, moving clears them) and quicksand in Super Mario and Zelda; chill building to a freeze in Path of Exile. A slow that ends as immunity to being moved is its own.
The Swamps of Sadness in The NeverEnding Story, where whoever slows and gives in is taken by the mire, and quicksand scenes generally; chill stacking toward a freeze in Diablo and Path of Exile.

name: Under Seal
idea: A wax seal is pressed on a body. While it holds, every timer on that body stops: no condition on it expires, no cooldown advances, and nothing new can be added. The seal breaks on the first single hit worth 8% or more of the body's full life, or after 15 seconds; smaller hits leave it whole. On an enemy it keeps stacks in place under many small hits. On the player it holds every timed upgrade until the first hard blow.
source: A wax seal keeps a thing exactly as it was closed and shows the first tampering by breaking.
nearest: Buffs that last until you are next hit. This stops good and bad timers alike, works on enemies as well as the player, and ignores hits below a threshold.

notes.where: Temporal Chains in Path of Exile (effects on the cursed expire slower), Stop in Final Fantasy, and crowd control that breaks at a damage threshold in World of Warcraft. A full stop of good and bad timers that small hits do not break is its own.

Sleeping Beauty's castle and Miss Havisham's stopped clocks, everything held exactly as it was until the spell is broken; stasis fields in science fiction (Vinge's bobbles); sleep effects that break on a hard hit; Temporal Chains in Path of Exile slowing the expiry of effects.

name: Listing
idea: A blow that lands on a moving body from the side (more than 50 degrees off its heading) makes it list: for 5 seconds its heading is turned 25 degrees toward the side it was struck from, so it curves past its target. A second blow from the same side doubles the lean to 50 degrees. A blow from the opposite side rights it at once. Bodies walking the bottom in deep water cannot list.
source: A hull whose ballast shifts to one side lists and will not hold a straight course until the load is trimmed back.
nearest: Confusion effects that scramble enemy movement. This is a fixed lean, set and cancelled by which side the blow comes from, so the player bends a crowd's path by choosing a flank.

notes.where: Only ships that list in naval games and ordinary directional knockback or confusion; I know no status that leans a walker's heading toward the side it was struck from and is cancelled from the other side.

Nothing close. Distantly: a sheepdog turning a flock by working one flank, a matador's side-step bending the bull's line, the one-oared boat that circles in cartoons. Confusion and knockback effects in games do not hold a fixed lean set by the side struck.

name: Thief
idea: A stray spark lodged in the victim. On the player: one in three pickups collected falls out 1 metre behind and must be gathered again; it never ends by itself and is pinched out only by standing still for 1 second. On an enemy: for 8 seconds it drops 10% of its eventual loot each second while it lives, so a tough body can be emptied without being killed, and one that survives the 8 seconds has nothing left to drop.
source: Chandlers called a stray bit of wick in the flame a thief, because it made the candle gutter and waste its wax down the side.
nearest: Dropping rings when hit in Sonic. This is a steady leak not caused by hits, and its cure is the one thing a horde game punishes, standing still.

notes.where: Sonic's scattered rings for the player half; for the enemy half, treasure goblins shedding gold while alive in Diablo III and the Plunderblade and shiny drops of Monster Hunter. Standing still as the cure is its own.

Sonic's spilled rings; the leaking sack that lays a trail (Hansel and Gretel's crumbs, the cartoon burglar's swag bag); Steal and Mug in Final Fantasy and the treasure goblin of Diablo III shedding gold as it is hit, for loot taken from a living enemy.

name: Mudlark
idea: A foreshore scavenger on mud boards. Silt never slows or silts a Mudlark. Lifting the thumb is a verb: after 0.4 seconds still the Mudlark stoops, drawing in every pickup within 5 metres and turning up one buried find if any lies within 2 metres. Moving off again takes 0.3 seconds. Starting skill, Grubbing Hook: every 2 seconds it rakes a 2-metre arc on the side with more enemies; raked enemies that die on mud drop one extra pickup.
source: Mudlarks worked the Thames foreshore at low tide, stooping for coal, rope and copper, and crossed soft mud on boards strapped to their feet.
nearest: Pickup magnets in every horde survival game. Here gathering is bought with stillness, a deliberate stop inside the crowd, and not with a radius number.

notes.where: Archero, where lifting the thumb is the attack; stopping to mine in Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor and dig spots in Hades II. Stillness spent on gathering inside the crowd, not on attacking, is its own.

Mayhew's mudlarks and the 1950 film The Mudlark; Dodger, Pratchett's tosher working London's sewers for finds; the scavenger-rogue archetype. Standing still for a bonus exists as an occasional item in horde games (Statue and Barricade in Brotato), not as the way to gather.

name: Chandler
idea: The city's candle-maker, carrying a rod of hanging wicks. A wax vat stands where the vigil starts; a button moves it to the Chandler's feet (20-second cooldown). Each time the Chandler comes back within 2 metres of the vat after going at least 12 metres from it, they take a Dip: one coat, to a maximum of 8. Each coat adds 6% to all harm dealt and is lost in place of life when hit. Starting skill, Broach: five wicks lash 3 metres ahead every 1.5 seconds.
source: A dipped candle is built one coat at a time, each cooled away from the bath before the next dip.
nearest: Stacking buffs that fall off when you are hit. Here a stack is earned only by running a lap out from and back to a point the player places, so the thumb draws loops through the crowd.

notes.where: Charges lost in place of life (Baldur Shell in Hollow Knight, Sonic's rings) and a planted object you stay near for a bonus (banners in Path of Exile, Ley Lines in Final Fantasy XIV). Earning a stack only by a lap out and back is its own.

Mr. 3 (Galdino) in One Piece, whose Wax-Wax Fruit builds him a wax armour that is knocked away in the fight; Achilles dipped in the Styx; buffs that stack and fall off when hit. A lap out from and back to a vat the player places is not something I can find.

name: Warper
idea: One who moves hulks through the flooded streets with anchor and line. A Warper does not walk. Every 0.9 seconds a kedge is thrown 4.5 metres the way the thumb points and the Warper is hauled to it in 0.35 seconds; nothing can push or hold them during a haul, and the taut line harms whatever it crosses. Between hauls the Warper stands. Starting skill, Kedge: the anchor's landing harms everything within 1.2 metres of it.
source: Warping or kedging moves a ship by carrying an anchor ahead, dropping it and hauling the vessel up to it.
nearest: Dash moves and grappling hooks. Here there is no walking at all: throw-and-haul is the only way to move, its rhythm is fixed, and the thumb's job is to choose a new bearing every beat.

notes.where: Timbersaw's Timber Chain in Dota 2 and Nautilus's Dredge Line in League of Legends (an anchor thrown, the hero hauled to it, harm along the way); Dandara, who cannot walk and only leaps; moving on the beat in Crypt of the NecroDancer. A class that moves only by a fixed-rhythm automatic haul is its own.

Kedging as an escape in sea stories (USS Constitution in 1812, Patrick O'Brian's novels); the mobility gear of Attack on Titan, which fires anchors and reels the soldier to them; Nautilus's Dredge Line in League of Legends; hop-only movement in Frogger. None forbids walking outright on a fixed beat.

name: Dredgerman
idea: A dragger of the river bed, paid for what he brings up. A 5-metre drag-chain trails behind him along the path he has walked. Enemies the chain passes over take harm in proportion to the chain's speed at that point, so a wide fast turn whips the tail through a crowd and a straight walk barely scratches. Standing still, the chain sinks and does nothing. Starting skill, Creeper: a grapnel on the chain's end hooks in one pickup per second from the ground it crosses.
source: Thames dredgermen dragged the bed with chains and grapnels called creepers, for coal, metal and the drowned.
nearest: Damaging trails left behind the player in horde games. This is one rope with a tail that lags and whips, harmless in a straight line and strongest on a turn.

notes.where: Brutal.io and Flail Rider: a flail dragged behind the player on a tether that does nothing in a straight line and whips through a crowd on a sharp turn, harm by its speed. Hammerfight is the older game built on weapon speed alone.
notes.mutation: Make it a drag, not a flail: the chain lies slack and harmless along the path walked, and every few seconds it is hauled taut to a straight line, dragging every body and pickup caught in the bight to that line and harming them by the distance dragged. The player lays a loop round a crowd and the haul does the work.

notes.where: Gaffer Hexam dragging the Thames in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend; Marley's ghost trailing his chain; the playground game crack-the-whip; physics flails whose harm is their swing speed (Hammerfight). A lagging tail that bites only on a turn is its own.

name: Lanternman
idea: A night watchman with a dark lantern. His light, and every skill, reaches only into a 70-degree cone ahead of his direction of travel, at double reach; behind him is black. A button closes the shutter: skills stop, and every enemy farther than 3 metres loses him and walks to where the light was last seen. Opening it takes 0.5 seconds. Starting skill, Glare: every 3 seconds the cone flashes and lit enemies cannot change heading for 1.5 seconds.
source: A dark lantern throws its light one way only and has a slide that hides the flame without putting it out.
nearest: Stealth toggles and weapons that fire the way you face. Here one shutter trades all offence for being lost by the crowd, and aim is simply the direction of flight, so fleeing and fighting cannot be done at once.

notes.where: Facing-fired weapons in Vampire Survivors (Knife, Whip), the vision cone of Darkwood and the torch of Alan Wake, and aggro drops such as Feign Death in World of Warcraft with the last-known-position search of stealth games. One shutter trading all offence for being lost is its own.

Alan Wake's torch, where a cone of light is the weapon and a boosted flash stops the Taken, and the stun flash of Luigi's Mansion; dousing your lantern so the hunters lose you in Amnesia: The Dark Descent; the bullseye and hooded lanterns of Dungeons & Dragons; the dark lantern Holmes shutters in The Red-Headed League.
notes.mutation: Let the light itself do no harm: each lit body throws a shadow down the cone and skills land only in those shadows, so the front rank becomes the lens that aims at the ranks behind, and the Lanternman fights by choosing whose shadow falls on whom.

name: Bell Diver
idea: A diver who works under a lowered bell. In water at least waist deep a button takes the Diver under: unseen and untouched by surface enemies, walking the bottom at 80% speed, moved by the undertow and not the surface current. Skills do not cast under water. Air lasts 8 seconds, 4 in deep water, and refills in 2 seconds at the surface. Starting skill, Pull-down: every enemy the Diver walks beneath (within 1 metre) is dragged under and harmed, double in deep water.
source: A diving bell's trapped air is squeezed to half its volume at ten metres, so the deeper the dive the less it gives.
nearest: Burrow moves, as Rek'Sai's in League of Legends. Here nothing bursts on surfacing: the harm is done by walking beneath the crowd, the air is halved by depth, and a different current from the surface steers the hidden walk.

notes.where: Weaver's Shukuchi in Dota 2 (unseen, harming each enemy passed through), Rek'Sai's burrow, the burrow-moving Roach of StarCraft II, and Sonic's air countdown. Air halved by depth and a hidden walk steered by a second current are its own.

Jaws and the drowners of folklore (Jenny Greenteeth, the kelpie, the Inferi dragging Harry under the lake in Half-Blood Prince): an unseen thing beneath the surface pulls victims down as it passes. Walking the bottom under trapped air is Jack and Will beneath the upturned boat in Pirates of the Caribbean; going under out of sight is Pyke's Ghostwater Dive in League of Legends and Dive in Pokemon.
notes.mutation: Drop the drag-under: let the bell's spilled air lift whatever he walks beneath, so surface bodies bob helpless and are carried off by the surface current while he goes the other way on the undertow. He then sorts a crowd between two currents instead of playing the shark.

name: Lamplighter
idea: The city's lamplighter, with a pole. Every district has lamp posts about 15 metres apart. Passing within 1.5 metres lights one for 40 seconds. Every lit lamp within 12 metres of the Lamplighter casts their skills as well, at 35% strength, at enemies inside its own 4-metre pool of light. Each enemy that walks through a pool takes 1 second off that lamp. The thumb walks a round. Starting skill, Taper: a 3-metre thrust every 1.5 seconds that lights whatever it touches.
source: A lamplighter walked a fixed round at dusk, lighting each street lamp in turn with a pole.
nearest: Captured towers that then fire for you. Here the towers copy the player's own skills, are worn down by the crowd, and stay alive only while the player keeps walking the round.

notes.where: Marauder sentries in Diablo III and spell totems in Path of Exile, which cast the hero's own skills, and captured map turrets; the light havens of Alan Wake. Fixed lamps on a timer the crowd wears down, kept alive by walking a round, are its own.

D. M. Cornish's Monster Blood Tattoo, whose second book is Lamplighter: lamplighters walk a fixed stretch of road at dusk with a pole, lighting the lamps and fighting the monsters on it. Also the lamplighter of The Little Prince bound to his round, the street lamps that are safe havens in Alan Wake, and captured towers that fire for you.
notes.mutation: Have each lamp keep what he did as he passed it, not his whole kit: it repeats on a loop the exact casts made inside its pool on his last visit, so a lamp is a recording of one stretch of the round and the player composes the district by which skill fired where.

name: Strandliner
idea: For a Mudlark. After every ebb the last high-water line stays drawn across the district as a strip of wrack 1.5 metres wide. Pickups gathered on the strip are worth double, enemies killed on it drop one extra, and a stoop made on it turns up a find without one being buried there (once per 10 metres of strip each tide). The strip is erased when water next covers it, so its place is new with every tide.
source: The strandline, the band of wrack left by the last high water, is where foreshore searchers look first.
nearest: Bonus zones marked on an arena floor. This is a thin line that the tide itself draws and redraws, so the best route is different every toll.

notes.where: Bonus-experience and gold zones on arena floors, and the shoreline where shells wash up in Animal Crossing and Stardew Valley. A thin strip redrawn by each tide is its own.
Beachcombers and wreck-pickers working the strandline in shore fiction; bonus strips marked on an arena floor in games. No story or creature repeats it; the tide redrawing the line is the fresh part.

name: Founder
idea: For a Chandler. At 8 coats, a return to the vat with the button held is a Pour and not a Dip: all 8 coats are melted out and one Bronze takes their place for the rest of the vigil. A Bronze is a coat that cannot be knocked off and counts double. Coats then start again from nothing, leaving the Founder bare until re-dipped. The number of Bronzes is limited only by how many times the player dares to stand bare.
source: In lost-wax casting the wax model is melted out of the mould and metal takes its exact place.
nearest: Cashing a stack in for a permanent bonus, as with kill stacks in League of Legends. Here the trade is made at a place, on purpose, and its price is going unprotected until eight more laps are run.

notes.where: Prestige in idle games (ascension in Cookie Clicker: melt the run for a permanent multiplier), stack items made permanent at full count (Tear of the Goddess into Seraph's Embrace), bank-or-ride combos in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater. Banking that leaves the banker bare is its own.

Talos, the bronze man whose making reads like lost-wax casting, and Achilles dipped in the Styx; stacks cashed into something permanent (Nasus and Veigar in League of Legends). Going bare by choice, at a place, is its own.

name: Body-finder
idea: For a Dredgerman. Enemies killed by the drag-chain stay hooked to it, up to 8. Each hooked body adds 12% to the chain's harm and takes 3% off walking speed. Hauling them to any river stair pays for them in the legacy currency: one unit a body, three at the stair on the far bank from where the vigil began. A keeper's blow shakes every body off. Stairs are marked on the ground from the start.
source: Thames dredgermen were paid a reward and inquest money for each drowned body they brought ashore.
nearest: Carrying a flag or a delivery in capture modes. Here the cargo is the player's own kills, it is weapon and burden at once, and the better payer is always across the district.

notes.where: Dome Keeper, where the haul trails behind on tethers and slows you until delivered; bounty skulls carried to a turn-in in Sea of Thieves; the idol in Spelunky. Kills that are weapon, burden and pay at once are its own.

Gaffer Hexam, paid for the drowned he hauls from the Thames in Our Mutual Friend; Achilles dragging Hector behind his chariot; bounty hunters hauling bodies in for pay (The Hateful Eight) and resurrection men paid by the corpse; carry-and-deliver cargo in capture modes.

name: Wrecker
idea: For a Lanternman. The button no longer shutters the lantern; it sets it down. Every skill casts from the lantern and every enemy walks to the lantern, not the player. The Wrecker walks dark, harmless and unseen beyond 2 metres, free to gather. The lantern has a quarter of the Wrecker's life; knocked over, it smokes for 2 seconds and must be reached in that time, or else relit by a 1-second touch. Picking it up is instant.
source: Wreckers were said to set false lights ashore so that ships would steer for them.
nearest: Totem builds in Path of Exile, where a placed object casts for you. Here it is all or nothing: every skill and every enemy's attention goes with the one light, and the player becomes a blind looter in the dark.

notes.where: Totem play in Path of Exile: a planted object with its own life casts your skills while Decoy Totem holds the monsters and you gather. The Engineer's sentry in Team Fortress 2 and sentries in Diablo III are the same seat.
notes.mutation: Let the false light wreck and not fight: the lantern casts nothing, and bodies steering for it walk a straight line, cannot turn aside and gain speed all the way. They are harmed by what they run onto (pillars, hulks, deep water, each other at the lamp) in proportion to that speed, so the skill is choosing a spot with rocks between.

notes.where: The wreckers' false light of Cornish legend (du Maurier's Jamaica Inn, the fire lit by the founders in Carpenter's The Fog); the flare thrown to draw the tyrannosaur in Jurassic Park and the pipe bomb in Left 4 Dead; spell totems and decoy totems in Path of Exile. The all-or-nothing split is the new part.

name: Tenebrist
idea: For any class. At every toll the Tenebrist must put out one of their own lights: the player picks one skill, reserved effect or in-run upgrade to go dark until the vigil ends. Every light still burning gains 12%, compounding. Once per vigil a light may be hidden and not put out: it comes back at the toll after next, at double strength for one toll. A Tenebrist down to one light pays nothing more.
source: At Tenebrae fifteen candles on a triangular hearse are put out one by one, and the last is hidden and then shown again.
nearest: Banishing options or removing cards to thin a deck. Here the loss is forced on a clock, it takes what is already in use, and everything left grows with each loss.

notes.where: Egocentrism in Risk of Rain 2 (every 60 seconds one of your other items is eaten and the stack grows) and Madness and Ceremonial Dagger in Balatro (each blind a Joker is destroyed and the multiplier rises). Deck-thinning and Banish are the milder forms.
notes.mutation: Give the dying light's strength to one heir, not 12% to all: the player names which burning light inherits the whole of what the darkened one did. The vigil becomes a line of succession ending in one overgrown flame, and the hidden candle comes back to inherit from it.

notes.where: Haydn's Farewell Symphony, where each player snuffs his candle and leaves, and Tenebrae itself; The One (2001) and Highlander, where each rival removed makes the survivors stronger; the blinded hero whose other senses sharpen (Daredevil); thinning a deck in card roguelikes.

name: Air-carrier
idea: For a Bell Diver. The Diver's air is no longer a private timer but a place: a dry circle 3 metres wide carried overhead like a bell. Inside it there is no water for anyone: currents do not push, wet conditions stop building, and brine bursts. The circle shrinks to 2 metres in waist-deep water and 1.5 in deep, and widens by 1 metre for 5 seconds each time the Diver touches a pocket of air trapped under a vault.
source: A diving bell carries a room of dry air down with it, smaller the deeper it goes, and Halley topped his up from sunk barrels of air.
nearest: Aura circles around the player. This one changes which rules the ground obeys inside it, and its size is set by the depth the player chooses to stand in.

notes.where: The water shield of Sonic 3 and Noita's Freeze Field and circle fields, a carried bubble that changes what liquid does; Cloud Nine in Pokemon cancelling weather for all. A bubble sized by the depth stood in, which bursts brine on those who enter, is its own.

The carried pocket of dry air: Aang's air bubble in Avatar: The Last Airbender, the Bubble-Head Charm in Harry Potter, the parted Red Sea in small; Sonic topping up from air bubbles under water. A dry circle that changes the ground's rules and is sized by depth is in none of them.

name: Snubber
idea: For a Warper. When a haul's line bends round a pillar, post or mooring ring, the Warper swings round it at the line's length and does not travel straight, sweeping everything the line crosses, and lands on the far side. One full turn of line round a post snubs it: for 3 seconds nothing, not a bore and not a keeper, can move the Warper, and whatever pushes them is shoved back as hard as it pushed.
source: One turn of rope round a bollard lets a single person hold a ship, because the friction multiplies with every turn.
nearest: Swinging on a grapple line in platform games. Here it is flat, the swing is the attack, and wrapping the post turns movement into being immovable.

notes.where: The ninja rope of Worms, which wraps round terrain, the flat swing round a post in Sling Drift, and Snake Pass coiling a pole for grip. A wrap that turns movement into being immovable and returns pushes is its own.

The snowspeeder's tow cable wound round the walker's legs in The Empire Strikes Back; the dally round the saddle horn and the snubbing post of Westerns; Spider-Man's swing; tetherball. Wrapping a post to become immovable is its own.

name: Panner
idea: For any class. Standing still for 1 second boils the water off a pan 2.5 metres wide round the character; it stays dry for 6 seconds. A pan is dry ground for everything: brine bursts on enemies that enter, silt cannot settle, and floating bodies ground and must walk. Up to 3 pans exist at once. A pan made in deep water lasts 3 seconds and leaves a ring of salt crust that slows whatever crosses it for 5 seconds.
source: Salters boiled and dried sea water in shallow pans until only a crust of salt was left.
nearest: Ground areas laid down by skills. These do no harm themselves; they change which rules the ground obeys, and they are placed by choosing where to stop.

notes.where: Surfaces in Divinity: Original Sin, where fire dries a water tile and the status rules change with it; stand-still zones like Bustling Fungus in Risk of Rain 2. A harmless patch placed by choosing where to stop is its own.

The Red Sea standing back to leave dry ground, and firebenders flashing water to steam in Avatar; ground zones laid by skills in action games. A harmless zone that only changes which rules the ground obeys is hard to place in any story.

name: Sounding Lead
idea: Every 4 seconds a lead on a line drops on the nearest enemy within 6 metres: one heavy hit, +50% for each band of water depth over the victim. The tallow in its base brings up a sample: for 8 seconds all of the character's skills deal 30% more to that enemy's kind. The lead holds one sample; each cast replaces it. The player chooses the sample by which kind they are passing closest to as the cast comes due.
source: A sounding lead's hollow base was armed with tallow to bring up a sample of the bottom, so the pilot knew what lay beneath.
nearest: Marking a quarry type for bonus damage. Here the mark is taken by the strike itself, is always the nearest body, and is overwritten every 4 seconds, so it is steered and not chosen from a menu.

notes.where: The ranger's favoured enemy in Dungeons and Dragons and Hunter's Mark in World of Warcraft; bonuses against a monster family in Diablo. A mark taken by the strike, always the nearest body, overwritten every cast, is its own.

The bloodhound given a scrap of its quarry's scent; the witcher's blade oils, each good against one kind of monster; the ranger's favoured enemy and Hunter's Mark in Dungeons & Dragons. A mark taken by the strike and overwritten every cast is its own.

name: Lee Eddy
idea: Whenever the character passes within 1.5 metres of a pillar, post or grounded hulk at walking speed or faster, an eddy 2.5 metres wide forms on its far side for 5 seconds (one per obstacle). An eddy does not pull. Any enemy that walks into it is carried once round and let go heading back the way it came for 1.5 seconds, into those behind; each collision harms both. Open ground gives nothing; a colonnade gives a chain of eddies.
source: Eddies turn behind piers and pillars, and inside an eddy the water runs upstream.
nearest: Whirlpool skills that suck enemies in. This pulls nothing: it turns pursuers round into their own crowd, and it exists only where the player brushes past an obstacle.

notes.where: Whirlwind and tornado towers in Bloons TD that blow the line back the way it came, fear effects that turn enemies round, and knock-into-others harm from Poseidon in Hades. An eddy born only by brushing an obstacle is its own.

Being pixy-led, or stepping on the Irish stray sod: the walker is turned about and sent back the way he came; Turn Undead in Dungeons & Dragons; Charybdis and Poe's Maelstrom for the whirl. Eddies that exist only where the player brushes an obstacle are new to me.

name: Sweep-wire
idea: Every 10 seconds a buoy is thrown 7 metres to the side with more enemies and a wire runs from it to the character for 6 seconds. The buoy drifts with the current; the wire follows the character. Each enemy the wire passes over is harmed once per half-second, in proportion to the wire's speed at that point, and not at all where it is still. Circling the buoy sweeps the wire like a clock hand; running straight away from it does nothing.
source: Salvors found sunk wrecks by towing a wire between two boats and sweeping the bed with it.
nearest: Beams linking the player to a drone or pylon. Here the far end drifts on the tide, the line is harmless when still, and its harm is exactly the speed the player gives it.

notes.where: Tether lines that harm what crosses them: the Electropylon Driver of Returnal, Loader's pylon in Risk of Rain 2, beams strung between two ships in cooperative shooters. A far end adrift on the tide is its own; the harm-by-speed rule is the flail's, as in water-15.

The snapped cable that scythes through the ballroom in Ghost Ship (2002); the nanofilament strung across the canal in The Three-Body Problem; the harbour chain raised at the Blackwater in A Clash of Kings; tether beams between the player and a drone in games.

name: Stylus
idea: The path walked in the last 3 seconds is written on the ground as a faint groove. The groove does nothing until the character crosses it. Crossing wipes it: every enemy within 0.7 metres of any part of the groove is struck at once, harder for each metre of groove up to 12. A new groove starts from the crossing point. Walking in a straight line never fires it.
source: A wax tablet is written with a stylus and rubbed out with its flat end, or wiped clean by warmth.
nearest: Fire trails left behind the player. This trail is inert until the player cuts back across their own line, so it pays for loops and figure-eights and gives nothing to a straight retreat.

notes.where: Qix, Volfied and Paper.io, where closing your own line is the attack, the capture loops of Pokemon Ranger, and Snake, where crossing yourself is the event. Striking along the groove, not inside a loop, is its own.

The magic circle that has power only when its line is closed, with Okami's brush loops and Pokemon Ranger's capture loops; the light-cycle trails of Tron, deadly to cross. A trail that fires along its whole length when its maker cuts back across it is not quite any of these.

name: Undertow
idea: Every 7 seconds, for 2 seconds, a strip 4 metres wide and 10 long ahead of the character runs two ways at once. Light bodies (the swarm) ride the surface 4 metres away from the character. Heavy bodies (elites, anything ballasted or mired) are dragged along the bottom 4 metres toward the character. Both are harmed for the distance moved. The strip points where the thumb points at the moment it starts.
source: Undertow pulls along the bottom against the flow at the surface.
nearest: Knockback skills and pull skills. This does both in one cast and sorts a mixed crowd by weight, bringing the dangerous few close and sending the many away.

notes.where: Pull skills and push skills everywhere; vacuums that take the small and leave the heavy (Luigi's Mansion, the Suck Cannon of Ratchet and Clank); spells with opposite effects by type, as healing harms the undead. One cast that sends the swarm out and drags the heavy in is its own.

Winnowing: the wind carries the chaff away and drops the grain at the thresher's feet; gold-panning; the rip current of sea thrillers. Separate push and pull skills are ordinary; one cast that sorts a crowd by weight is not.

name: High-water Mark
idea: The skill remembers the largest single hit the character has dealt since the last toll: the mark, shown as a line on its icon. Every 9 seconds it strikes the enemy with the most life within 8 metres for exactly the mark, with no multiplier applied. Each toll wipes the mark to nothing. The skill is as good as the one best blow the player can arrange early in each tide.
source: Flood heights were cut into church walls as high-water marks, each a record that stood until a greater flood.
nearest: Abilities that return a share of recent damage, like Zed's Death Mark in League of Legends. Here the store is a single best hit per toll, the player's to engineer, and it is replayed whole without scaling.

notes.where: Ignite in Path of Exile, built from the single strongest hit; Zed's Death Mark in League of Legends and Bide in Pokemon, which store damage and replay it. A per-toll record replayed whole is its own.

Bide and Counter in Pokemon and Zed's Death Mark in League of Legends, stored harm paid back; Echo of myth, who can only repeat; flood marks cut on church walls. Replaying one record blow per toll, unscaled, is its own.

name: Loose Pew
idea: At the first toll after the skill is taken, a pew 3 metres long floats up beside the character and stays for the vigil. It drifts with the current, turning as it goes, and whatever it strikes is harmed and shoved in proportion to its speed. The character moves it by walking into it: it takes the character's velocity for 2 seconds. On dry floor it grounds and lies still until water returns. Raising the skill adds a second pew.
source: In a flooded church the pews float off their fixings and knock about with the water.
nearest: The bouncing football weapon in Survivor.io. This one is not automatic: it goes where the tide and the player's shoulder send it, and it stops dead when the water leaves.

notes.where: The minecarts of the Dairy Plant in Vampire Survivors (touch one and it runs through the crowd), the football of Survivor.io, and props kicked into enemies in Half-Life 2 and Dark Messiah. One lasting piece of drift the player shoulders about is its own.

The kicked Koopa shell in Super Mario and the football in Survivor.io; furniture adrift in Titanic's flooding saloons and every flood scene. A battering object that only the tide and a shoulder can steer is its own.

name: Sluice
idea: Every 12 seconds the skill finds the deepest and the shallowest water within 9 metres of the character and joins them with a channel 1.5 metres wide for 3 seconds. Water runs from deep to shallow at 6 metres per second, carrying enemies and pickups (not the character) and harming what it carries. Afterwards both ends stand at the middle depth for 8 seconds. With level water all round, it does nothing.
source: Water in two flooded rooms stands at different heights until an opening joins them, then rushes from the higher to the lower until level.
nearest: Line-shaped push skills. This one is aimed by the ground and not by the caster, exists only between unequal water, and leaves the depths changed afterwards.

notes.where: Water finding its level in Noita, floodgates in Dwarf Fortress and From Dust, and the wave pushes of Hades. As a skill aimed by the ground that leaves both depths changed, I know no match.

Heracles turning two rivers through the Augean stables; the Ents loosing the Isen on Isengard; the flood at the Ford of Bruinen; the drained city of New Londo in Dark Souls. A channel aimed by the ground that leaves both depths changed is new.

name: Starling
idea: While the character stands still, enemies pressing within 3 metres build a head: 1 point each half-second for every 5 enemies, to 20. When the character steps away the head is let go through the spot they left: a race 2 metres wide and up to 10 long, running from the side where the crowd was densest out through the other, harming and sweeping everything in it by the head stored. Moving before any head has built releases nothing.
source: The starlings of Old London Bridge held the tide back until the river stood six feet higher on one side and ran through the arches as a rapid.
nearest: Attacks charged by standing still. Here the charge is the crowd itself leaning on the player, and the release is aimed by which side the player lets them through.

notes.where: Charges built by standing still (Brotato, Halls of Torment) and gauges filled by pressure taken (Galio's Shield of Durand in League of Legends, the V-Gauge of Street Fighter V). A charge that is the crowd's own lean, aimed by its densest side, is its own.

Horatius and every held bridge; the matador stepping aside; the judo maxim of yielding so that the pusher's own force throws him; the dead heaped against the wall in World War Z. Attacks charged by standing still are ordinary; charging one with the crowd's own press is not.

name: Pier-scour
idea: Always on. Any enemy that passes within 1.2 metres of the character without touching them is harmed once, by the closing speed between the two: 1 metre per second is a scratch, 8 or more is full harm. Running with the crowd alongside does nothing; running head-on through a gap in it rakes both sides. Each enemy can be raked once per second. Touching an enemy cancels the harm to it.
source: A river scours its bed deepest where the water speeds past the sides of a pier.
nearest: Graze scoring for near misses in bullet-hell shooters. Here the near miss is the attack itself, against bodies and not bullets, sized by how fast the two pass each other.

notes.where: Graze in Touhou and the Buzz system of Psyvariar, the speed bonus on blows in Mount and Blade, and the Garlic aura of Vampire Survivors. A near miss that is the attack itself, sized by closing speed, is its own.
The single-stroke passing duel of samurai film and anime, where two run past each other and one falls; the joust; the Road Runner's wake; graze scoring in bullet-hell shooters.

name: Bell-buoy
idea: Every 14 seconds a buoy with a bell is dropped at the character's feet and drifts with the current for 12 seconds. It rings only when jostled: each enemy that bumps it, and each metre it drifts, makes one ring, at most 4 a second. Each ring harms everything within 3 metres. In an empty lane it is silent; in a packed one it never stops. Dropped upstream of a crowd, the tide carries it through them.
source: A bell-buoy has no ringer: the swell rocks it and the bell sounds by itself.
nearest: Proximity mines and placed turrets. This has no trigger and no aim of its own: it answers crowding ring for ring and goes wherever the water goes.

notes.where: Pinball bumpers, which answer every knock, thorns and retaliation totems, and drifting sea mines. An emitter rung by crowding and carried by the tide is its own.

Southey's The Inchcape Rock and Kipling's The Bell Buoy for a bell the swell rings; bells that harm or bind the dead in Garth Nix's Sabriel and in church-bell folklore; drifting sea mines. A pulse that answers jostling ring for ring is its own.

name: Snuffer
idea: Every 5 seconds a bell-mouthed snuffer on a pole comes down, 1.2 metres wide, on the enemy within 5 metres that carries the most dangerous death effect, or failing that the weakest. Everything under it that is below 25% life goes out: removed with no death effect, no burst, no split and no smoke, so nothing can relight it. Enemies above 25% are untouched. It rewards wounding a crowd without finishing it.
source: A snuffer puts a flame out without smoke, and a church snuffer is a small bell on a pole.
nearest: Culling strikes that finish low-life enemies. The point of this one is what does not happen afterwards: a death that sets nothing off.

notes.where: Culling Strike in Path of Exile and the Old Guillotine of Risk of Rain 2; deaths that set nothing off, as exile in Magic: The Gathering, Silence and transform in Hearthstone, 'Slain Monsters Rest in Peace' in Diablo II and frozen exploders in Deep Rock Galactic. The pairing, aimed at death effects, is its own.

The kill that forecloses what follows: exile in Magic: The Gathering and Polymorph or Silence against Deathrattles in Hearthstone (removed, so no death trigger and no return); balefire in The Wheel of Time; salt-and-burn in Supernatural; burning the bodies before they rise as Crimson Heads in Resident Evil. Culling strike supplies the threshold.
notes.mutation: Let the snuffer keep what it smothers: each death effect it prevents is held under the bell, and all of them are poured out together the next time it comes down on an enemy above 25%, so the player harvests the crowd's own bursts and spends them where it matters.

name: Votive Round
idea: Every 8 seconds a votive is set at the character's feet and burns 16 seconds. It does nothing while the character is away. When the character comes back inside its 2-metre light it flares and is spent: harm to everything within 3 metres, greater for every second it has burned. A votive that burns out unvisited gives nothing, and each enemy that walks over one takes 2 seconds off it. The best round returns to each light just before it dies.
source: A votive candle is lit and left to burn while its giver goes away.
nearest: Delayed mines. These are set off only by the player's own return, ripen with time and are eaten by the crowd, so the skill is a circuit walked against a clock.

notes.where: The Engineer's pressure mines in Risk of Rain 2, which arm up to full strength over time, Zyra's seeds in League of Legends, woken by coming back with a spell, and the Demoman's stickies. Mines set off only by the player's return and eaten by the crowd are its own.

The plate-spinner running back to each pole before it falls; the lamplighter of The Little Prince; votive candles left burning in any church scene; delayed mines in games. Ripening charges that only the player's return can spend are its own.

name: Reflected
idea: The bound skill casts a second time, mirrored to the opposite side of the character, whenever the character stands in still water (current under 0.5 metres per second) at least ankle deep. In moving water or on dry ground there is no second cast. Cost: the skill is 20% weaker everywhere. Slack water at each toll, eddies and standing pools are the places where it pays.
source: Still water doubles every flame with a reflection; moving water breaks the image.
nearest: Multi-cast supports that repeat a skill. This repeat belongs to the ground, so the modifier is really an instruction about where to stand.

notes.where: Terrains and weather in Pokemon that boost a move only on the right ground, Spell Echo and while-stationary supports in Path of Exile. A repeat that belongs to still water is its own.

The reflection as a second self: Dark Link stepping out of the still pool in Ocarina of Time's Water Temple, Narcissus, the Mirror Image spell; multi-cast supports in Path of Exile. Tying the repeat to slack water is the new part.

name: Twelfths
idea: The bound skill repeats by the state of the tide. The 75 seconds between tolls are six parts of 12.5 seconds, and the skill casts 0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 0 extra times in them. Cost: its cooldown is 30% longer. It is strongest at mid-tide and plainest in the seconds around each toll, exactly when new danger arrives.
source: The rule of twelfths: a tide moves one, two, three, three, two and one twelfths of its range in its six hours.
nearest: Buffs on a repeating timer. This follows the run's own clock in a curve the player can learn, so fights are planned for mid-tide and caution for the toll.

notes.where: Convention of Elements in Diablo III, a bonus on a fixed repeating clock that players learn and fight around; the Balance Druid's Eclipse in World of Warcraft and turn-count relics in Slay the Spire are the same learnable cycle.
notes.mutation: Count the extra casts from the speed of the water at the character's feet, not from the clock: none in slack water, one in a stream, two in a race. Mid-tide is still the strong time, but arches, channels and eddies let the player find fast or slack water at any moment, so it is a rule about where to stand as well as when.

notes.where: Power that waxes and wanes on a clock: Gawain's strength growing until noon (Escanor in The Seven Deadly Sins), werewolves and the moon, waterbenders at the full moon in Avatar. No story uses the rule-of-twelfths curve itself.

name: Lagan
idea: The bound skill no longer acts when it casts. Each cast is sunk under a small buoy at the place it would have struck, to a maximum of 12 buoys (the oldest is lost). At every toll all buoys release together, each at double strength. Cost: the skill does nothing between tolls, and enemies must be standing over the buoys when the bell sounds.
source: Lagan is cargo sunk on purpose and marked with a buoy so that its owner can find it again.
nearest: Trap and mine supports in Path of Exile, which store a skill until something triggers it. Here neither enemy nor player triggers it; the toll does, turning the most dangerous moment of each tide into the player's own.

notes.where: Remote mines in Path of Exile and the Demoman's stickies in Team Fortress 2: casts stored where they would land and all let go together later, for more. Released by the clock and not the player it is the time bomb: Future Sight in Pokemon, Delayed Blast Fireball in Dungeons and Dragons.
notes.mutation: Sink each cast where the character stands and let the buoys drift on the current until the toll, releasing wherever the tide has carried them and stronger for every metre travelled. The player sows casts upstream of where the crowd will be at the bell and has to read the stream, which no mine or time bomb asks.

notes.where: Everything timed to the stroke of the bell: Cinderella's midnight, the synchronised charges of a heist film; remote mines and trap supports in Path of Exile; Zilean's time bombs in League of Legends. A store that only the run's own toll releases is its own.

name: Armed
idea: The bound skill takes on the ground under its first victim. On silt it lays 3 stacks of Silted on everything it hits. In deep water its victims take the blow a second time as weight. In a current it carries them 3 metres downstream. On dry stone it throws up salt crust that slows crossing bodies for 3 seconds. Cost: the skill's own harm is 25% lower, and the rider is whatever the ground happens to give.
source: The tallow on a sounding lead comes up carrying whatever the bottom is made of.
nearest: Skills that take an element from the weapon equipped. This reads the floor under the victim, so one socket gives four effects depending on where the fight is led.

notes.where: The Geomancer of Final Fantasy Tactics and Final Fantasy V, whose one command gives a different attack and rider by the terrain underfoot, and Secret Power and Nature Power in Pokemon, whose effect is read from the ground of the battle.
notes.mutation: Have the skill carry the ground with it and not just read it: it takes a sample from under the character at the cast and lays a 3-second patch of that ground under its victims, deep water on dry stone, a dry pan in the shallows, silt in a clear channel. The rider is terrain moved from one place to another, which sets off the wet and dry rules there.

notes.where: The Absorbing Man of Marvel comics, who takes on the nature of whatever he touches (and Kevin Levin in Ben 10); Secret Power and Nature Power in Pokemon, one move whose effect is decided by the ground the fight stands on.
notes.mutation: Make it carry ground rather than copy it: the skill takes its rider from the floor under the character at the cast and delivers it only onto a victim standing on a different floor, so it does nothing on uniform ground and pays for fighting across an edge of wet and dry, silt and stone.

name: Thief in the Wick
idea: The bound skill casts 50% faster. Cost: every cast spills one experience pickup the character had already gathered this level, dropped 1.5 metres behind, and the level bar falls with it. Spilled pickups can be collected again. The skill therefore lays a trail of the player's own gains through the crowd that follows them.
source: A thief in the candle makes it burn bright and fast and wastes the wax down its side.
