nearest: Supports that trade a resource cost for speed. Here the cost is not spent but dropped on the floor behind, recoverable only by turning back into the pursuit.

notes.where: Sonic's rings scattered to be gathered again, the dropped gold bags of Shovel Knight, and guns that fire your own money (the Microtransaction Gun in Enter the Gungeon). A per-cast cost dropped behind into the pursuit is its own.

Burning the candle at both ends; Sonic's spilled rings; Hippomenes dropping golden apples behind him in the race with Atalanta; the leaking sack that lays a trail. Speed bought by spilling your own gains into the pursuit is its own.

name: Shuttered
idea: The bound skill acts one way only: within 45 degrees of the direction the character is moving, at double reach. Targets outside that cone are ignored and area shapes are cut to it. Standing still, it points where the character last moved. Cost: the skill does nothing to what chases from behind, which in flight is everything.
source: A shielded lantern throws its light one way and leaves the rest in the dark.
nearest: Narrow-cone and facing weapons. As a socket it turns any automatic skill into one that works only while the player is advancing on the enemy.

notes.where: The Knife and Whip of Vampire Survivors, which fire only the way you face, and narrowing supports in Path of Exile; it also repeats the cone of water-16. As a socket on any automatic skill it is its own.

Facing weapons: the Knife and Whip of Vampire Survivors strike the way the character moves; Cyclops's visor and the blinkered horse; narrower-but-longer cone trade-offs in action role-playing skill trees. The same dark-lantern cone is already the Lanternman's.
notes.mutation: Fix the sector to the world, not the feet: the skill reaches double into one compass sector, set by where the character was heading as the toll struck and held for the whole tide like a lighthouse's sector light, so the player fights by where they stand and not by which way they run.

name: Resist
idea: The first time the bound skill touches an enemy it bites three times as hard and leaves a film of wax on it. The skill can never harm a waxed enemy again; the film lasts until the next toll. Cost: against a keeper or any long-lived enemy it lands one blow per tide. It makes a skill a harvester of fresh arrivals and useless as a finisher.
source: In wax-resist work acid or dye bites only where there is no wax; whatever has been waxed is spared.
nearest: First-hit bonuses. Here the bonus is paid for with total immunity afterwards, which changes what the skill is for.

notes.where: Bonuses against untouched enemies (Crowbar in Risk of Rain 2, Ambush in Diablo III) and per-target lockouts (Braum's stun immunity in League of Legends, diminishing returns in World of Warcraft). A triple bite paid for with immunity until the toll is its own.

The Borg adapting after the first phaser hit; 'the same technique never works twice on a Saint' in Saint Seiya; Doomsday, who cannot be killed the same way twice; bonuses against still-healthy enemies such as Ambush in Diablo III. Choosing that immunity as the price is its own.

name: Leading Lights
idea: Holds 20% of the pool. Two lights are kept burning: one on the district's bell tower, one on the gate that opened most recently. The straight line through them is the channel, drawn faintly on the water. While the character is within 1 metre of that line their skills reach 50% farther, and pickups lying within 3 metres of the line slide along it to them. When a new gate opens the channel swings round to it.
source: Leading lights are two beacons a pilot keeps in line, one above the other, to hold the safe channel.
nearest: Aura buffs kept up by reserving a pool. This one works only on a line across the map, so holding it is a commitment to fight along a bearing.

notes.where: Ley Lines in Final Fantasy XIV, a placed zone you must stand in to cast better, reserved auras in Path of Exile, and lanes in arena battle games. A bonus that exists only on a bearing between two landmarks is its own.

Ley lines: straight alignments between landmarks (Watkins's church towers and beacons in The Old Straight Track) along which, in fantasy from The Raven Cycle to the Geomantic Web of Total War: Warhammer, power runs and magic is stronger for whoever stands on them.
notes.mutation: Give the line no power of its own and pay for pilotage: reach grows the longer the character keeps under way along the line with the two lights held one above the other, and falls to nothing the moment they stray or stop, so it rewards holding a bearing through the crowd, not standing on a seam of power.

name: Flotsam Line
idea: Holds 15% of the pool. Pickups that fall on water float: they drift with the current, never expire, and collect in eddies behind pillars and in still corners, where they raft together into one pickup worth the sum plus 10% per item, up to 20 items. Pickups on dry ground are unchanged. The character stops chasing drops and harvests the lee of pillars.
source: Flotsam drifts with the tide and gathers in the eddies behind piers.
nearest: Pickup magnets and auto-collect. This sends loot away from the player to known places and pays a premium for going to fetch it.

notes.where: Water streams carrying drops to one collection point in Minecraft farms, experience gems merging in Vampire Survivors, and Brotato doubling what was left on the ground. Loot sent away to the lee of pillars at a premium is its own.

The Sargasso Sea of sea stories, where every drifting hulk ends up; Poohsticks; experience gems merging into one large gem in Vampire Survivors. Loot sent away to known lees and paid at a premium is its own.

name: Votive for Another
idea: Holds 30% of this character's pool, in and out of vigils, for as long as it is kept. The player names one other standing character. That character gains one extra option at every level-up and a light 1 metre wider. If the holder dies the votive goes out and the named character is Unlit for its next vigil: one option fewer at every level-up. A character can hold one votive and be named by one.
source: A votive candle is lit and left to burn for someone else.
nearest: Link skills in MapleStory, where one character lends a bonus to another. Here the gift is paid from the holder's pool at every moment, and the holder's death turns it into a debt.

notes.where: Link Skills in MapleStory and soldier bonds in XCOM 2: War of the Chosen, where a bondmate's death hurts the survivor. A gift paid from the holder's pool that turns to a debt on death is its own.

The life-token of folktale (the knife that rusts when a brother is in peril in Grimm's The Two Brothers) and Meleager's brand; bonded pairs where one's death maims the other (soldier bonds in XCOM 2, dragon and rider); Link Skills in MapleStory.

name: Cerecloth
idea: Holds 25% of the pool. The character is wound in waxed cloth and water cannot mark them: no wet condition (Brined, Silted, Dead Water) can be put on them, and currents move them half as far. Being sealed, they also cannot be rinsed, healed or refilled by any water: fonts, rain and air pockets do nothing. Heavy blows count 25% more, the wrap holding air to be squeezed.
source: The dead were wound in cerecloth, linen soaked in wax to keep water and air out.
nearest: Immunity auras with a drawback attached. This is one physical fact with both of its faces, sealed out and sealed in.

notes.where: Shroud in Magic: The Gathering (cannot be targeted by anyone, your own spells included), spell immunity in Dota 2 that also refused allied spells, and the Warforged of Dungeons and Dragons, immune to much and healed by half. Path of Exile keystones are built this way: an immunity paired with the loss of its matching benefit.
notes.mutation: Make the wrap seal in whatever is on the character when it is wound: switching it on stops every wet condition already on them from acting or expiring, and switching it off lets them all resume. It becomes a way to carry Brine sealed across dry ground to a font, at the price of the pool and the heavier blows.

notes.where: Odysseus's crew with beeswax in their ears, deaf to the Sirens and to everything else; the wrapped mummy; anti-magic heroes whom healing magic cannot reach either; two-faced keystones such as Chaos Inoculation in Path of Exile.

name: The Pour
idea: Offered as a blank. On taking it, wax is poured into the water under the character and sets in a shape the water decides. In a current: Long, every skill +25% reach. In still water: Round, +25% area. In deep water: Heavy, +25% harm and -10% casting rate. On dry ground it does not set and the pick is wasted. The offer names all four outcomes, so the choice is made by where the character is standing as the level arrives.
source: In wax divination molten wax is poured into cold water and sets at once into a shape that is then read.
nearest: Mystery upgrades with a random result. This result is not random; it is read from the ground, so the choice is made with the thumb before the menu opens.

notes.where: Pokemon: Burmy's cloak, set by the ground of its last battle, and Eevee or Magneton evolving into different forms by where they stand when they level up. Stat growth in Final Fantasy Tactics, decided by the job held at the moment of the level, is the same rule.
notes.mutation: Pour it hot and let it set over the next 10 seconds: the share of that time spent in current, still water and deep water becomes the share of reach, area and harm in the finished shape, and every second on dry ground is wax lost. The pick is a short run the player makes through the water, with a blended result no menu or map spot would give.

notes.where: Pokemon evolutions decided by where the creature stands when the level arrives: Eevee by the Moss Rock or the Ice Rock, Magneton in a magnetic field, Burmy's cloak taken from the ground of its last battle. The wax-in-water divination (lead-pouring, St Andrew's Eve wax) is the dressing.
notes.mutation: Do not pick from four named shapes: let the wax record the next three seconds of the character's own motion, with distance carried becoming reach, turning becoming area and depth becoming weight, in proportion, so every Pour is a one-off casting of that moment.

name: Low-water Find
idea: For the rest of the vigil, pickups gathered within 2 metres of the waterline (the moving edge between wet and dry ground) count double, and one buried find surfaces somewhere on the waterline at each ebb. The waterline moves all through every tide. A second copy widens the band to 3 metres. Away from the edge it gives nothing.
source: Mudlarks follow the water's edge down the foreshore as the tide falls, because that is where things are newly bared.
nearest: Bonus-experience zones. This is a line that travels across the map on a schedule the player can read.

notes.where: Moving objective zones (Crazy King in Halo, Hardpoint in Call of Duty) and shoreline spawns in Animal Crossing; it also repeats water-19. A bonus band that walks the map with the tide is its own.

The thing bared only at low water: wrecks and causeways shown by the ebb in shore tales (the Nine Lives Causeway in The Woman in Black); bonus zones in arena games. A reward line that travels with the water's edge is its own.

name: Shoot the Bridge
idea: Each time the character passes through a gap narrower than 3 metres (between pillars, piers or hulks) with at least 4 enemies within 2 metres, they gain a stack: +3% harm and +1% speed for the vigil, to 25 stacks. Passing the same gap again within 10 seconds gives nothing. Being hit inside a gap loses 3 stacks.
source: Watermen shot the arches of Old London Bridge on a running tide for the fare and the dare, while the cautious got out and walked round.
nearest: Stacking bonuses for kills or near misses. These are earned only by threading the map's narrow places with the crowd at the player's shoulder.

notes.where: Near-miss and oncoming boosts in Burnout, named gaps in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, slalom gates. Stacks earned by threading narrow places with the crowd at the shoulder are its own.

Running the gauntlet; the Argo shooting the Clashing Rocks; the Millennium Falcon threading the asteroid field; near-miss boost in Burnout. Stacks earned only at the map's narrows with the crowd at the shoulder are its own.

name: Nail in the Candle
idea: Take no upgrade now. A nail is pressed into the candle at the second toll from this one. When that toll sounds the nail drops: the player receives two picks at once, each showing one extra option, and the first of them is doubled in effect for one toll. Nails already set are shown on the candle and several may wait on one toll. Dying before a nail drops loses it.
source: A nail pushed into a candle clock falls onto a plate when the wax burns down to it: a set alarm.
nearest: Skipping an upgrade for a later reward. Here the payment falls at a known toll, just when danger steps up, and the player can load one toll with several nails.

notes.where: Chaos boons in Hades (pay now, blessing after a set number of chambers), the Invisible Joker and interest in Balatro, saving for interest in Teamfight Tactics. Loading one known toll with several nails is its own.

The time-locked vault and the marshmallow test; Faust's bargain turned round (pay now, collect at the appointed bell); Chaos boons in Hades and the Invisible Joker in Balatro, which pay out after a set count; interest in Teamfight Tactics.

name: Jetsam
idea: The offer shows the most valuable find the character is carrying unbanked. Taking the pick throws that find overboard for good. In return the character takes two upgrades now, and every later offer in this vigil shows one extra option. It is not offered when nothing is carried. A character who banks often will rarely see it; one who hoards will see it often.
source: Jetsam is cargo thrown over the side on purpose to save the ship.
nearest: Paying gold or health for power in roguelike shops. The price here is the single best thing the player was trying to carry out alive.

notes.where: N'loth in Slay the Spire (give up a relic for better offers from then on), devil deals in The Binding of Isaac, altars in Spelunky. The price being the best unbanked find is its own.

The sacrifice of the dearest thing: Polycrates throwing his most prized ring into the sea, Agamemnon and Iphigenia, the Soul Stone's price in Avengers: Infinity War; devil deals in The Binding of Isaac and N'loth trading away a relic in Slay the Spire.
notes.mutation: Do not buy generic power with it: let the jettisoned find be burned for itself, its own properties coming back as in-run upgrades at double strength for this vigil only, so the player chooses to use the keepsake up now rather than carry it home.

name: Turn of the Tide
idea: The next toll's tide is reversed: a flood becomes an ebb or an ebb a flood, and it holds for two tolls before the pattern resumes. The offer shows which tide was coming. It lets a character who needs dry ground, or deep water, keep it for 150 seconds through the next rise in danger. It cannot be taken twice in a row.
source: Between spring and neap the same shore is bared wide or hardly at all, and the tide table decides what work can be done.
nearest: Arena or weather modifiers chosen between rounds. This is taken mid-run in place of an upgrade and changes the map's water, not the character.

notes.where: Rain Dance and Sunny Day in Pokemon (spend the turn to set the field for five turns), the Rod of Seasons and the Sun's Song in Zelda. Taken mid-run in place of an upgrade to hold the tide, it is its own.

Commanding the tide and the weather: Canute's failed order, Prospero's storm, the wind-knots witches sold to sailors, the Sun's Song turning night to day in Ocarina of Time; choosing the next room's modifier in roguelikes.

name: Tide-marked
idea: At each toll the deepest water the character stood in for 3 seconds during the tide just ended is marked on them: no mark gives nothing, ankle +6%, waist +12%, deep +20% to harm and casting rate, until the next toll. The mark is drawn as a line across the figure. Each tide the player decides how deep to wade, once, for the sake of the next 75 seconds.
source: Flood water leaves a tide mark on every wall at the height it reached.
nearest: Buffs refreshed each wave for taking a risk. Here the risk is a depth the player wades to once per tide, and the result is worn as a visible line on the figure.

notes.where: Opt-in risk for the next reward (Shrine of the Mountain in Risk of Rain 2, flawless doors in Dead Cells) and buffs renewed each wave. One wade per tide worn as a line is its own.
Achilles held by the heel in the Styx, protected exactly as far up as the water reached; flood marks on walls; risk-for-buff choices refreshed each wave in horde games.

name: Drifter
idea: A swollen body afloat, face down. It does not chase. It moves with the current at the current's speed plus a paddle of 0.5 metres per second toward the nearest living thing, so it arrives from upstream, stalls at slack water and comes back the other way when the tide turns. In eddies it circles. Each Drifter touching the player takes 15% off their speed and presses each second. Read: pale spheres bobbing in lanes. Answer: cross the stream, never stand down-current.
source: A drowned body sinks, then rises days later and travels with the tide.
nearest: Hazards riding conveyor belts or river currents. These are the horde itself, and their only legs are a tide the player can read.

notes.where: Jellyfish that float slowly at the player in Risk of Rain 2, the wind-driven Angry Tumbler of Terraria, logs and hazards on river currents in Frogger. A horde whose only legs are a readable tide is its own.

The floater: the bloated drowned dead of zombie fiction and games (Dead Island's Floater, the drowners of The Witcher, the Drownies of Sunless Sea), and the dead that come in with the tide (the sea-floor walkers washing ashore in World War Z, the revenants of The Fog). Hazards riding a current supply the movement.
notes.mutation: Keep the tide as its only legs but make it something the flood lifted, not something that drowned: a raft of wax-fused hassocks and coffin boards with a passenger aboard, which can be boarded, ridden or broken up as it passes.

name: Wick-walker
idea: A grave-wax body with a lit wick, wasting 2% of its life each second. Any hit above 5% of its life, or water over its head, puts it out: it stands as an unlit stub, harmless, and worth double tallow if it is left whole. A lit Wick-walker passing within 1 metre relights a stub. Read: a walking flame that casts real light. Answer: put them out far apart, keep the lit away from the stubs, or simply outlast them.
source: Adipocere, grave wax, forms on bodies in wet airless places and keeps their shape; one candle is lit from another.
nearest: Enemies that rise again unless dealt with, like the Crimson Heads of Resident Evil. Here revival is contact with a living flame, and every one of them is dying on its own clock.

notes.where: Fire Keese in Zelda, which relight at any flame, Fallen revived by a Shaman in Diablo II, Crimson Heads in Resident Evil, Darklings in Slay the Spire. An enemy dying on its own clock and worth more left unlit is its own.

Corpse candles of Welsh folklore (a walking flame that foretells a death), Litwick, and the life-candles of Godfather Death; the Fallen Shaman raising the Fallen in Diablo II and the Crimson Heads of Resident Evil for the dead put down but not out. Revival by a passing flame, on a body that is burning itself away, is its own.

name: Belled
idea: A drowned diver still walking inside a diving bell: a cone on two legs. On dry ground and in shallows the bell covers it and no harm reaches it. In water waist deep or more the air inside is squeezed, water rises in the bell, and it takes full harm, double in deep water. It walks straight at the player at 1.2 metres per second and brings the rim down on a 1.5-metre circle shown 1 second ahead. Answer: lead it into the deep.
source: A diving bell's air is squeezed smaller the deeper it goes, until the water inside reaches the diver.
nearest: Shielded enemies that must be flanked or stripped. This shield is ended by the ground, and the cure is taking the fight into the water the player would rather avoid.

notes.where: Armour that softens only on the right ground (Agnaktor and Lavasioth in Monster Hunter), enemies harmed by water in Minecraft, shield bubbles that must be entered in Path of Exile. A shield ended by depth the player would rather avoid is its own.

The lumbering dead diver in brass: BioShock's Big Daddy, Captain Cutler's ghost in Scooby-Doo; Antaeus, unbeatable only while he stands on his own ground, and the knights drowned by their armour on the ice in Alexander Nevsky. A bell on legs whose shield is squeezed off by depth is new.

name: Cered
idea: A body wound in waxed cloth. Wax floats: on water of any depth it runs on the surface at 5 metres per second, faster than the player; on dry ground it shuffles at 1. No wet condition stays on it. It harms by ramming, in proportion to its speed at contact, so on water it hits hard and on stone hardly at all. Read: a white cylinder riding high with no wake. Answer: meet it ashore, where it is the slowest thing in the district.
source: The dead were wrapped in cerecloth, waxed linen, and wax and tallow float.
nearest: Fast flanking enemies. Its speed and its harm are both properties of the surface under it, so one step onto stone turns the hunter into the easiest kill.

notes.where: Zerg on and off creep in StarCraft, sharks and crocodiles that are deadly in water and helpless ashore (Maneater, Far Cry), ramming chargers. Speed and harm both read from the surface is its own.

The shambling bandaged Mummy crossed with a pond-skater or the basilisk lizard that runs on water; the seal and the crocodile, terrors afloat and helpless ashore. Speed and harm both read from the surface underfoot is its own.

name: Salter
idea: A body crusted white with salt, walking in water only. Its touch, and the brine it flings in a 2-metre splash shown 0.8 seconds ahead, put Brine stacks on the player (to 10). Brine does nothing while the player stays in water. Stepping onto dry ground costs 2% of full life per stack at once. One second in a fresh-water font rinses it all. Read: white cubes that stop at the water's edge. Answer: know where the font is before going ashore.
source: Salt dries into crust and does its damage only as its host dries out.
nearest: Enemies that apply a stacking damage-over-time. These deal nothing themselves; they turn the safe ground into the thing that hurts.

notes.where: Raid debuffs cleansed only at a marked pool (World of Warcraft, Final Fantasy XIV) and wet-then-punished in Magicka and Divinity: Original Sin. It is water-06 on an enemy; safe ground made the thing that hurts is its own.

Lot's wife, the salt vampire of Star Trek's The Man Trap, Aquaman's old weakness of dying if kept out of the water, and the Little Mermaid's knives underfoot on land. An enemy that deals nothing itself and arms the safe ground is its own.

name: Bedded
idea: The dead under the silt. At ebb the bared foreshore shows them as low cone mounds among the finds. A mound wakes if anything living steps within 1 metre, and every mound still asleep wakes together when the returning water covers it. Woken, they are slow, heavy and hard to move. Read: cones ringed with dry cracks; a woken one has lost its cone. Answer: thread the mounds to take the finds at low water, and be gone before the flood.
source: Mudlarks searched the foreshore at low tide, and silt buries and keeps whatever lies still in it.
nearest: Sleeping enemies woken by coming near. These are a field the tide arms on a timer, laid across the richest ground in the district.

notes.where: Sleepers laid over the loot: draugr in the barrows of Skyrim, Decayed Guardians in Breath of the Wild, Armos statues, sleeper zombies in 7 Days to Die, the Witch in Left 4 Dead. The wake-all on a clock is nightfall in Dying Light and Minecraft.
notes.mutation: Tie the waking to the taking, not to nearness: the mounds never stir at ebb, but each find lifted from the foreshore unbeds the nearest mound, which rises only when the returning water covers it. The flood then brings exactly as many heavy dead as the player took finds, from the places they were taken.

notes.where: The dead asleep in their mounds who wake when disturbed: Tolkien's barrow-wights, the Norse mound-dwellers, the draugr sitting dormant among the treasure in Skyrim's barrows; the Stalchildren that rise from Hyrule Field when night falls; the egg field of Alien. The flood plays the part of nightfall.
notes.mutation: Wake them by drying, not by footsteps: each mound hatches once it has lain bare for ten seconds and beds down again when covered, so a line of waking follows the ebb down the shore and the only quiet ground is the strip the water has just left.

name: Stone-belly
idea: A body sunk with ballast stones and tied to a buoy so it could be found again. In deep water it walks the bottom unseen and can be harmed only by weight from above; just its buoy shows, a red sphere gliding on the surface over it. It comes up to strike in the shallows, slowly, with a wide swing shown 1.2 seconds ahead. Hitting the buoy 3 times cuts the line: it loses the player and wanders. Answer: fight it in the shallows or cut its buoy.
source: Lagan is goods sunk on purpose and buoyed for recovery, and weighted things walk the bottom.
nearest: Burrowing enemies that surface to attack. This one is tracked by a float the player can strike to blind it.

notes.where: Burrowers with a surface tell (Molduga in Breath of the Wild, the fin and barrels of Jaws games) and river Zoras that surface to strike. A float the player can cut to blind it is its own.

The yellow barrels that track the unseen shark in Jaws, and the dorsal fin generally; Bootstrap Bill sunk tied to a cannon and the cursed crew walking the sea bed in Pirates of the Caribbean; the wolf drowned with a belly of stones in Grimm. Striking the float to blind the walker is the part I cannot place.

name: Kiddle
idea: A fish weir: two fences of stakes 6 metres long meeting in a V, a wicker cone at the point, facing the current. While water moves, anything drifting or walking down-current between the arms is funnelled into the cone, where it is pressed each second and can leave only against the current at quarter speed. Enemies and pickups are caught as well as the player. At slack water it holds nothing and gives up every pickup it has caught. It cannot be destroyed.
source: Fish weirs and eel bucks are funnels that a fish swims into with the tide and cannot find its way out of.
nearest: Static trap hazards. This one is also the district's loot collector, dangerous for most of each tide and a prize at the turn.

notes.where: Water-funnel mob grinders in Minecraft, which also gather the drops, one-way conveyors into crushers in Mario, pinball outlanes. A trap that is the district's loot collector and opens at slack water is its own.

The antlion's pit and the Sarlacc, a funnel you slide into and cannot climb out of; the lobster pot; crusher-and-conveyor hazards in games. A trap that is also the district's loot collector and empties at slack water is its own.

name: Bucket-chain
idea: A dredger still turning. Along a fixed line 30 metres long a chain of buckets passes every 20 seconds, the line darkening for 2 seconds first. Everything on the line (enemies, pickups, the player) is scooped, carried to the spoil heap at its end in 3 seconds and dumped, taking a modest hit. A player may ride it on purpose to cross the district or to dump a crowd, and the spoil heap is where its scooped pickups lie.
source: A bucket dredger lifts the bed in an endless chain of scoops and drops it on a spoil heap.
nearest: Trains or carts that cross an arena on rails. This one moves what it hits to a known place, so it is transport, crowd disposal and loot collector by turns.

notes.where: Stage hazards that carry fighters off in Super Smash Bros. (Spirit Train, Big Blue), minecarts in Vampire Survivors, conveyor tiles in Bomberman. A sweep that moves crowd, loot and player to one known heap is its own.

The conveyor to the furnace in Toy Story 3 and the sawmill belt of the serials; the mine cart of Temple of Doom; trains that cross an arena on a timetable in action games. Its use as transport and crowd disposal is the fresh part.

name: Ex-voto
idea: A heap of wax limbs left at a shrine, walking. Every 5 seconds it raises one limb for 1 second and lobs it 6 metres. A wax leg takes 30% of the struck player's speed for 6 seconds; a wax hand shrinks their pickup radius to nothing; a wax eye halves their light. Each limb thrown is gone from the heap: after three it is a bare frame that falls to one hit. Read: the raised shape, cylinder, box or sphere, names what is about to be taken.
source: Wax models of legs, hands and eyes were hung at shrines as offerings for the healing of that part.
nearest: Casters that throw a random debuff. Here the shape in the air tells which faculty is at stake, and the enemy spends its own body to do it.

notes.where: Bone-throwing skeletons in Castlevania, which spend themselves, crippled limbs in Fallout (leg for speed, head for sight), and the Like-Like of Zelda, which takes one named thing. The raised shape naming the faculty at stake is its own.

The heap-of-bodies monster (Legion in Castlevania, The One Reborn in Bloodborne, Gravelord Nito); the wax poppet of sympathetic magic, turned round so that the wax limb takes the matching limb's power; the Black Knight losing limbs in Monty Python. Spending its own body on three readable thefts is its own.

name: Keeper of the Hearse
idea: The keeper bears a triangular frame of 15 candles, each lighting one 24-degree sector. Phase one: a candle flares 1.2 seconds, its sector is swept with harm, the candle dies and the sector goes dark. Touching the frame within 2 seconds relights it through its smoke and wounds the keeper. Phase two, at 5 candles: two flare together. Last: the final candle is hidden for 5 seconds of dark and three rings of noise, each a clap 0.8 seconds ahead; shown again, the keeper takes triple harm for 6 seconds.
source: At Tenebrae fifteen candles on a hearse are put out one by one, the last is hidden, a great noise is made in the dark, and the candle is shown again.
nearest: Boss fights that black out the arena. Here the dark arrives sector by sector, the player can win each sector back through the smoke, and the last phase is dodged by ear.

notes.where: Clock-sector sweeps in Final Fantasy XIV and World of Warcraft raids, the Lost Sinner's dark arena in Dark Souls II, which the player can light, torch-relighting bosses in Zelda, shrinking arenas. Winning sectors back through the smoke and a last phase dodged by ear are its own.

Tenebrae itself; Zhuge Liang's seven-star lamps in Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a life staked on keeping the lamps alight; the lights put out one by one for a fight in the dark in Wait Until Dark and The Silence of the Lambs; clock-face sector attacks in raid bosses.

name: Keeper of the Unpoured Bell
idea: Phase one: the keeper is a wax model with eight faces, each recording the harm done to it. It drips molten wax in shadowed circles (1 second warning) that set into pillars. Phase two, at half life: the wax is run out and bronze takes its exact place. Faces most harmed in wax are thin and take double; untouched faces take a fifth. The bronze turns its thin faces away at 30 degrees a second and swings a 4-metre arc shown 1 second ahead. Sculpt the flaw, then reach it.
source: In lost-wax casting every mark made on the wax model is reproduced exactly in the metal that replaces it.
nearest: Bosses with a weak point on the back. Here the player makes the weak point in the first phase, and the second phase is cast from that work.

notes.where: Sectioned armour in MechWarrior and BattleTech, where the damaged side is turned away from you, and wounds and tenderised parts in Monster Hunter. Sculpting the flaw in one phase and having the next cast from it is its own.

Talos, the bronze giant with one weak place; the bell-founding tales (Hearn's The Soul of the Great Bell, the casting in Andrei Rublev); part-breaking and wounds in Monster Hunter, where the hunter's earlier hits make the weak point. A second phase cast from the first phase's damage is its own.

name: The Lock-keeper
idea: Fought in a lock chamber 24 metres long. Phase one, filling: the water rises one band every 15 seconds while the keeper heaves ballast stones, each a shadow circle 1 second ahead. Phase two, in deep water: paddles open and a race runs down one of three lanes, its water streaking 1.5 seconds first; anything in it is swept to the far gate and pressed there. Phase three: the gates open and a bore crosses the chamber every 12 seconds. The only lee is within 3 metres behind the keeper.
source: A lock's gates are held shut by the water and its paddles let the levels equalise in a rush; the lee of a pier is the one still place in a race.
nearest: Arena bosses with lane attacks. Here the room's water level is the phase counter, and the final shelter is the boss's own lee, inside his reach.

notes.where: Leviathan in Final Fantasy XIV (water surging across the deck) and the raid habit of hiding behind a pillar from a room-wide blast; rising-water arenas in Zelda and Mario. Water level as the phase counter and the boss's own lee as the shelter are its own.

The flooding chamber of adventure serials (the trash compactor, every rising-water trap); the sluice-keeper of Sayers's The Nine Tailors; the stock boss rule of sheltering behind the boss or in the storm's eye. Water level as the phase counter is the fresh part.

name: Keeper of the Sunk Bell
idea: The keeper waits inside a great bell hung over deep water and cannot be harmed outside it. Every 20 seconds the bell's shadow falls on the player for 1.5 seconds, then it drops: everything in its 5-metre circle is sealed in with the keeper for 10 seconds, in air. A candle inside is the only light and the measure of the air; when it dies, all inside take harm each second. The player may snuff it early to save air and fight blind. Phase two: two candles, half the air.
source: A candle lowered into a vault or carried in a diving bell shows the state of the air: it dims and dies before a person does.
nearest: Arena bosses that trap the player in a dome. Here being trapped is the only way to hurt it, and the fight's clock is a flame the player may choose to put out.

notes.where: Mordekaiser's Realm of Death in League of Legends and the brain room of Yogg-Saron in World of Warcraft: taken into a sealed space on a hard clock, the only place the boss can be hurt. A clock that is a flame the player may put out is its own.

Hauptmann's play The Sunken Bell; the candle guttering in a sealed vault (The Cask of Amontillado) and the submarine crew dousing lights to save air; the cage match of Thunderdome and duel realms such as Mordekaiser's in League of Legends; being swallowed to strike from inside (Jonah, Jabu-Jabu).

name: The Nave
idea: A flooded nave 60 metres long between two rows of cylinder pillars, box pews adrift. Five colours: drowned green water, slate stone, candle gold, lichen-white tide marks, soot. The water sloshes end to end on a 24-second beat: the west end is deep while the east is ankle deep, then the reverse. The crossing in the middle never changes depth but has the fastest flow. Tide-mark bands on each pillar show how high the water will come there. Pews ride the slosh and knock down what they meet.
source: Water in a closed basin rocks end to end as a seiche, rising and falling at the ends and running fastest through the level middle.
nearest: Arenas with rising and falling hazards. This depth is a standing wave the player can ride, always shallow somewhere for a player who keeps time.

notes.where: Tide levels in Salmon Run (Splatoon), the tides of Mario Kart beach tracks, tilting stages in Super Smash Bros. A standing wave with a level, fast middle is its own.

The drowned cathedral of Ys (Debussy's La cathedrale engloutie) and New Londo in Dark Souls for the place; tilting-deck fights such as Leviathan's barge in Final Fantasy XIV for the slosh. A standing wave the player rides end to end is its own.

name: The Bridge of Starlings
idea: A bridge of nine arches on boat-shaped piers (tapered boxes) cuts the district in two. Five colours: pewter water, rust, pale ashlar, tar black, one signal red. The water stands one depth band higher on the side the tide comes from, and each arch is a race 3 metres wide running to the low side, reversing at every toll and still for 6 seconds at the turn. Crossing means shooting an arch: 9 metres per second through, harmed on the way. Enemies cross the same way, in bursts.
source: Old London Bridge's starlings dammed the tide until the river stood six feet higher on one side and its arches ran like weirs.
nearest: Maps split by chokepoints. These chokepoints run one way for 70 seconds and then turn round, so the two halves take turns at being the trap.

notes.where: One-way doors and conveyors on timers in Bomberman and Zelda dungeons, rapids chutes in Donkey Kong Country. Chokepoints that run one way for a tide and then turn round are its own.

Old London Bridge as fiction has it; the Clashing Rocks and Charybdis, a strait that opens and reverses on a rhythm; one-way gates on a timer in arena maps. Two halves taking turns as the trap is the fresh part.

name: The Strand
idea: Mudflats under a wall of river stairs (stepped boxes), with mooring posts and three stranded hulks (tapered boxes). Five colours: mud brown, tin-grey water, bone, weed green, one buoy red. At each ebb the water draws 30 metres back, baring silt that slows everyone not on boards and showing buried finds as glints. At each flood the hulks float and ground again somewhere new, so the walls of the map change every second toll. The stairs are always dry.
source: A grounded hull lifts on the flood and settles wherever the ebb leaves it, and the foreshore exists only at low water.
nearest: Day and night map states. Here the two states alternate every 75 seconds and the water reshuffles the obstacles each time.

notes.where: Low tide in Salmon Run opening the foreshore, Levolution in Battlefield 4, day and night map states. Hulks that float and ground somewhere new each flood are its own.

The marshes and prison hulks of Great Expectations, the tidal sands of The Riddle of the Sands, the causeway of The Woman in Black; the maze whose walls move each night in The Maze Runner; day and night map states.

name: The Wick
idea: On the shared tree each character marks one unbroken path of 8 of its allocated nodes as its wick, in order. During a vigil the wick burns one node per toll: at the first toll node one counts triple until the second toll, then node two, and so on. At the eighth toll, when the keeper arrives, node eight is the one alight. Past eight the wick starts again. Re-marking the wick is free between vigils.
source: A candle marked in bands is a clock: each band's turn to burn comes at a known hour.
nearest: Keystone nodes in a passive tree. Here the player schedules which ordinary node is tripled at which toll, so a path through the tree is also a timeline through the run.

notes.where: Convention of Elements in Diablo III (a bonus that rotates on a clock) and the fixed cast order of a wand in Noita. Scheduling which ordinary node is tripled at which toll is its own.

Nothing close. Distantly: the canonical hours of a Book of Hours, one office to each bell in fixed order; an Advent candle burned a band a day; a step sequencer's moving light. No tree I know lets the player schedule which node is alight at which toll.

name: Wax and Bronze
idea: Every node is first taken in wax: it works at half strength and can be wiped and moved at will, for nothing. A character may pour a cluster: every wax node in it turns to bronze, working at full strength and never refundable, and every node of that cluster left untaken is closed to that character for good. The tree is drafted in wax, tried in a vigil, and committed one cluster at a time.
source: A wax tablet is wiped clean by warmth, but a lost-wax casting can never be altered once the metal is poured.
nearest: Respec points in passive trees. Here trial is free and unlimited but only half real, and commitment is the act that gives full value and removes options.

notes.where: Free respecs in Diablo III against permanent exclusive picks (Ascendancy in Path of Exile, policy trees in Civilization V). Trial at half strength and a commitment that closes the rest of a cluster are its own.

Pencil then ink, wet clay then fired pot; the choice that closes the other doors for good (the Grail knight's 'choose wisely'); free respec set against permanent ascendancy choices in Path of Exile. Half-strength trial nodes are not something I have met.

name: Confluence
idea: Each node's strength depends on the flow reaching it. Flow is 100% at the tree's source and loses 4% for each node travelled along the character's allocated path, so a long thin line ends weak. A node fed by two separate allocated paths is a confluence: flow there is restored to 100% and the node itself counts 25% more. Good trees are braided, not strung.
source: Silt drops where a channel's flow slackens and is scoured clear where two streams join and the water speeds up.
nearest: Travel nodes in the Path of Exile tree. Here distance itself weakens whatever lies at the end of it, and closing a loop is what pays.

notes.where: Only redstone signal strength in Minecraft (falling one per block until a repeater restores it) and supply-range falloff in strategy games; I know no character tree that weakens nodes by path length or pays for closing a loop.

Potency thinning with distance from the source and restored where two lines join: vampire generations in Vampire: The Masquerade, the Bene Gesserit crossing of bloodlines in Dune; redstone signal fading block by block until a repeater restores it in Minecraft; travel nodes in Path of Exile.

name: Ebb and Flood Banks
idea: The tree is drawn as a river with two banks. Nodes on the flood bank work only during flood tolls and nodes on the ebb bank only during ebb tolls, each at 180% strength; nodes in the channel between always work at 100%. A character built on one bank is formidable for 75 seconds and plain for the next 75. A character built on both is two builds that take turns.
source: A tidal shore is two places, the one the flood covers and the one the ebb bares, taking turns twice a day.
nearest: Stance builds and day-and-night builds. Here the switch is not chosen in play; it is the run's clock, and the planning is how much of each tide to be strong in.

notes.where: Night Stalker in Dota 2, formidable for one half of the clock and plain for the other, and the Sun Stone, Moon Stone and Celestial Stone of Terraria (works by day, by night, always); Solar and Lunar Eclipse for the Druid in World of Warcraft.
notes.mutation: Let the ground, not the clock, decide which bank is live: flood-bank nodes work while the character stands in water and ebb-bank nodes while on dry ground. The tide then sets how much of each ground a district offers at that toll, and the player chooses a build by where the thumb goes.

notes.where: Two natures that take turns on the world's clock: Ladyhawke, Castor and Pollux, the Oak King and the Holly King, the Summer and Winter courts; Night Stalker in Dota 2, strong by night and plain by day. Laying it out as two banks of one tree is its own.

name: Dips
idea: An item is a core with up to 7 dips of wax laid one over another, each holding one property. Only the outer 3 dips work; the rest lie dormant beneath. To change an item the player either adds a dip at a district's vat (a new random property of that district's kind goes on top, pushing the fourth one under), or pares the outer dip off, destroying it and bringing a dormant one back up. Nothing in the middle can be touched.
source: A dipped candle is built in coats, one over another, and can only be pared from the outside in.
nearest: Adding and removing random affixes with crafting orbs in Path of Exile. Here the properties are a strict stack, last on first off, and an item carries a buried history that can be dug back to.

notes.where: Adding and removing random affixes in Path of Exile, and the sealed affix of Last Epoch, set aside under the working ones. A strict last-on, first-off stack with a buried history is its own.

The palimpsest and the pentimento, where older layers lie buried under the new and can be recovered; the Defect's orb slots in Slay the Spire, where a new orb pushes out an old one; affix crafting in Path of Exile. A strict last-on-first-off stack of properties is new to me.

name: High-water Grade
idea: No item has a rarity. Every item has a mark: the highest toll it has been worn through and then banked at a gate. All of its properties are scaled by the mark, 6% per toll. A new find has mark 0 whatever it is. The mark rises only by wearing the item deeper into a vigil than it has been before and getting out; it is cut into the item and shown as lines. Dying loses the item and its mark together.
source: A flood's high-water mark is cut into the wall and stands until a higher flood.
nearest: Legendary gems levelled in Diablo III rifts. Here the mark is the item's only grade, it replaces rarity outright, and it is earned by carrying the thing itself into danger and out again.

notes.where: The Item World of Disgaea (an item grows by how deep you dive and get out), legendary gems ranked by Greater Rift depth in Diablo III, weapons that grow and can be lost in Dark Cloud. A record of depth as the only grade is its own.

Notches cut on a gun and kill marks on a fuselage; the named sword whose worth is its history; Strange weapons in Team Fortress 2 and legendary gems ranked by rift depth in Diablo III. A depth record replacing rarity outright is the fresh part.

name: Tablet Lines
idea: Each item has 3 lines written in wax. Warming an item between vigils wipes one chosen line blank. A blank line is written by the next vigil: the game counts twelve deeds (kills in deep water, kills on dry ground, metres hauled by current, seconds stood still, tolls outlasted, and so on) and the deed the character led in, against its own average, writes the line as that deed's property, stronger the wider the lead.
source: A wax tablet is written with a stylus and wiped clean by warmth to be written again.
nearest: Rerolling one affix at the enchanter in Diablo III. Here nothing is rolled: the player writes the line by how they play the next run.

notes.where: Weapon affinities in Vagrant Story, shaped by what the weapon is used on, challenge perks in Fallout: New Vegas, growth by use in The Elder Scrolls. A line written by the deed you led in against your own average is its own.

The weapon written by its use: Vagrant Story, where a blade's affinities drift toward whatever it is used against; Fable III's weapons, which morph and unlock bonuses according to the wielder's deeds; skills raised by use in The Elder Scrolls; Gryffindor's sword taking in what strengthens it.
notes.mutation: Take an impression, not a tally: once per vigil the player presses the tablet, and the blank line is written from exactly what is true in that second (depth, current, crowd at the shoulder, life missing), so the line is a staged moment and not a season of habits.

name: Sealed Lots
idea: Finds come up sealed with wax. A sealed item can be worn as it is: the seal's device names its kind and it gives a fixed, modest, known effect. Breaking the seal shows what is really inside: three properties that may be better or worse, and it can never be sealed again. Sealed items bank at double worth toward the legacy currency, broken ones at single. A keeper's blow breaks one worn seal at random.
source: A wax seal proves a thing unopened and cannot be remade once it is broken.
nearest: Unidentified items in Diablo. Here the unopened state is a usable, bankable item in its own right, so identifying is a gamble the player may decline.

notes.where: Unidentified items in Diablo and NetHack (wearable unread in NetHack), unidentified sets paying double in the chaos recipe of Path of Exile, sealed crates worth more unopened. A sealed state that is a usable item, and a gamble the player may decline, is its own.

Mint in the box: Pandora's jar and Urashima's casket, Stinky Pete in Toy Story 2, sealed weapon cases in Counter-Strike and unopened booster packs, worth more shut; unidentified items in Diablo, and Path of Exile's vendor recipes paying double for unidentified sets.
notes.mutation: Let the seal ripen what it hides: every toll the item is worn unbroken improves the three properties inside, and a keeper's blow that breaks it early spoils them, so the question is how long to lay it down, not whether to scratch a ticket.

name: The Bore
idea: At a spring toll the water draws back for 4 seconds with a rising roar, then one wave crosses the whole district along its main channel at 9 metres per second. Everything it meets, enemies, pickups and the player, is carried 15 metres and harmed, except in the lee of a pillar or wall: a strip 2 metres wide and 4 long behind each. Three whelps follow at 1-second gaps, each carrying 3 metres. For 12 seconds after, the current runs upstream.
source: A tidal bore arrives as a single wave followed by a train of smaller ones called whelps, and the river runs backwards behind it.
nearest: Hazard waves that cross the screen. This one moves the loot and the horde as well as the player, and the map's pillars become the only places to stand.

notes.where: Tidal Wave from Leviathan in Final Fantasy XIV and raid blasts dodged behind a pillar in World of Warcraft; screen-crossing hazard waves. A wave that carries loot and horde too, with whelps and a reversed stream after, is its own.

The sea drawing back before the wave in tsunami stories (Hearn's A Living God, The Impossible); sheltering behind a pillar from the dragon's breath, and line-of-sight mechanics in raid bosses; screen-crossing hazard waves. Moving horde and loot along with the player is the fresh part.

name: Sale by Candle
idea: A niche lights with an inch of candle, a pin stuck in it, and a find on show. The lot goes to the player if they are standing in the niche's 2-metre light, with no enemy in it, at the instant the pin drops. The pin drops between 10 and 16 seconds after lighting; the wax round it visibly softens in the last 3. Each second spent in the light stakes 4% of carried coin, lost if the lot is not won.
source: At an auction by candle the lot went to whoever had bid last when a pin stuck in the candle fell.
nearest: Stand-in-the-circle shrines. Here presence costs money by the second, the deciding instant is uncertain, and one enemy in the light at that instant voids the sale.

notes.where: Stand-in-the-circle objectives (the teleporter in Risk of Rain 2, events in Diablo IV), Tail Tag in Fall Guys (hold it at the final instant), musical chairs. Presence staked by the second on an uncertain instant is its own.

Musical chairs, and the last-second bid at any auction scene; stand-in-the-circle shrines in action role-playing and horde games. The real auction by candle is rarely told, and its uncertain instant is the fresh part.

name: Votive of the Fallen
idea: In a district where one of the player's earlier characters died, an unlit votive stands at the spot. If the living character lights it (1 second of touch) it must burn through one full toll: every enemy passing within 0.5 metres takes 3 seconds off it, and it can be relit through its smoke within 2 seconds of going out. If it lasts, it returns one item the dead character was wearing, with its marks.
source: A votive candle is lit for the dead and must be left to burn itself out.
nearest: Corpse runs to recover lost goods in Dark Souls. Here recovery is a 75-second defence of a small flame by a different character, not a touch.

notes.where: ZombiU and bones files in NetHack, where a later character recovers the dead one's goods at the death spot; corpse runs in Dark Souls; stand-and-defend recoveries like the Black Box in Deep Rock Galactic. A 75-second defence of a flame is its own.

The vigil over the dead: Khoma keeping three nights in the church in Gogol's Viy while the candles gutter; corpse runs in Dark Souls and ZombiU, and the Shrieker returning lost trinkets in Darkest Dungeon; hold-the-point events. Winning the goods back by guarding a flame with a different character is its own.

name: A Hulk Refloats
idea: On a flood toll a grounded hull 9 metres by 3 lifts and drifts across the district on the current for 20 seconds, pushing everything before it. Its deck is dry ground with two finds on it, reached from either side amidships, and nothing that swims can climb it. When the tide slackens it grounds wherever it is and stays there as a wall until the next flood lifts it.
source: A stranded vessel floats off on the next high tide and goes wherever the stream takes it.
nearest: Moving platforms. This one is also a plough through the horde, a refuge, and afterwards a lasting change to the map.

notes.where: The destroyer that breaks loose and grounds on the island in Paracel Storm (Battlefield 4), moving-platform refuges, stage hazards that plough through fighters. A hull that regrounds as a new wall each flood is its own.

Noah's ark lifting on the flood and grounding where the water leaves it; the Demeter driving ashore at Whitby in Dracula, and ghost ships generally; moving platforms and refuges in games. A drifting wall that stays where it grounds is the fresh part.

name: Squall
idea: Rain falls for 25 seconds. Fresh water lies over the salt: every body in water, the player included, is in Dead Water, moving on one shared 3-second beat of held and surge. The rain rinses all brine from everyone and wets all dry ground ankle deep, so nothing counts as dry until 10 seconds after it stops. Flames outside a lantern go out and may be relit.
source: A layer of fresh water over salt makes dead water, which holds a vessel as if by a hand.
nearest: Weather events that slow everyone. This puts player and horde on the same pulse, so the skill is acting in the surge.

notes.where: The Rain spell of Divinity: Original Sin (douses fire, wets everyone, primes other statuses), storms in Breath of the Wild, rain in Pokemon. Player and horde put on one pulse is its own, by way of water-05.

The storm that douses every torch and the rain that washes clean, as stock as weather gets; one shared tempo for player and horde in Crypt of the NecroDancer and in Red Light, Green Light. Putting both sides on the dead-water beat is its own.

name: Strata
idea: The permanent tree's currency is not a number but layers. Every vigil, fatal or not, lays one layer of silt on the shared tree, as thick as the tolls that character outlasted. A node of cost N can only be planted in a single layer at least N thick, and each layer holds one node. Long vigils make deep layers for great nodes; a death at the second toll still lays a thin layer that holds a small one. The tree's side view is the record of every run.
source: Every tide leaves a film of silt, and a flood plain is built layer by layer, each one the record of one flood.
nearest: Meta-currencies banked after each run in roguelites. Here runs are not summed into one purse: each run is its own slot of its own size.

notes.where: Rogue Legacy: Charon takes whatever gold is left at the gate, so runs are never summed and an upgrade must be afforded by one run alone. Cells handed in or lost between levels in Dead Cells follow the same rule.
notes.mutation: Let layers join or part by how the vigil ended: a vigil banked alive may be merged with the bed beneath it into one thicker bed, while a fatal one sets as a hard crust that no node can root through. A node needs one unbroken bed as deep as its cost, so the unit of saving is the run of survivals between two deaths.

notes.where: Rogue Legacy, where Charon takes all unspent gold at the castle door, so each run's haul must pay for an upgrade by itself; the nine cities of Troy and the flood-plain record for the image of one layer per event.
notes.mutation: Give each layer a kind as well as a thickness, taken from how the vigil ended (in deep water, on dry stone, at a keeper, at a gate), and let nodes root only in the kind they need, so what a run can buy depends on where and how it ended and not only on how long it lasted.

name: The Mask Wall
idea: When a character dies a wax death mask is cast, holding one line: the stat in which that character stood furthest above the average of all the player's characters. The mask becomes a new node on the permanent tree, placed on the branch of the district where it died. Any later character whose path passes through it gains that line at half strength. The permanent tree is therefore grown from the dead themselves, one node per death.
source: Wax death masks and funeral effigies were made of the dead and kept in the church.
nearest: The graveyard in Darkest Dungeon and the lineage in Rogue Legacy, which only record the dead. Here each death adds a working node, shaped by how that character differed from the rest.

notes.where: Legacies in Sunless Sea (the dead captain passes on one distinctive thing), relics of dead heroes in Massive Chalice, the lineage of Rogue Legacy. A working tree node shaped by how the dead differed from the rest is its own.

The mask of the dead that lends the dead one's strength: the Goron and Zora masks of Majora's Mask, the Roman wax ancestor masks, the Hall of Faces in A Song of Ice and Fire; in games, Sunless Sea's legacy handing the next captain half of one of the dead captain's stats, and Rogue Legacy's heirs.
notes.mutation: Make the mask a mould, not a gift: it adds nothing, but lifts any wearer who falls below half the dead one's mark in that stat up to that floor and drops away once they outgrow it, so the dead shore up what the living lack.

name: Enter on the Tide
idea: Each district's wall keeps the player's high-water mark: the deepest toll any character, living or dead, has reached there. Legacy currency is paid mostly for raising a mark: a toll beyond the old mark pays ten times a toll below it. The permanent tree sells tide tables: with one, a new character may enter that district at any toll up to half its mark, with the levels and picks it would have earned, chosen in a row.
source: Flood heights were cut into walls as records, and a tide table lets a pilot arrive at the hour he wants.
nearest: Starting at a later wave in arcade games. Here the right is earned by the dead characters' record, and the skipped upgrades are still chosen by the player.

notes.where: Shortcuts in Spelunky and Greater Rift level select in Diablo III (start deeper, up to your record), and heat bounties in Hades, which pay only for a new best. Skipped levels still chosen in a row is its own.

Flood marks and records made to be broken; level select and continue-from-wave in arcade games (Tempest), rifts opened up to the highest cleared in Diablo III, heat records in Hades. Choosing the skipped picks in a row is the fresh part.

name: The Toll is the Turn
idea: Each toll is the turn of the tide. Odd tolls begin a flood, even tolls an ebb, and the water moves by the rule of twelfths through the 75 seconds: slow, faster, fastest, fastest, slower, slow. Three seconds either side of each toll the water is slack and nothing drifts. Every fourth toll is a spring tide with double the range; the eighth, the keeper's, is the highest water of the vigil.
source: A tide moves by the rule of twelfths, stands slack at each turn, and runs highest at springs.
nearest: Wave timers in horde games. Here the timer is also a physical thing the player stands in, with a readable curve inside every interval.

notes.where: Salmon Run in Splatoon, where each wave has its own tide level, tide levels in Donkey Kong Country and New Super Mario Bros., seasons in Don't Starve. A tide that moves through each interval on a readable curve, with slack and springs, is its own.

The plot run by the tide table (The Riddle of the Sands, the causeway of The Woman in Black); Salmon Run in Splatoon, a horde mode whose waves come at high or low tide; wave timers generally. A readable twelfths curve inside every interval is its own.

name: Sea-locks
idea: A gate is a lock, held shut by the water against it. It can open only when the level is the same on both sides, which is at slack water: for 6 seconds around a toll, and only at the one gate on the side the tide is leaving. So the question is put once per toll, at a known place, at the moment danger rises: stand in the lock as the bell sounds and bank, or let it close and owe another 75 seconds.
source: A lock's mitre gates are pressed shut by the higher water and cannot be moved until the levels are equal.
nearest: Timed extraction points in extraction shooters. Here the window is welded to the danger step, so leaving and escalating are the same instant.

notes.where: Loop Hero: the campfire tile is the one place to retreat with everything, reached once per loop at the moment the loop counter and the danger step up. Timed exits in Escape from Tarkov and the portals of Dark and Darker are the window alone.
notes.mutation: Give the lock a capacity set by the tide in place of a yes or no: each slack it banks finds up to that toll's range, two at a neap and six at a spring, and the character goes through only with the last of them. A hoard has to be sent out over several tolls or saved for a spring, and what to send first is the question.

notes.where: The door that opens only at the appointed moment and place (Durin's Day in The Hobbit, causeways passable at low water); in games, Exfil in Call of Duty Zombies, offered every few rounds at a fixed site as the rounds step up, and the camp tile in Loop Hero, where each lap asks whether to bank or go round again harder.
notes.mutation: Hold to the physical rule and let the player use it: any gate opens the moment the water stands level on both sides, so the toll gives one opening per tide, but a character who can level water elsewhere (a sluice, a pan, a grounded hulk) can make a way out off the clock.

name: The Banded Candle
idea: Each in-run upgrade is written on one band of the character's candle, newest at the foot. The candle burns one band per toll from the top, and an upgrade taken at toll N burns out at toll N plus 8. So for the first eight tolls power only grows; after the keeper, the oldest upgrades start to go while danger keeps rising. Every fifth level offers a Dip: one chosen band is re-coated for eight more tolls.
source: A candle marked in bands burns them away in order, and a dipped candle can always be given another coat.
nearest: Boons that last a set number of rooms in Hades. Here every upgrade expires on the same clock, in the order taken, which gives an endless run its shape.

notes.where: Chaos boons and curses in Hades that last a set number of chambers, the oldest item falling off the inventory in Loop Hero, set rotation in Hearthstone. Every upgrade expiring on one clock in the order taken is its own.

Magic that runs out at the bell (Cinderella) and gains that fade in turn (Flowers for Algernon); Perishable jokers in Balatro and food that spoils in Don't Starve; boons that last a set number of rooms in Hades. Every upgrade on one clock, in the order taken, is the fresh part.

name: Lagan for the Next
idea: A character may sink any carried find under a buoy where it stands (2 seconds, still). A buoyed find is no longer carried: it weighs nothing and cannot be lost. It also cannot be banked. It stays in that district, on that spot, through every later vigil, showing only at ebb, until any of the player's characters hauls it up (2 seconds) and carries it to a gate. A dying character's last act can be to buoy its best item for its successor.
source: Lagan is goods sunk on purpose with a buoy, and the law leaves it the property of whoever sank it.
nearest: Shared stashes, and bloodstains in Dark Souls. This cache is made on purpose before death, lies in the hostile map itself, and must be raised under tide and horde by another character.

notes.where: Buried stashes in DayZ and Rust: goods hidden on purpose in the hostile map, kept through your death and dug up by your next character. Storehouses in Shiren the Wanderer and buried treasure in Sea of Thieves are the same cache.
notes.mutation: Let the water work on what is sunk: for each vigil a find lies under its buoy it takes one crust, a property of that district's kind laid over its own, and after three it can be hauled only at a spring ebb. The buoy is a slow workshop in hostile ground as well as a bequest, and leaving a thing down longer is a real choice.

notes.where: Buried treasure left for the heir: Treasure Island, Faria's hoard passed to Dantes in The Count of Monte Cristo; in games, NetHack's bones files, the stash a new survivor reclaims in Project Zomboid, buried stashes in DayZ, and the bloodstain of Dark Souls.
notes.mutation: Let the water work on what is left in its keeping: each vigil a find lies sunk rewrites one of its properties after that district's kind (a sea-change), so lagan is a slow craft and the question is when to raise it, not only whether it is safe.

name: Poured from the Run
idea: The one-sitting run builds a wax model. If it clears all five districts alive, the player may pour it: the character becomes a standing character. Its in-run upgrades are melted out and lost; its levels, tree path and worn items take their exact place as the standing character's start. A run that dies leaves only its legacy currency. One pour per completed run, and a poured character can never re-enter the one-sitting mode.
source: In lost-wax casting the wax model is destroyed and a lasting metal copy stands where it was.
nearest: Promoting a run's character into a persistent roster. Here the temporary layer is exactly what is lost, and only a completed run can be cast.

notes.where: Legacy in Wildermyth (heroes of a finished campaign join a lasting roster, keeping some things and losing others) and league characters passing one way into Standard in Path of Exile and Last Epoch.
notes.mutation: Make the casting reproduce the run's marks, as lost-wax does: each district cleared without a heavy blow casts clean, fixing one node of the path at full strength for good, and each district survived at under a fifth of life casts a flaw, a named weakness to that district's water. The player pours how they played and may refuse a flawed casting.

notes.where: The run that is made real when it succeeds: Pinocchio, and the apprentice's masterpiece; in games, Wildermyth promoting a finished campaign's heroes into the legacy roster, and league characters migrating to Standard in Path of Exile and Diablo, one way only.
notes.mutation: Cast the other layer: what the pour keeps is the run's set of in-run upgrades, frozen as the standing character's fixed innate kit, while levels and worn items are what melt away, so each standing character is the lasting shape of one whole run.

name: Ballast of Finds
idea: Every unbanked find carried is ballast. Each one takes 1.5% off walking speed and 4% off the distance any current, bore or blow moves the character. A button jettisons the heaviest: it is thrown 5 metres ahead as a strike worth its value, floats, and drifts with the current as flotsam that can be caught again downstream. A heavily laden character is slow, immovable and one button from being light.
source: Ships carried ballast stones to stand steady, and threw cargo overboard to float free in danger.
nearest: Carry weight in extraction games. Here weight is also the character's steadiness against the water, and shedding it is an attack that leaves the goods adrift, not gone.

notes.where: Death Stranding, where cargo weight meets river currents and a dropped load drifts downstream to be chased, the idol of Spelunky as treasure and thrown weapon, carry weight in extraction games. Weight as steadiness against the water is its own.

The thief dragged down by his own loot (The Treasure of the Sierra Madre, the Cave of Wonders); cargo and ballast thrown out to stay up, as in the balloon that opens Verne's The Mysterious Island; Gil Toss in Final Fantasy, money thrown for harm equal to its worth; encumbrance. Weight as steadiness against the water is the fresh part.

name: Tallow or Beeswax
idea: Every in-run upgrade can be taken in tallow, free, or in beeswax, for 15% of the coin the character carries. A tallow upgrade smokes: each one held takes 25 cm off the character's light. A beeswax upgrade does not. With light under 2 metres, pickups and gate lamps beyond it are not drawn. A character who never pays ends the vigil strong and nearly blind; one who always pays stays bright and banks little.
source: Tallow candles were cheap, smoky and stinking, while beeswax burned clean and cost many times more.
nearest: Boons that come with a curse, as from Chaos in Hades. Here every upgrade has the same two prices, and the cheap price is one shared thing that shrinks: the circle the player can see.

notes.where: The torch in Darkest Dungeon (dimmer is richer and riskier), Light Radius in Diablo, boons with a curse from Chaos in Hades. Every upgrade offered at the same two prices, one of them sight, is its own.

Curse of the Dead Gods, where every offering can be paid for in gold or taken free at the cost of creeping corruption; Darkest Dungeon's torch, light traded against reward; the quick and easy path of the dark side. Tallow against beeswax is true social history, rarely told.
notes.mutation: Tie the smoke to the casting, not the owning: each tallow skill dims the character's light for two seconds every time it fires, so the dark flickers on the build's own rhythm and can be read and played in the gaps, and beeswax buys silence in that rhythm.

name: The Undercroft
idea: A grid of vaulted rooms 10 metres square joined by wooden doors, each room holding water at its own height. Five colours: wet black, tallow yellow, verdigris, chalk, ember. A door swells shut while its sill is under water and stands open while it is dry, so at flood the district is sealed cells and at ebb every door opens at once. When a door opens between unequal rooms the higher drains into the lower in a 3-second rush. Crowds heap against shut doors and pour through at the turn.
source: In a flooded building timber doors swell shut, and water stands at different heights in different rooms until something joins them.
nearest: Arenas whose gates open and close on a timer. Here the tide works every door at once through one physical rule, and each opening also levels the water of two rooms.

notes.where: Compartments in Barotrauma and FTL, where doors hold water or air between rooms and opening one equalises them; the Water Temple in Zelda; room-lock doors in The Binding of Isaac. A tide that works every door by one rule is its own.

Watertight doors and flooding compartments in Titanic and submarine films; the dead pressed against the mall doors in Dawn of the Dead; arenas with gates on a timer. Doors worked by their own swelling, each opening levelling two rooms, is its own.

name: Float-light
idea: Holds 20% of the pool. The character rides like a nail-weighted candle, higher as it burns down: for each quarter of life missing, water counts as one band shallower for them and currents carry them 25% farther. At full life nothing changes. A wounded character is therefore lifted out of the deep and swept along: harder to press, harder to pin down, and harder to steer.
source: A candle weighted with a nail floats upright and rides higher in the water as it burns away.
nearest: Low-life bonuses. Here missing life changes how the water treats the character, a shift in physics with a gain and a loss in it, not a damage bonus.

notes.where: Super Smash Bros., where the more hurt a fighter is the farther it is thrown, and low-life bonuses in Path of Exile. Missing life changing how the water treats the body is its own.

Swimming a witch (the guilty float); the nail-weighted candle that rides higher as it burns; low-life builds in Path of Exile and berserker thresholds. Missing life changing how the water treats the body is the fresh part.
